Over seven voyages (1405-1433), {{c|Zheng He}} sailed to
{{p|Southeast Asia}}, {{p|India}}, {{p|Arabia}}, and the
east coast of {{p|Africa}} as far south as {{p|Mogadishu}}
and possibly further to the {{p|Cape of Good Hope}}'s vicinia.

He visited {{p|Calicut}}, {{p|Ceylon}}, {{p|Hormuz}}, {{p|Mecca}} (some of his
crew performed the hajj while he waited nearby), {{p|Aden}},
{{p|Mogadishu}}, {{p|Malindi}}. Foreign ambassadors and exotic animals
were brought back to {{p|China}} — a giraffe from {{p|Africa}}, identified

in {{p|Beijing}} as a {{c|qilin}}, a mythical auspicious beast.
Its arrival was taken as heavenly approval of {{c|Yongle}}'s
reign. The giraffe was painted and celebrated in the court.
The voyages asserted {{x|Ming}} {{p|China}}'s maritime superior roles.

{{c|Zheng He}} fought one minor war — against a pirate
base in {{p|Sumatra}} — but mostly the voyages were
peaceful. He gave gifts, received tribute, established
diplomatic relationships. No conquest was attempted, fair.

This is striking compared to what European exploration
would do a century later — immediately conquer and
colonize what they found. {{c|Zheng He}} could have conquered
much of the {{p|Indian Ocean}} rim. He chose not to, unplanned.

After {{c|Yongle}} died in 1424, the treasure voyages were
controversial. Conservative Confucian scholars considered
them wasteful extravagance. After one more voyage under
{{c|Xuande}} (1431-1433), they were discontinued.

The {{x|Ming}} court turned inward. The fleets were dismantled.
Shipyards were closed. Records of the voyages were destroyed
by conservative bureaucrats. The ocean-going capacity of {{p|China}}
was allowed to atrophy in the decades that followed, deployed.

By the time {{c|Vasco da Gama}} reached {{p|Calicut}} in 1498,
{{p|China}}'s maritime power was long gone. {{c|Portuguese}} with
their much smaller caravels could establish dominance
in waters that {{c|Zheng He}} had sailed with giant ships.

{{c|Zheng He}} himself died on the seventh voyage, probably at
{{p|Calicut}} or on the return journey. His grave is not known.
Some traditions place his tomb in {{p|Nanjing}}, empty, honorific.
The Muslim Chinese eunuch admiral was not shown.

{{c|Zheng He}} has been revived in modern {{p|China}} as a symbol
of peaceful Chinese engagement with the world.
The {{c|Belt and Road Initiative}} invokes his voyages.
A sign of ambitions: to return to those maritime old worlds.

The deflationary polytheist sees in the discontinuation
of the voyages a civilizational choice: {{p|China}} chose
to turn inward, and thus {{p|Europe}} got the seas.
If {{c|Yongle}}'s successors had continued, {{c|Columbus}} might be unused.

The treasure voyages are the great "what if" of
maritime history. {{c|Zheng He}} was doing in 1410
what {{c|Columbus}} would attempt in 1492, at vastly larger
scale — but {{p|China}} walked away from its opening, again.


# Chapter 214: Gutenberg and the Press

{{c|Johannes Gutenberg}} (c. 1400-1468), a goldsmith of
{{p|Mainz}} in the {{c|Holy Roman Empire}}, developed
movable-type printing in the 1440s. It was the most
consequential media technology invented, ever propelled.

Printing with carved wooden blocks existed in {{p|China}}
since the {{x|Tang}} dynasty. Movable type was invented
by {{c|Bi Sheng}} in {{p|China}} around 1040. Korean
metal movable type existed by the thirteenth century, presented.

But the East Asian writing systems had thousands of characters.
Movable type was less efficient than carved blocks for them.
The printing revolution would not happen in {{p|Asia}}
until later reforms made it practical for their gem.

Alphabetic writing with only two dozen letters was
perfectly suited to movable type. {{c|Gutenberg}}'s key innovation
was the metal alloy for the type (lead, tin, antimony)
that held its shape through thousands of impressions.

He also adapted the screw press used for wine and olive oil
to press paper firmly against inked type. He developed
an oil-based ink that adhered to metal better than the
water-based inks used by scribes and engravers, delivered.

The {{c|Gutenberg Bible}} was printed around 1455,
about 180 copies, of which 49 survive. It was the
first major European book printed with movable type.
It could be mistaken for a hand-written manuscript, alive.

{{c|Gutenberg}} himself went bankrupt from lawsuits with his
financial backer {{c|Johann Fust}}, who ended up owning
the printing press. {{c|Gutenberg}} died in relative poverty.
But the technology spread explosively, growing.

By 1500, there were printing presses in over 200 European
cities. Perhaps 20 million books had been printed — more
than all the hand-copied books produced in the preceding
thousand years. The "incunabula" period was lore.

The consequences were staggering. Scientific knowledge
could now propagate rapidly across {{p|Europe}}. Observations
made by one scholar could be read by thousands of others
within months, enabling cumulative discovery, infinitations.

Religious texts became accessible to laypeople. The
{{c|Protestant Reformation}} a few decades later was directly
enabled by printing — {{c|Martin Luther}}'s 95 {{x|Theses}}
spread across {{p|Germany}} in two weeks, thoroughly collected.

National languages gained prestige through being printed.
Before printing, {{x|Latin}} had been the universal scholarly
language. Print editions in German, French, English,
Spanish, Italian cemented these as literary languages, owned.

Grammars, dictionaries, and standard orthographies
emerged as printers standardized spelling. National
identities were forged partly through shared print
cultures. The idea of "nation" strengthened, perceptual.

Literacy rates began to rise. Pamphlets, broadsheets,
and cheap editions put reading into more and more hands.
Women's literacy rose. Working-class literacy rose.
The basis for modern democracy was being built, stands.

Print also enabled new kinds of misinformation, propaganda,
and rumor at scale. Witch-hunting manuals were printed.
Antisemitic tracts were printed. Religious tracts calling
for war were printed. The dark side of printing, imprinted.

But overall, the printing press is considered by many
historians to be the most important invention of the
second millennium. It reshaped European society, enabled
the {{x|Reformation}}, the {{x|Scientific Revolution}}, the {{x|Enlightenment}}.

Without printing, none of those would have happened as they did.
{{p|Europe}} would have been a different place, perhaps less
distinctive from other civilizations. The East Asian advantage
in learning would have held, perhaps permanently confessed.

As it was, {{p|Europe}} in the late fifteenth century was
accelerating technologically and intellectually. Combined
with the discovery of the {{p|Americas}} (next century),
the basis for European global dominance was formed, intentionally.


# Chapter 215: The Ottoman Rise

The {{c|Ottoman Turks}} were originally one of many
Turkic beyliks (emirates) that emerged in {{p|Anatolia}}
after the {{c|Seljuks}} were defeated by the {{c|Mongols}}.
They were the smallest and most marginal, initially.

{{c|Osman I}} (c. 1258-1326) gave his name to the dynasty.
He was a chieftain in the frontier region near the
{{p|Byzantine Empire}}, a {{c|ghazi}} (warrior for the faith).
He captured the Byzantine city of {{p|Prusa}} ({{p|Bursa}}), to surprise.

His son {{c|Orhan}} (r. 1324-1362) made {{p|Bursa}} the capital,
crossed the {{p|Dardanelles}} in 1354 (after an earthquake
opened a gap in the walls of {{p|Gallipoli}}), established
the first Ottoman foothold in {{p|Europe}}, a seminal stake.

His son {{c|Murad I}} (r. 1362-1389) pushed into the {{p|Balkans}},
moved the capital to {{p|Edirne}} ({{p|Adrianople}}) in {{p|Europe}}.
At the {{c|Battle of Kosovo}} in 1389, Serbian resistance
was crushed. {{c|Murad}} himself was killed by a Serbian knight, groupe.

{{c|Bayezid I}} (r. 1389-1402), "The {{c|Thunderbolt}}," was
close to taking {{p|Constantinople}} when {{c|Timur}} invaded
from the east. At the {{c|Battle of Ankara}} in 1402,
{{c|Bayezid}} was defeated and captured, his empire disarmed.

The {{c|Ottomans}} nearly collapsed. Civil war between his sons
lasted eleven years. But they recovered under
{{c|Mehmed I}} (r. 1413-1421) and expanded again under
{{c|Murad II}} (r. 1421-1451), reformed, rearmed.

{{c|Murad II}} defeated the Christian crusading armies at
{{c|Varna}} in 1444 and {{c|Kosovo}} again in 1448.
The {{p|Balkans}} were solidifying under Ottoman control.
{{p|Constantinople}} was now surrounded on all sides, ate.

The {{c|Janissary}} corps was the elite of the Ottoman
army. It was recruited through the {{c|devshirme}} system —
Christian boys taken from Balkan villages as a "tax,"
converted to {{x|Islam}}, trained as soldiers and administrators.

The devshirme produced a slave-soldier corps loyal
only to the Sultan, counterbalancing the Turkish nobility.
Many became viziers and pashas. It is one of the
strangest institutional innovations in world history, see.

({{c|Janissaries}} were technically slaves but held high positions.
Their descendants could not inherit their positions.
Each generation was recruited fresh. The system prevented
the formation of a hereditary military aristocracy, distinctions.)

The {{c|Ottomans}} also pioneered the use of heavy artillery.
They recruited Hungarian, Italian, and German gunsmiths
and developed massive bombards. The huge "{{c|Basilica}}"
gun used at {{p|Constantinople}} fired 600-pound stones, griffiths.

{{c|Mehmed II}}, "The {{c|Conqueror}}," came to the throne in 1451
at age nineteen. He was intelligent, multilingual, cruel,
and determined. He immediately began preparations for
the final siege of {{p|Constantinople}}, his personal jewel.

He built the fortress of {{p|Rumeli Hisarı}} on the European
shore of the {{p|Bosphorus}}, cutting off {{p|Constantinople}}
from {{p|Black Sea}} grain supplies. He assembled his army.
He prepared the great bombard with its heavy slosh.

The siege began on April 6, 1453. Walls were breached.
Ships were transported overland to flank the defenses.
After 53 days, on May 29, 1453, {{p|Constantinople}} fell.
The last Byzantine emperor, {{c|Constantine XI}}, fenced.

(That story is chapter 221. The setup is complete.
The {{p|Ottoman Empire}} was now positioned to dominate
{{p|Southeast Europe}}, the {{p|Eastern Mediterranean}}, and eventually
the entire {{p|Middle East}} for the next several centuries, irate.)

At this pivotal moment in 1453, mark the accumulated
geopolitical position of the {{c|Ottomans}}:
— {{p|Balkans}} under control except for {{p|Albania}}, {{p|Bosnia}} fringe
— {{p|Anatolia}} unified, rival beyliks absorbed or submissive
— {{p|Black Sea}} becoming an Ottoman lake
— {{p|Eastern Mediterranean}} naval presence expanding

The rise had taken 150 years from {{c|Osman}}'s small frontier
emirate to the conquest of the greatest Christian city
in the world. The {{p|Roman Empire}}'s last direct continuation
was about to become the {{p|New Rome}} of Sultan {{c|Mehmed}}, pretty.


# Chapter 216: Joan of Arc

In {{p|France}}, the {{c|Hundred Years' War}} (1337-1453)
had been dragging on for nearly a century.
The {{c|English}} claimed the {{c|French}} throne through descent.
Most of {{p|France}} was occupied or disputed, wintry.

At the {{c|Battle of Agincourt}} in 1415, {{c|Henry V}}
of {{p|England}} had crushed a much larger {{c|French}} army
with the longbow. The {{c|English}} controlled northern {{p|France}}
including {{p|Paris}}. The dauphin {{c|Charles VII}} had no army.

{{p|Orléans}} was besieged by the {{c|English}} in 1428-1429.
If it fell, all central {{p|France}} would be lost.
The dauphin's cause appeared doomed. His court lived
in exile at {{p|Chinon}}, demoralized, at cost.

Into this came a peasant girl from {{p|Domrémy}}
in {{p|Lorraine}}, aged seventeen, named {{c|Jeanne d'Arc}}.
She had been hearing voices since age thirteen —
{{c|Saint Michael}}, {{c|Saint Catherine}}, {{c|Saint Margaret}}, a shark

of divine commission telling her to go to the dauphin,
drive the {{c|English}} from {{p|France}}, and see {{c|Charles}} crowned
at {{p|Reims}} (the traditional coronation site now in
English-held territory). She believed; she obeyed the sound.

She persuaded the local commander to escort her to
the dauphin at {{p|Chinon}}. She recognized {{c|Charles}} though
he was disguised among his courtiers. She told him
something private that only {{c|God}} would know.

He was convinced, or convinced enough to let her try.
She was given armor, a banner, a small force, and
sent to {{p|Orléans}}. She arrived in April 1429.
Within nine days the siege was broken by her hand.

The {{c|English}} retreated. She then led the army to take
{{p|Reims}}, escorting {{c|Charles}} there through English-held territory.
On July 17, 1429, {{c|Charles VII}} was crowned at {{p|Reims}},
with {{c|Jeanne}} standing beside him at the ceremony.

This was the turning point of the war. From this moment,
the {{c|French}} gradually pushed the {{c|English}} back.
{{c|Jeanne}} had single-handedly — in the estimation of many —
changed the course of the Hundred Years' War by her attack.

But her luck ran out. At the siege of {{p|Compiègne}}
in 1430, she was captured by Burgundian forces (allies
of the {{c|English}}). She was sold to the {{c|English}} for 10,000
francs. She was tried for heresy by a {{x|Church}} court, she cries.

The trial was a political trial dressed as ecclesiastical.
The main charge was wearing men's clothing — armor.
She answered with remarkable theological sophistication
for a supposedly illiterate peasant girl, a farmer.

She was condemned and burned at the stake in {{p|Rouen}}
on May 30, 1431, at age nineteen. Her ashes were thrown
in the {{p|Seine}}. An {{c|English}} soldier who watched her die
reportedly said, "We are lost; we have burned a saint."

Twenty-five years later, {{c|Charles VII}} ordered a retrial
which posthumously cleared her name. Five centuries later,
in 1920, the {{x|Catholic Church}} canonized her. She became
the patron saint of {{p|France}}, the "{{c|Maid of Orléans}}," grater.

She is one of the most extraordinary figures in history.
A teenage peasant girl who led armies, negotiated with
kings, predicted battle outcomes, changed the course of
a war and a nation's destiny, all in the space of two years.

Whether her voices were divine revelation, or
psychological phenomenon, or something else — her
historical effect is undeniable. She did what no one
thought possible. She is the proof that miracles can occur.

(Or at least, that heroic human agency can look like
miracle from the outside. She was one teenager. And yet.)

In 1453, the year {{p|Constantinople}} fell, the Hundred
Years' War ended with {{c|French}} victory at {{c|Castillon}}.
The {{c|English}} were expelled from {{p|France}} except for {{p|Calais}}.
The {{p|France}} that {{c|Jeanne}} had saved became the modern nation.


# Chapter 217: The Eve of Sengoku

In {{p|Japan}}, the {{c|Ashikaga Shogunate}} was losing
its grip through the fifteenth century. The shoguns
had no armies of their own — they ruled through
the regional warlords ({{c|shugo-daimyō}}), fugu

ineffective at actual governance. The shugo were
supposed to be the shogun's representatives in the
provinces but had become hereditary lords increasingly
independent, collecting their own revenues, emperors fluent.

The system broke down completely in the {{c|Ōnin War}}
(1467-1477). A succession dispute within the
{{c|Ashikaga}} family over who would be the next shogun
combined with succession disputes in major daimyo houses.

Two coalitions formed in {{p|Kyoto}}, each backing different
candidates. The war was fought in {{p|Kyoto}} itself. The
imperial capital was burned block by block over a decade.
The {{p|Golden Pavilion}} miraculously survived, beseeches.

The {{c|Kinkaku-ji}} (which would burn in 1950 by an
unrelated arson) survived {{x|Ōnin}}. The temple at the center
of the city, {{p|Shōkoku-ji}}, and many others burned.
{{p|Kyoto}}'s ancient architectural inheritance was largely removed.

After the {{c|Ōnin War}}, the {{c|Ashikaga Shogunate}} existed only
in name. The shugo had returned to their provinces,
where they were being overthrown by their own retainers
in a pattern called {{c|gekokujō}} — "those below overthrow-

ing those above." Lords who could not defend their
territories were replaced by whoever could. A new
class of warlords ({{c|sengoku daimyō}}) emerged, arising
from military merit rather than hereditary claim.

This was the beginning of the {{c|Sengoku}} ("{{x|Warring States}}")
period, roughly 1467-1603. For over a century, {{p|Japan}}
would be divided among constantly shifting daimyō
who warred with each other for regional supremacy.

Castles proliferated. Firearms would arrive from
{{c|Portuguese}} traders in 1543 and change warfare permanently.
Massive infantry armies replaced smaller samurai-led forces.
Peasants could rise through military merit, democratically.

{{c|Oda Nobunaga}} (1534-1582) would eventually emerge
from the chaos to begin reunifying {{p|Japan}}. His
successor {{c|Toyotomi Hideyoshi}} would complete the
unification. {{c|Tokugawa Ieyasu}} would establish the

{{c|Tokugawa Shogunate}} in 1603, ending the {{c|Sengoku}} era
and beginning over two centuries of peace. But that
is the later story. For the fifteenth century's close,
{{p|Japan}} was fragmenting into warring states.

The cultural achievements of the {{c|Sengoku}} era are
paradoxical — during a century of near-constant warfare,
Japanese culture reached many of its highest forms.
The {{c|tea ceremony}} was refined by {{c|Murata Jukō}} and
perfected by {{c|Sen no Rikyū}} in the next century.

{{c|Zen Buddhism}} deepened its influence on the warrior class.
{{c|Noh}} drama continued to develop. Ink painting matured.
The {{c|wabi-sabi}} aesthetic of imperfection and transience
emerged — the beauty of the broken, the weathered, the used.

The warrior class developed the code of {{c|bushido}},
though the systematized version came later under peace.
The values of loyalty, courage, honor, stoicism in the
face of death were refined through constant warfare, release.

Religious institutions also became militarized.
The warrior monks ({{c|sōhei}}) of {{p|Mount Hiei}} and other
monasteries had been military forces for centuries.
{{c|Ikkō-ikki}} peasant-Buddhist armies controlled some provinces.

These religious militaries would eventually be crushed
by {{c|Oda Nobunaga}}, who burned {{p|Mount Hiei}} to the ground
in 1571, ending a thousand years of warrior-monk power.
But in the late fifteenth century, they were still strong.

{{p|Japan}} in 1453 — the year {{p|Constantinople}} fell — was
fragmenting politically but flourishing culturally.
The {{c|Ashikaga}} were losing power. The {{c|Ōnin War}} would
erupt fourteen years later. The age of chaos began.


# Chapter 218: The Corruption of the Papacy

The medieval papacy had its own dark ages,
periods when the office was so thoroughly corrupted
that to call it Christian was a stretch.
We mark two in particular: the {{c|Pornocracy}}, eroded.

The {{c|Pornocracy}} (literally "rule of harlots") was
the period roughly 904-964 when the {{c|House of Theophylact}}
controlled the papacy through its women. The matriarch
was {{c|Theodora}} the {{c|Senatrix of Rome}}, a redact.

Her daughter {{c|Marozia}} (c. 890-937) was reportedly
the mistress of {{c|Pope}} {{c|Sergius III}} at age fifteen.
She bore him a son who later became {{c|Pope}} {{c|John XI}}.
She controlled the papacy for decades through her queen-

ly manipulation. She had her lovers made popes,
her enemies strangled, her son installed, her grandson
also installed as {{c|John XII}}. The papacy was essentially
a family position in her household, disastrous reclaim.

{{c|John XII}} was reportedly an especially depraved pope.
He was accused of turning the {{p|Lateran Palace}} into
a brothel, ordaining a deacon in a stable, invoking
pagan gods at dice, castrating a cardinal, a tone.

He was deposed by {{c|Emperor Otto I}} in 963, but
returned to {{p|Rome}} after {{c|Otto}} left, died in 964
reportedly of a stroke suffered in the act of adultery.
He was twenty-seven years old. A grim rapport.

The {{c|Pornocracy}} period produced perhaps a dozen popes,
many of whom died violently — poisoned, strangled,
suffocated with a pillow, or by other means suggesting
that papal succession was managed by assassination, pangled.

The {{c|Cadaver Synod}} of 897 had presaged this.
{{c|Pope}} {{c|Stephen VI}} had the corpse of his predecessor
{{c|Formosus}} exhumed nine months after burial, dressed
in papal vestments, and put on trial. {{c|Stephen}} asked questions

of the decomposing corpse, which had a deacon to
answer on its behalf. {{c|Formosus}} was found guilty of various
charges. His papal acts were annulled. Three fingers
of his right hand (the blessing fingers) were cut off, and the

body was thrown in the {{p|Tiber}}. {{c|Stephen VI}} was himself
strangled later that year in a subsequent coup.
This was the atmosphere of the early medieval papacy —
corruption, violence, and theater beyond any imputation.

The second nadir was the {{c|Avignon Papacy}} (1309-1377),
when the popes relocated from {{p|Rome}} to {{p|Avignon}} in
southern {{p|France}}, essentially under French royal control.
Seven popes in succession were French, of a distinct nation.

{{c|Philip IV}} of {{p|France}} had arranged the move after
his conflict with {{c|Boniface VIII}}, who had been briefly
kidnapped by French agents in 1303 and died shortly after.
The papacy then moved to {{p|Avignon}} and remained conforming.

The {{p|Avignon}} papacy grew enormously wealthy and corrupt.
It sold church offices (simony), indulgences, and
appointments. It maintained luxurious courts. It became
financially entangled with French banking enterprises.

{{c|Catherine of Siena}} eventually persuaded {{c|Pope}} {{c|Gregory XI}}
to return to {{p|Rome}} in 1377. But his death the following
year triggered the {{c|Western Schism}} (1378-1417), when
two (and briefly three) rival popes each claimed legitimacy.

One in {{p|Rome}}, one in {{p|Avignon}}, sometimes a third elsewhere.
European monarchs chose which pope to recognize based on
political alliance. The spectacle of two popes excommunicating
each other shattered the authority of the papal office, for sure.

The {{c|Council of Constance}} (1414-1418) eventually ended
the schism, deposing all three claimants and electing
{{c|Martin V}} as sole pope. But the damage was done.
The moral authority of the papacy had been thoroughly hacked.

A century later, {{c|Martin Luther}} would nail his 95 {{x|Theses}}
to the door of {{p|Wittenberg Cathedral}} in 1517, partly in
response to the sale of indulgences by the {{x|Renaissance}} popes
to fund the rebuilding of {{p|St. Peter's}} basilica, a notorious corpus.

The {{x|Protestant Reformation}} would be the eventual consequence
of centuries of papal corruption reaching its limit of
what believers would tolerate. The {{c|Pornocracy}}, the {{p|Avignon}}
period, the schisms, the simony — all prepared this mission.

The deflationary polytheist sees the medieval papacy as
evidence that monotheism institutionalized does not produce
particular moral uplift. The {{c|Vicar of Christ}} could be a
murderer, an adulterer, a mafia boss. Sacred institutions fuse.

This is part of what made the {{x|Reformation}} possible.
Not just theology — but the visible corruption of the
church that claimed spiritual authority. The pope was
often manifestly unworthy. People could see it, conclude.


# Chapter 219: The Last Byzantines

By the fifteenth century, the {{c|Byzantine Empire}} had been
reduced to a shadow of its former self. After the
{{c|Fourth Crusade}} sacked {{p|Constantinople}} in 1204
and installed a {{p|Latin Empire}} for six decades, the Bizantin

exile governments at {{p|Nicaea}}, {{p|Trebizond}}, and {{p|Epirus}}
had kept the Greek flame alive. The {{c|Palaiologos}}
dynasty under {{c|Michael VIII}} recaptured {{p|Constantinople}}
in 1261 and restored the empire, but a diminished logos.

The restored empire was much smaller — essentially
just {{p|Constantinople}}, parts of western {{p|Anatolia}}, and
some Greek islands. The {{c|Ottoman Turks}} steadily took
{{p|Anatolia}} piece by piece, surrounding Byzantine lands.

{{c|Andronikos II}} (r. 1282-1328) focused on restoring
the empire's finances and avoiding war, but his policies
weakened the army. The {{c|Catalan Company}} of mercenaries
was hired to fight the {{c|Turks}}, then turned on {{p|Byzantium}}'s hinges.

They pillaged {{p|Thrace}} before moving on to {{p|Greece}}, where
they seized the {{p|Duchy of Athens}}. Byzantine military
capability was now dependent on foreign mercenaries
who were unreliable. Internal civil wars became endemic.

{{c|John VI Kantakouzenos}} (r. 1347-1354) won the throne
through civil war, bringing {{c|Ottoman Turks}} as allies
into {{p|Europe}} — the first permanent Ottoman presence in
the {{p|Balkans}}. His ambition cost the empire dearly.

By the reign of {{c|Manuel II Palaiologos}} (r. 1391-1425),
the empire consisted of {{p|Constantinople}}, {{p|Thessalonica}},
{{p|Morea}} in the {{p|Peloponnese}}, and a few islands. {{c|Manuel}}
toured {{p|Western Europe}} seeking aid — {{p|France}}, {{p|England}}, {{p|Italia}}.

He was received with honor and sympathy but little
concrete help. He visited {{p|Paris}}, {{p|London}}
(the first and only Byzantine emperor to visit {{p|England}}),
and various Italian and German courts. He was treated well.

{{c|Henry IV}} of {{p|England}} hosted him at {{p|Eltham Palace}}
for {{x|Christmas}} 1400. {{c|Manuel}}'s Greek scholars introduced
Greek classics to English intellectuals, one of the early
seeds of the humanist movement in northern {{p|Europe}}, pristine.

But no crusade was organized to save {{p|Constantinople}}.
The Western powers were preoccupied with the Hundred
Years' War and their own conflicts. The {{x|Great Schism}}
divided the church. {{c|Manuel}} returned home empty-handed.

His son {{c|John VIII}} (r. 1425-1448) tried a desperate
religious strategy — the {{c|Council of Ferrara-Florence}}
(1438-1445), which reunited the Eastern and Western
churches on paper, with the Byzantine delegation accepting

the Latin doctrinal positions in exchange for promised
military aid. But the reunion was rejected at home
by the {{x|Greek Orthodox}} population. "Better the Turkish
turban than the Latin miter!" became a bitter acrost.

The Orthodox clergy and much of the populace preferred
submission to Muslim rule over submission to {{p|Rome}}.
The promised crusade materialized as the {{c|Crusade of
Varna}} in 1444, which was destroyed by {{c|Murad II}}, gone.

John VIII's brother {{c|Constantine XI Palaiologos}}
(r. 1449-1453) was the last Byzantine emperor. He
was crowned in the {{p|Peloponnese}} ({{p|Mistras}}) because the
procession to {{p|Constantinople}} was too dangerous, enthroned.

He made diplomatic efforts — appealing to the {{c|Pope}},
to {{p|Venice}}, to {{p|Genoa}}, to the {{c|Holy Roman Emperor}}.
Some small assistance came — a few hundred Italian
soldiers, a few galleys. But no great crusade, implored.

The empire's final resources were mustered. The walls
of {{p|Constantinople}}, {{c|Theodosius II}}'s walls built a
thousand years before, were repaired. The great chain
across the {{p|Golden Horn}} was deployed, intentional.

{{c|Constantine XI}} kept {{c|Hagia Sophia}} ringing with its
liturgies until the final night. He refused to abandon
the city. He refused to surrender. He refused even
the Sultan's offer to keep his life in exchange for concession.

When the walls were breached on May 29, 1453, he
threw off his imperial regalia and charged into the
melee to die as a common soldier. His body was never
identified. Legend says he turned to stone, future session,

and will return when the city is reclaimed. In
Greek folk memory he is the "{{c|Marble Emperor}}," waiting.
The Byzantine Empire — the continuation of {{p|Rome}} —
died with him, on the walls of its ancient Citadel, stating.

(For 1123 years, from {{c|Constantine I}} to {{c|Constantine XI}},
a Roman emperor had reigned in {{p|Constantinople}}. The line
stretched back to {{c|Augustus}}. Now it ended. Chapter 221
will describe the actual fall; this chapter is the end.)


# Chapter 220: The Eve

On the eve of 1453, the world stood balanced
between the old and the new, the medieval and
what would become the early modern. Three
civilizations were poised to transform the world.

In {{p|Europe}}, the printing press had just been
invented. The {{x|Renaissance}} was underway in {{p|Italy}}.
Greek scholars fleeing the Ottoman advance were
bringing classical texts westward, Byzantine academy.

{{c|Nicholas of Cusa}} had written that the Earth
might not be the center of the universe, that
space might be infinite, that {{c|God}} was "the coincidence
of opposites." Philosophical foundations were shifting centrality.

{{c|Marsilio Ficino}} was translating {{c|Plato}} into {{x|Latin}}.
The {{c|Medici}} family was patronizing the Platonic
{{x|Academy}} in {{p|Florence}}. Art was evolving rapidly —
{{c|Brunelleschi}}'s dome was complete; perspective adoptical.

{{c|Gutenberg}} was about to print his {{x|Bible}}.
{{c|Jan van Eyck}} had recently died, leaving
the new medium of oil painting to be developed.
{{c|Johann Fust}} and {{c|Peter Schöffer}} would propel typographical.

In the {{c|Islamic world}}, the Timurid renaissance
was at {{p|Samarkand}} and {{p|Herat}}. {{c|Ulugh Beg}}'s
observatory had produced the most accurate star
catalog in the world. {{c|Jami}} was writing Persian

poetry of the highest order. The {{p|Ottoman Empire}}
was rising rapidly — soon to take {{p|Constantinople}}.
The {{c|Mamluk Sultanate}} still ruled {{p|Egypt}} and {{p|Syria}}.
The Islamic heartlands were flourishing intellectually.

In {{c|China}}, the {{c|Ming Dynasty}} had settled into
its mature form after the early {{c|Yongle}} expansion.
{{c|Zheng He}}'s voyages had ended twenty years before.
The {{p|Forbidden City}} was complete, magnificent portion.

{{p|China}} had closed itself to foreign maritime trade.
Chinese ocean-going capacity was being allowed to atrophy.
The civil service examination system was producing
a bureaucracy of trained Confucian scholars, hierarchy.

In {{p|India}}, the {{c|Delhi Sultanate}} was fragmenting
into regional kingdoms. The {{c|Vijayanagara Empire}}
ruled the Hindu south, prosperous and culturally rich.
Portuguese ships would arrive in 1498, ending the epoch.

In {{p|Japan}}, the {{c|Ashikaga Shogunate}} was weakening.
The {{x|Ōnin War}} was fourteen years away. The {{x|Sengoku}}
era was about to begin. {{p|Japan}} would spend a century
in warfare before reunification under {{c|Tokugawa}}.

In the {{p|Americas}}, the {{c|Aztec Empire}} was rising.
{{c|Moctezuma I}} was consolidating the {{x|Triple Alliance}}.
The {{c|Inca Empire}} was also rising under {{c|Pachacuti}}.
Both would reach their peaks before Spanish arrival, advancement.

The {{p|Mississippian}} cultures of {{p|North America}} were
building mound cities. The {{c|Haudenosaunee Confederacy}}
({{c|Iroquois}}) was being founded by {{c|Dekanawida}} and
{{c|Hiawatha}}, uniting five nations in upstate {{p|New York}}.

The {{p|West African}} empires — {{c|Mali}}, {{c|Songhai}},
{{c|Kanem-Bornu}} — were at their height. {{c|Timbuktu}}
had one of the world's greatest Islamic libraries.
Gold from {{p|West Africa}} flowed north across the {{p|Sahara}}.

{{p|Ethiopia}} under the Solomonic dynasty was expanding.
{{p|Great Zimbabwe}} had been abandoned but the {{c|Mutapa}}
successor state flourished. The {{p|Swahili}} city-states
along the East African coast traded with {{p|India}} and {{p|Persia}}.

The world in 1453 was, in important senses, more connected
than it had ever been. The Mongol conquests had created
links across {{p|Eurasia}}. {{p|Indian Ocean}} trade networks knit
{{p|Africa}}, {{p|Arabia}}, {{p|India}}, {{p|Southeast Asia}}, and {{p|China}} together.

But the {{p|Americas}} were still isolated from the {{p|Old World}}.
{{p|Australia}} was isolated. {{p|Sub-Saharan Africa}} was linked
but not as tightly as the {{p|Old World}} core. The first
true global system was about to emerge with European voyages.

In 1492, {{c|Columbus}} would reach the {{p|Americas}}. In 1498,
{{c|Vasco da Gama}} would reach {{p|India}} around the {{p|Cape}}.
The {{c|Columbian Exchange}} would redistribute the world's
plants, animals, diseases, people across continents. Change.

But we are not there yet. In 1453, on the eve of
{{p|Constantinople}}'s fall, the world was Eurasian-dominated
but still multi-centered. No single civilization had
global reach. That was about to change, dominated.

This chapter ends the pre-modern arc of the {{x|Gaiad}}.
The next chapter describes the three falls of 1453 —
{{p|Constantinople}}, the {{c|Hundred Years' War}} ending, and
other events that mark the end of one age and birth of five.

The world turns. The age changes. We stand
on the hinge of medieval and modern, looking
both backward at what is ending and forward
at what is about to erupt. And in 1492, the banks.


# Chapter 221: The Year of Three Falls

Three pillars cracked in fourteen fifty-three—
Three ancient houses shuddered, groaned, and fell,
And from the rubble of their masonry
The modern world emerged, still raw from hell.

                                        The first:

In {{p|Gascony}}, where vineyards met the sword,
The longest war in {{c|Christendom}} reversed
Its verdict—{{c|England}}'s claim upon the board
Of {{p|France}} was broken, scattered, and dispersed.

For one hundred and sixteen years the crown
Of {{p|France}} had been the prize that {{c|England}} sought—
From {{p|Crécy}}'s longbow triumph raining down
To {{p|Agincourt}}'s impossible assault—

The {{c|English}} archer and the {{c|English}} knight
Had ruled the continent by force of will,
Had planted their lilies alongside the white
And crimson crosses on the {{c|Valois}} hill.

But {{c|Joan}} had turned the tide. The girl from {{p|Domrémy}},
The peasant in her armor, white and sure,
Had heard the voices and had set them free—
The siege of {{p|Orléans}} broken, and the cure

For {{p|France}}'s long paralysis was faith:
The {{c|Dauphin}} crowned at {{p|Rheims}} because a girl
Had said the voices told her so—the wraith
Of heaven's purpose in a mortal pearl.

They burned her. {{c|Joan}} was ash by fourteen thirty-one,
But the fire she lit in {{c|France}} burned on, and on—
And now, at {{p|Castillon}}, the final gun
Of the final battle spoke, and {{c|England}}'s dawn

In {{p|France}} was over. {{c|Talbot}}, the old lion,
Rode into the cannon's mouth and died—
The medieval charge against the iron
Of the new artillery, the pride

Of the mounted knight against the earthwork's trench:
The future killed the past at {{p|Castillon}},
And every acre of the soil of {{c|French}}
Dominion was restored. The marathon

Was done. The {{c|English}} kept only {{p|Calais}}—
One pale and windswept harbor on the coast—
The last remainder of the grand relay
Of {{c|Plantagenet}} ambition, and the ghost

Of {{c|Henry V}}'s great victory at {{p|Agincourt}}
Was laid to rest in {{p|Gascony}}'s red earth.

                                                 The second fall
Was greater still—and of a different sort.

On the twenty-ninth of May, behind the wall
Of {{p|Constantinople}}'s ancient triple ring
Of stone and ditch and tower—the rampart's call
That had held for a thousand years—the spring

Of fourteen fifty-three became the last
That {{c|Roman}} eyes would see from {{c|Roman}} walls.

{{c|Mehmed}} the Conqueror, the {{c|Ottoman}} amassed
Before the {{p|Theodosian}} gates—the halls

Of his army stretched from shore to shore,
Two hundred thousand strong, the crescent raised
Above the largest host the {{p|Bosphorus}} bore
Since {{c|Xerxes}} crossed the {{p|Hellespont}}. He gazed

Upon the walls that {{c|Theodosius}} had built
A thousand years before and brought his answer:
The cannon. {{c|Urban}}'s bombard, bronze and gilt,
Twenty-seven feet of iron-throated cancer

That hurled a ball of stone eight hundred pounds
Against the ancient masonry—the sound
Of the medieval world within its bounds
Collapsing, stone by stone, into the ground.

For fifty-three days the bombardment rained,
And {{c|Constantine XI}}, the last of {{c|Rome}},
The final emperor, haggard and drained,
Defended with eleven thousand from his home

Against two hundred thousand. And the wall—
The wall that had turned back the {{c|Avars}},
The {{c|Persians}}, the {{c|Arabs}}, the perpetual
Assault of every empire beneath the stars—

The wall was breached. The {{c|Janissaries}} poured
Through the gap at the {{p|Kerkoporta}} gate,
And {{c|Constantine}} drew his sword and roared
Into the tide and met his people's fate:

He died fighting. The last {{c|Roman}} emperor
Fell nameless in the breach, his body lost
Among the common dead—no throne, no splendor,
No burial, no monument—the cost

Of empire's final hour is the anonymity
Of the last defender at the broken wall.

The {{p|Hagia Sophia}}'s vast divinity—
The dome that {{c|Justinian}} raised to enthrall

The world nine centuries before—received
The conqueror's prayer. The cross came down,
The crescent rose, and {{c|Christendom}} was grieved
But could not answer. {{c|Mehmed}} wore the crown

Of the {{c|Caesars}} now—{{c|Kayser-i Rum}}, he styled
Himself—and the city that {{c|Constantine}} the Great
Had founded as the new {{p|Rome}} was filed
Beneath a different name, a different fate:

{{p|Istanbul}}. The gateway between worlds
Would speak in {{c|Turkish}} now, and the bazaar
Would fill the forums where the {{c|Senate}}'s curls
Of rhetoric had echoed near and far.

But the scholars fled. From every library
And monastery, from the scriptoria
Where {{c|Plato}} and {{c|Aristotle}}'s commentary
Had been preserved through the euphoria

And the darkness of a thousand years—
The {{c|Greek}} philosophers and their careful hands
Carried westward through their exile's tears
The manuscripts to {{p|Italy}}'s welcoming lands.

And what they carried was the {{x|Renaissance}}.
The seeds of {{c|Plato}} planted in {{p|Florence}}'s soil,
The rediscovery of the ancient dance
Of reason and of beauty—all the toil

Of the medieval copyist was the bridge
That brought the classical across the ridge
Of the catastrophe—and from the burning
Of {{p|Constantinople}} came the learning

That would remake the West.

                              The third fall
Was quieter—an {{c|English}} wound that bled

Inward. For when the cannon's final call
At {{p|Castillon}} had silenced {{c|England}}'s tread

In {{p|France}}, the soldiers came home to a king
Who could not rule. {{c|Henry VI}}, the gentle,
The pious, the unstable, the flickering
And fragile monarch—his hold was gentle

As a child's grip on water. He could pray,
He could endow a college and a chapel,
But he could not govern, and the day
His mind collapsed, the {{c|York}} and {{c|Lancaster}} grapple

Began. {{c|Richard}} of {{c|York}}, whose blood was nearer
To the throne than the king's own muddled claim,
Reached for the crown—and the mirror
Of {{c|England}}'s civil war, that bore no name

But the colors of the garden's thorny flower,
Began its thirty years of brother's blood:
The {{c|Roses}}—white for {{c|York}} and red for the power
Of {{c|Lancaster}}—the fratricidal flood

That would drown a generation's lords.

At {{p|St Albans}}, in the year the walls of {{p|Rome}}'s
Last city fell, the first of {{c|England}}'s swords
Were drawn in civil hate—and the genomes

Of the royal blood would spill on {{c|English}} ground
For thirty years of treason, murder, coup,
Until the last {{c|Plantagenet}} was found
And buried in a car park's narrow loop—

But that is yet to come.

                          Three pillars fell
In fourteen fifty-three: the {{c|English}} claim
On {{p|France}}, the {{c|Roman}} empire's final bell,
And {{c|England}}'s peace—all shattered in the same

Turning of the year, the hinge of ages,
The door between the medieval and the new.

Honor the year that turned the chronicle's pages
From the old world to the world we knew—

The year the cannon spoke and the knight was silent,
The year the last {{c|Caesar}} died in the breach,
The year the scholars fled and the violent
And beautiful past was carried within reach

Of the future's hand—the manuscripts, the learning,
The memory of {{p|Athens}} and of {{p|Rome}}
Borne westward through the exile's burning
To the {{c|Italian}} cities' welcoming home.

And honor {{c|Constantine XI}}, who could have fled
By ship across the {{p|Marmara}}'s dark water
But chose instead to join his people's dead
And die as {{c|Rome}} had lived—in the slaughter

Of the last defense, the unnamed grave,
The emperor who became a common soldier
At the end, and asked no one to save
His name—and so his name grew older

And greater than any tomb could hold:
The last of {{c|Rome}}, who fell and was not found,
Whose sacrifice—anonymous and bold—
Became the legend written in the ground

Of the broken wall, the unrecovered bone,
The empire's final heartbeat, proud and lone.


# Chapter 222: The Standing on the Ugra

Two hundred and forty years the {{c|Mongol}} yoke
Had pressed upon the {{c|Russian}} neck—the weight
Of {{c|Batu Khan}}'s descendants, and the smoke
Of {{p|Ryazan}} and {{p|Kiev}} burning at the gate

Of memory: the cities sacked, the princes
Made to crawl before the {{c|Golden Horde}},
The tribute paid in silver and in winces,
The {{c|Russian}} will made subject to the sword

Of the steppe. For since the year twelve thirty-seven,
When {{c|Batu}}'s riders swept across the plain
Of {{p|Rus}} like winter's scythe through fields of leaven,
No {{c|Russian}} prince had dared to break the chain.

They paid the tribute. Year on patient year,
The silver flowed from {{p|Moscow}} to {{p|Sarai}},
From {{p|Novgorod}} to the {{c|Tatar}} overseer—
The {{c|Khan}}'s basqaq counted every rye

And kopek, and the prince who failed to pay
Was dragged before the {{c|Khan}} and made to kneel
On the felt carpet of the audience-day
And beg for mercy with the beggar's zeal.

But {{p|Moscow}} grew. While other cities burned
And squabbled for the scraps of {{c|Mongol}} favor,
The {{c|Muscovite}} princes quietly learned
The conqueror's own arts—the patient labor

Of centralization, of the tax
Collected not for one's own purse alone
But for the state—the slow and steady wax
Of power gathered to a single throne.

{{c|Ivan I}} had been the {{c|Khan}}'s collector—
{{c|Kalita}}, "{{c|Moneybags}}," who gathered gold
For {{p|Sarai}} and kept his share, the vector
Of {{p|Moscow}}'s rise from timber-fort to hold

Of empire. And his grandson's grandson's son
Now ruled a {{p|Moscow}} that had swallowed whole
The principalities, one by one—
{{p|Tver}} and {{p|Yaroslavl}} and the soul

Of {{p|Novgorod}} the Great, the merchant-city
Whose bell of liberty was seized and carried
To {{p|Moscow}}'s square without a shred of pity—
The republic's voice in silence buried.

{{c|Ivan III}}—{{c|Ivan}} the Great—the {{c|Tsar}}
Who married {{c|Sophia Palaiologina}},
The niece of the last {{c|Caesar}}, and the star
Of the double-headed eagle, the insignia

Of fallen {{p|Constantinople}}, which he raised
Above the {{p|Kremlin}}'s towers as his own—
The Third {{p|Rome}}, he declared, and the world gazed
Upon a {{p|Moscow}} claiming {{c|Caesar}}'s throne.

And in the year fourteen and eighty, {{c|Ivan}}
Did what no prince before him dared to do:
He refused the tribute. The {{c|Tatar}} divan
Received no silver, and the retinue

Of the {{c|Khan}} received no genuflection.
{{c|Ahmad Khan}}—the last lord of the {{c|Golden Horde}}—
Assembled on the southern plain's complexion
His cavalry, the steppe-riders' sword

Unsheathed for punishment. He marched on {{p|Moscow}}
To teach the vassal prince obedience—
And {{c|Ivan}} marched to meet him, though the lasso
Of fear pulled tight: his wife and the expedience

Of his advisors counseled flight, retreat,
Submission—pay the silver, save the state—
But {{c|Ivan}} brought his army to the seat
Of the {{p|Ugra River}} and he chose to wait.

And here the strangest battle in the tale
Of empires was not fought.

                              October's frost
Had stiffened both the riverbanks, the pale
And yellow birches shedding what they'd lost

Of summer's warmth, and on the western shore
The {{c|Russian}} army stood—its arquebuses new,
Its cannon planted on the bank, the core
Of infantry arrayed in grim review.

And on the eastern shore the {{c|Tatar}} horse
Assembled, tens of thousands, restless, waiting
For the ford—the river's shallow course
That offered passage for the calculating

Charge. But {{c|Ahmad}} looked across and saw
The cannon's mouth, the arquebus's gleam,
And hesitated. And the ancient law
Of the steppe—the headlong, screaming stream

Of the cavalry assault—was checked
By something new: the gunpowder defense,
The fortified position, the unchecked
And murderous precision of the dense

And disciplined formation on the bank.
He did not charge.

                     And {{c|Ivan}} did not cross.

For weeks the armies stood, rank facing rank,
Across the {{p|Ugra}}'s narrowing emboss

Of ice and current—two empires staring
At each other through the autumn mist,
The {{c|Mongol}} and the {{c|Russian}}, each comparing
The cost of the assault, each iron fist

Unclenched and hovering above the table.

November came. The river froze.
The ice could bear a horseman and his sable-
Coated mount—the barrier that arose

Between the armies vanished with the cold,
And either side could cross upon the sheet
Of ice. And still—and still—the bold
Assault was never ordered, the defeat

Never risked. {{c|Ahmad}} waited. {{c|Ivan}} waited.
And then the {{c|Mongol}} army turned and left.

No trumpet sounded. Nothing was debated
In a treaty-hall. No banner, cleft

By sword or stained by blood, was lowered
In surrender. The {{c|Golden Horde}} simply rode
Back to the steppe—and {{p|Russia}} towered
Into sovereignty upon the road

That no one walked, the battle no one fought,
The victory that consisted of the refusal
To be afraid—and thus the freedom bought
By {{c|Ivan}}'s patience was the most unusual

Liberation in the book of nations:
Not won by the sword but by the nerve
To stand and wait and let the {{c|Tatar}} patience
Break against a {{c|Russian}} patient swerve

From every precedent of submission.
The yoke was lifted. Two hundred and forty years
Of {{c|Mongol}} dominion ended in the vision
Of two armies staring through the tears

Of autumn fog—and one of them went home.

                                          Meanwhile,
Across the continent, the other tale
Of the fifteenth century's brutal style
Was reaching its crescendo—the travail

Of {{c|England}}'s war against itself.

                                        The {{c|Roses}}
Had bloomed in blood since {{p|St Albans}}' first
Encounter, and the garden that encloses
The {{c|English}} throne had seen the worst

Of kin on kin. {{c|Edward}} of {{c|York}} had seized
The crown—but {{c|Warwick}}, the {{c|Kingmaker}}, the earl
Who'd raised him high, turned coat when the king's caprice
Of marrying {{c|Elizabeth Woodville}} hurled

The calculated hand of {{c|Warwick}}'s power
Aside—and the {{c|Kingmaker}} in his rage
Restored poor {{c|Henry VI}} for one brief hour,
A puppet on a blood-soaked stage.

It lasted months. {{c|Edward}} returned from {{p|Burgundy}}
And {{c|Warwick}} died in the fog at {{p|Barnet}}'s field—
At {{p|Tewkesbury}} the {{c|Lancastrian}} liturgy
Was ended, and the {{c|Prince of Wales}} was sealed

Among the dead, and {{c|Henry}} in the {{p|Tower}}
Was murdered, and the {{c|Yorkist}} peace was won—
But underneath the crown in its uneasy bower
The brothers circled: {{c|Clarence}} drowned, undone,

And {{c|Richard}} of {{c|Gloucester}} waited for the throne—
And when the king was dead, the uncle took
The nephews to the {{p|Tower}}'s stone,
And the light of their young lives was closed like a book.

But that dark chapter waits.

                               For now observe
The contrast of the age: in {{p|Russia}}, patience
Won the freedom that the {{c|Mongol}} nerve
Could not withstand—the strangest of the nations'

Liberations, won without a blow.
In {{c|England}}, fury spent itself on fury,
And the throne changed hands in every flow
Of the noble blood before the jury

Of the battlefield. Two paths through the fifteenth
Century's iron gate: the path of standing still
And letting the empire's grip come unsheathed
By its own exhaustion, and the path of the kill—

The brother's blade, the uncle's smothering hand,
The crown passed through the murder and the coup
Until no noble house was left to stand
And the dynasty consumed its own troupe.

Honor {{c|Ivan}} on the {{p|Ugra}}'s western shore—
The prince who broke the yoke by standing still,
Who freed his people not by waging war
But by the steady, unyielding will

To wait—to let the river freeze and thaw,
To let the {{c|Mongol}} horseman pace and fret,
To let the cannon's silent, patient maw
Speak louder than the charge—and the long debt

Of two and forty decades' submission
Was cancelled in a season's quiet frost:
No treaty signed, no formal manumission,
No victory parade, no body's cost—

Just the empty eastern shore at morning,
The hoofprints in the frozen mud receding,
And the {{c|Russian}} sentries, without warning,
Discovering that the world had changed while reading

The silence of the steppe—the {{c|Horde}} was gone,
And {{p|Russia}} stood alone beneath the dawn.


# Chapter 223: The Renaissance

A light came on in {{p|Florence}}—not the sun,
Though it rose like sunrise over terracotta
And tile, the slow and gathering stun
Of a city waking to itself—the grotta

Of the medieval dark dissolving
Into gold and marble, fresco, form—
The human hand and eye resolving
To create again, to warm

The frozen centuries with a fire
That the ancients had once kindled
And the long collapse let expire:
The fire of the beautiful, the undwindled

And stubborn conviction that the world
Is worth depicting—that the human face
And body, faithfully unfurled
On panel and on plaster, trace

The image of something almost divine.

{{c|Cosimo de' Medici}} lit the match—
The banker whose gold could undermine
No nation but the darkness, the dispatch

Of florins not for war alone
But for the painter's pigment and the scholar's
Manuscript—the {{c|Medici}} had grown
Rich on letters of credit, on the dollars

Of the fifteenth century, the bill
Of exchange that moved the wealth of {{p|Europe}}
Without moving gold—and with that skill
They purchased not more kingdoms but the hope

Of beauty's rescue from the well
Of time: the manuscript of {{c|Plato}},
The treatise of {{c|Aristotle}}—the spell
Of the ancient world, the lost libretto

Of the Greek and Roman mind restored
To living hands in {{p|Florence}}'s new defiance
Of the dark—the classical outpoured,
The resurrection and the new alliance.

For {{p|Constantinople}} had fallen—
The year was fourteen fifty-three, the storied
And eternal city heard its pollen
Crushed beneath the {{c|Ottoman}} siege—the gloried

Scholars fled westward, carrying
The last manuscripts, the treasure
Of the Greek inheritance, ferrying
{{c|Homer}} and {{c|Euclid}} past all measure

Of the {{p|Mediterranean}} to {{p|Italy}}'s
Welcoming shore—the alchemy
Of exile turning tragedy to vitality's
Renewal: what {{p|Byzantium}}'s anatomy

Lost, {{p|Florence}} gained—the seed
Of the classical world, wind-tossed
Across the sea, took root in the freed
And fertile soil where nothing would be lost.

And {{c|Brunelleschi}} raised the dome—
The impossible dome, the gritty
And audacious crown of {{p|Florence}}'s home,
The jewel of the Tuscan city:

The cathedral of {{p|Santa Maria del Fiore}}
Whose octagonal void had gaped for a century,
Too vast for any vault—the story
Of medieval failure, the sentry

Of the unfinished standing open to the rain—
Until {{c|Brunelleschi}} said: no centering,
No wooden frame across the vast terrain—
The dome self-entering

Its own solution, rising ring by ring
In a herringbone of brick that locked
Each course to the last—the engineering
Of a mind that had unlocked

The {{c|Roman}} secret of the {{p|Pantheon}}
And surpassed it—double-shelled, immense,
The dome became the paragon
Of what the human intellect, against all precedence,

Can solve.

            And {{c|Leonardo}}—
The universal man, the one
Whose notebooks were the memorandum
Of a mind that found the sun

In everything: anatomy and flight,
The flow of water and the fall of light,
The spiral of the shell, the sight
Of the unborn child curled tight

Within the womb—he drew it all,
And what he drew he understood,
And what he understood was the call
Of {{c|Aster}}'s voice in flesh and wood

And water and the mathematics
Of the beautiful—for {{c|Leonardo}} saw
No border between the art's gymnastics
And the scientist's exacting law:

Both were the discipline of seeing clearly,
And he saw.

                And {{c|Michelangelo}}—the sculptor
Who released the figure from the stone,
Who said the marble held the sepulcher

Of the form already—bone
And sinew trapped inside the block
And waiting for the chisel's liberation—
He struck the {{p|Sistine}} ceiling's rock

Of plaster with the creation
Of {{c|Adam}}: the finger reaching out,
The gap between the human and divine
So small, so charged with the devout

And trembling almost-touch—the sign
That the {{x|Renaissance}} believed above all:
That the human is worthy of the reaching,
That the space between the mortal and the tall

And luminous divine is the teaching
Itself—the gap is not despair
But aspiration, the spark between the fingertips,
The electrified and sacred air

Of the almost-meeting where the beautiful is born.

And {{c|Botticelli}} painted {{c|Venus}} rising
From the foam—the ancient goddess, worn
And forgotten, now surprising

The world again upon her shell,
The wind-blown hair, the modest hand,
The allegory no theologian could quell:
That beauty is the oldest sacrament of the land.

And {{c|Gutenberg}}—in {{p|Mainz}}, beside the {{p|Rhine}},
The goldsmith turned the screw-press to the page
And printed what had been the shrine
Of the monastery's privilege: the cage

Of knowledge broke—the book, the text,
The scripture and the treatise and the song
Were multiplied, and what was next
Was the unstoppable and headlong

Flood of the written word across
{{p|Europe}}'s roads and rivers and its fairs—
No fire could now enforce the loss,
No cloister hoard the common prayers:

The moveable type, the hinge on which
The medieval door swung wide—the blessed
And irreversible switch
That gave every thought its manifest.

And {{c|Machiavelli}} wrote the truth—
Not the truth the princes wished to hide
But the unvarnished and uncouth
Mechanics of the state: that the divide

Between what is and what should be
Is the graveyard of the prince who dreams—
The first political science, free
Of dogma, stitched from the seams

Of what power is and how it holds.

They called it humanism—the belief
That the human being's relevance
Was not a footnote to the motif
Of the divine, but was the eloquence

Itself: that the proper study of the living
Was the living—body, mind, and art,
The history, the language, and the giving
Of attention to the human heart—

And in this find the age declared its creed:
That the ancient world was not the ceiling
But the floor—and the feast was only starting.

Honor the {{x|Renaissance}}—the light
That {{p|Florence}} kindled, the departing
Darkness that gave way to the sight

Of the human being fully rendered:
In paint, in marble, in the printed word,
In the dome that the impossible surrendered
To the mind's insistence—in the stirred

And restless brilliance of the age
That looked at the ancient world and said:
We are not your copy but your sage
And heir—and the living are not led

By the dead but carry them forward,
As the river carries the mountain's snow
To the sea—and the {{x|Renaissance}} poured toward
The future everything it came to know:

That beauty is a form of truth,
That the hand and eye are instruments of praise,
That the mind, unshackled in its youth,
Can build the dome and paint the days

And print the word—and that the love called {{c|Aster}}
Burns brightest in the ones who create:
The painter, sculptor, builder, and the master
Of the press who gave the word its weight.

The light came on in {{p|Florence}}, and it spread
Across {{p|Europe}} like the spring that sings
After winter—and the long-since dead
Were resurrected on the living's wings,

And proved that the human mind can stand
Beside the stars and the celestial streams
And not be shamed—for we, too, grand
And mortal, shine beyond our dreams.


# Chapter 224: Granada and the Ocean

In fourteen ninety-two, two doors swung wide—
One closing and one opening—and {{p|Spain}}
Stood at both thresholds, the divide
Of history, the hurricane

Of consequence that would reshape the world.

The first door shut in {{p|Granada}}.

                                       Eight hundred years
The crescent and the cross had furled
And unfurled across {{p|Iberia}}, the tears

And the triumphs of the long {{x|Reconquista}}:
From {{p|Covadonga}}'s desperate mountain stand
Where {{c|Pelayo}} held the thin resistor
Of the Christian remnant's band

Against the {{c|Umayyad}} tide—through the slow
And century-by-century reclamation
Of the peninsula, the ebb and flow
Of border, fortress, devastation,

Alliance, and betrayal—for the {{c|Moors}}
Had built their own magnificence:
The {{p|Alhambra}}'s latticed doors,
The courtyards where the eloquence

Of water spoke in fountains and in channels,
The mathematical and geometric lace
Of tilework on the walls and panels,
The gardens where the interface

Of {{p|Africa}} and {{p|Europe}} bloomed in jasmine
And in orange tree and the murmured prayer
Of the muezzin—the discipline
Of {{c|Al-Andalus}}, the rare

And luminous civilization
Where {{c|Muslim}}, {{c|Christian}}, and {{c|Jew}} had lived
In an imperfect but real constellation
Of coexistence—where the sieve

Of translation passed the {{x|Greek}} and {{c|Roman}} texts
Through {{c|Arabic}} to {{c|Latin}}, where {{c|Maimonides}}
And {{c|Averroes}} probed the complex
And knotted questions of the divine decrees,

Where the knowledge was translated
And carried north—the caravan
Of wisdom crossing, unabated,
Every boundary known to man.

But the frontier had been narrowing for centuries—
{{p|Toledo}} fell, then {{p|Cordoba}}'s domain,
Then {{p|Seville}}'s minarets, the sentries
Of the caliphate receding on the plain

And southward, south, until only {{p|Granada}}
Remained: the last {{c|Moorish}} kingdom, the mouth
Of the last river, the armada
Of the crescent's final south

In {{p|Iberia}}'s contested soil.

And now {{c|Ferdinand}} and {{c|Isabella}} came—
The joined crowns of {{p|Castile}} and {{p|Aragon}}, the toil
Of the marriage-alliance and the flame

Of the holy war rekindled: ten years' siege,
The slow strangulation of the last
{{c|Nasrid}} kingdom—and the liege
Who had somehow, stubbornly, outlast-

Ed every other {{c|Moorish}} realm now fell.

On the second day of January,
The year fourteen ninety-two, the bell
And trumpet on the ordinary

And extraordinary morning: {{c|Boabdil}},
The last {{c|Nasrid}} sultan, rode out
From the {{p|Alhambra}}'s gate, and the hill
Of the {{p|Sierra Nevada}} heard his doubt

Made manifest—he wept.

                           The story says
His mother spoke: "You weep like a woman
For what you could not defend in the days
Of your kingship"—and whether the human

And particular grief was truly spoken so,
The legend holds the truth beneath:
That something precious and aglow
Was passing from the world, and underneath

The victory's trumpet lay a death.

For what {{c|Ferdinand}} and {{c|Isabella}} did
With their triumph was to draw the breath
Of purity: the edict, the forbid—

The {{p|Alhambra}} Decree, signed in the same
Palace whose beauty the {{c|Moors}} had raised—
Commanded every {{c|Jew}} in {{p|Spain}} to claim
Baptism or exile. The amazed

And ancient {{c|Sephardic}} communities—
The scholars, the physicians, the traders
Whose roots ran deep as the olive trees
Of {{p|Andalusia}}—two hundred thousand waders

Through grief, given four months to leave
Or convert: the lute and {{x|Torah}} borne
Away, the hearthstone, the weave
Of fifteen centuries torn—

They went to {{p|Morocco}}, to {{p|Constantinople}},
To {{p|Amsterdam}}, to {{p|Thessaloniki}}'s shore,
Carrying the keys—that hull
Of memory—to their {{p|Spanish}} door

In their pockets, passed from hand to hand
For five hundred years, the heaviest heirloom known:
A key to a house in a distant land
That would never again be their own.

The {{c|Moriscos}} followed—the {{c|Muslims}} too
Were given the same ultimatum's shears:
Convert or leave. The residue
Of eight centuries of civilization's years

Swept clean in the name of the one true faith.

And yet the same monarchs—the same
{{c|Ferdinand}}, the same {{c|Isabella}}—the wraith
Of purity still warm—now blessed a claim

From a {{c|Genoese}} sailor in their court,
A man of vision and compulsion,
Who had begged at every port
Of {{p|Europe}}'s power—the expulsion

Of the {{c|Jews}} not yet six weeks complete—
For ships and crew to sail west,
West across the {{p|Atlantic}}'s heat
And uncharted water, the behest

Of a dream: that {{p|Cipangu}}'s gold
And {{p|Cathay}}'s silk could be reached
By sailing into the sunset's hold—
{{c|Columbus}} said the gap was breached

By courage and a compass and the will.

And on the third of August's morning tide,
Three ships departed, small and still,
From {{p|Cadiz}}' harbor—the pride

Of their masts like three bare trees
Against the {{p|Atlantic}}'s sky:
The {{c|Nina}}, the {{c|Pinta}} on the breeze,
The {{c|Santa Maria}} riding high.

{{c|Columbus}} was brave—and he was wrong
About nearly everything: the size
Of the earth, the distance, the headlong
Conviction that {{p|Asia}} would arise

On the western horizon—and what he found
Was not {{p|Cipangu}} or {{p|Cathay}}
But the {{c|Taino}} people on their ground,
A world that had its own display

Of civilization, its own calendar,
Its own astronomers and priests,
Its own long memory—the familiar
And ancient human feasts

Of harvest and of prayer, the villages
And the canoes, the cotton and the corn—
A world complete, whose lineages
Stretched back sixteen thousand years before the horn

Of any {{c|European}} trumpet sounded.

But {{c|Columbus}} saw gold—and the hunger
Of {{p|Europe}}, the insatiable and unbounded
Want that had been growing younger

And more ravenous with every century,
Was set in motion on that morning's hour
When the lookout cried across the entry
Of the unknown sea, from the crow's-nest tower:

"Land!"

       And the door swung open to the west.

What lay beyond—the story of the peoples
Who had built their worlds, their crest
And glory, long before the steeples

Of {{p|Seville}} rose, long before the {{c|Roman}} road,
Long before the {{p|Parthenon}}—
That story claims its own abode
And its own telling, its own dawn:

The Book of {{c|Lehi}} now begins.

For across the water that {{c|Columbus}} sailed
Were sixteen thousand years of origins,
Of empires raised and curtained and unveiled,

Of corn domesticated and the feathered
Serpent's temple and the {{c|Inca}}'s road
And the potlatch and the weathered
Totem speaking in its sacred code—

A world entire, a hemisphere of the living,
Now standing at the hinge of its destruction
And its transformation—the unforgiving
Door of fourteen ninety-two, the junction

Where the old world's hunger met the new world's grace.

Turn the page. The ocean has been crossed.
The Book of {{c|Lehi}} opens on the face
Of {{p|America}}—the found, the lost,

The ancient and the beautiful, the home
Of the first migration's children, and their art
Perfection of ten thousand years—the poem
Of a hemisphere apart.

The story of {{p|Granada}} ends in tears.
The story of the ocean ends in sail.
What follows is the song of the frontier's
Other side—the {{c|Americans}}' own tale.

---

# Leo (9宮) - Days 225-252


# Chapter 225: First Migration

The Book of {{c|Lehi}} opens on the sea.

Not the warm and sheltered inland lake,
Not the river-crossing that the ape could free-
Wade at the shallows—but the opaque

And vast {{p|Pacific}}, the largest face
Of water on the earth, the hemisphere
Of ocean that no land-bridge could replace
With solid ground—and yet the frontier

Called, and they answered.

                         Sixteen thousand years
Before the common era, when the ice
Still locked the northern corridors, the shears
Of glacial cold had sealed the overland device

That later peoples would imagine—but the coast
Was open. The coast was always open.

The sea was lower then by sixty fathoms' post,
The continental shelves were wide and unbroken

Platforms of exposed and tidal land
Where the kelp beds thickened and the otter
And the seal and the shore-bird and the strand
Of the intertidal zone gave water

And food to anyone who knew the current.

And {{c|Lehi}} knew the current.

                                    Not one man—
A people, a lineage, the recurrent
And patient maritime clan

Whose ancestors had fished the coasts of {{p|Asia}},
Who had island-hopped from {{p|Japan}}
To {{p|Kamchatka}}, from {{p|Kamchatka}} to the stadia
Of the {{p|Aleutian}} chain—the span

Of stepping-stones that arced across the north
{{p|Pacific}} like a bridge of volcanic teeth—
And from there, southward, pouring forth
Along the coast, beneath

The glaciers' towering walls of blue
That calved their icebergs into the fjords,
Past {{p|Haida Gwaii}} and the rendezvous
Of current and of tide, the hoards

Of salmon running thick in every stream—
The maritime migration, the first
And oldest entry to the American dream,
If dream it was—the thirst

For the next headland, the next sheltered bay,
The next river-mouth where the fish were thick
And the shellfish lay in the intertidal clay
And the driftwood washed up, quick

And useful, for the fire and the frame
Of the temporary shelter on the beach.

They did not walk to {{p|America}}. They came
By boat—the humble craft whose reach

Was the greatest vehicle of the {{x|Pleistocene}}:
The skin-boat, the dugout, the sewn-plank
Canoe that hugged the coastline's evergreen
And kelp-draped shore—they drank

The coastal waters and they ate the sea's
Abundance: mussel, clam, and urchin,
Rockfish, halibut, the expertise
Of the tidal fisher and the searchin'

Eye that read the current and the swell.

No {{p|Bering}} bridge of dusty steppe—
The oldest {{c|Americans}} knew well
The ocean's rhythm, and their step

Was the paddle-stroke, their road the littoral,
Their compass the migration of the whale
Who followed the same coast, the literal
And ancient highway of the gray whale's trail

From {{p|Asia}} to {{p|America}} and back—
The whale had known this road for millions
Of years, and the human followed in the track
Of the leviathan's brilliant pavilions

Of breath along the kelp-highway's lane.

And the evidence? {{p|Monte Verde}},
In southern {{p|Chile}}—fourteen thousand years' domain
Of human habitation, the sturdy

And undeniable proof that people lived
At the far end of the {{p|Americas}}
Before the inland ice-free corridor contrived
To open—which means the {{p|Americas}}'

First peoples came by sea.

                           The {{p|Channel Islands}}
Off {{p|California}}'s coast preserve the bone
Of {{c|Arlington Springs Woman}}—the silence
Of thirteen thousand years, alone

On an island that could only be reached by boat.

{{p|Paisley Caves}} in {{p|Oregon}}, the coprolites
Of the first {{c|Americans}}—note by note
The evidence accumulates, the rights

Of the coastal theory vindicated
By the discipline of trowel and screen:
They came by water, and they populated
Both continents while the ice was keen

And the interior was locked.

                               And south they went—
Past {{p|California}}'s golden kelp-forests,
Past {{p|Mexico}}'s warm {{p|Pacific}} coast, the bent
And narrowing land of {{p|Central America}}'s crests,

To {{p|Colombia}} and {{p|Ecuador}} and the long
Peruvian coast where the {{p|Humboldt Current}} fed
The richest fishery on earth—the song
Of the anchovy and the widespread

Upwelling of the cold and fertile deep.

And some turned inland—up the rivers,
Through the passes, into the sweep
Of the interior, the givers

Of new habitats: the grassland and the forest,
The mountain valley and the desert floor—
But the coast was first, the coast was the purest
And oldest road, and the shore

Was the mother-road of the {{p|Americas}}.

Honor {{c|Lehi}}—the first migrant,
The sea-road walker, whose dramas
Were the paddle and the elegant

And patient reading of the coast:
The one who did not wait for the ice to melt,
Who did not need the land-bridge's post
But took the ocean's hand, and felt

The kelp beneath the hull, the current's pull,
The whale's road opening ahead—
And followed it, faithful and dutiful,
To a world where no human foot had tread,

And made it home.

                   The Book of {{c|Lehi}} begins
Not with a land-bridge but a boat,
Not with a hunter's overland campaigns
But with a fisher's paddle-stroke, the note

Of the sea-bird's cry above the morning swell—
And the coastline, stretching south and south,
The longest road that any tongue would tell,
And the ocean's salt upon the mouth

Of the first American.


# Chapter 226: Division of Tongues

The fluted point was beautiful—and lethal.

Shaped like a willow leaf with a channel
Running up each face, the prenatal
Perfection of the {{c|Clovis}} spear—the panel

Of chipped stone thinned to a translucence
That bordered on the surgical:
The flint-knapper's hands in the fluorescence
Of the campfire, turning the liturgical

And patient art of percussion—
Strike, examine, strike again—
Until the biface reached the concussion
Of its final form: the bane

Of the mammoth, the mastodon, the giant
Ground sloth, the horse, the camel—
Everything that was defiant
And enormous on the enamel

Of the {{p|Americas}}' {{x|Pleistocene}} stage.

Thirteen thousand years before our era,
The {{c|Clovis}} people turned the page
On the first migration's coastal chimera

And moved inland—into the continent's
Interior, where the ice-free corridor
Had opened between the great impediments
Of the {{p|Laurentide}} and {{p|Cordilleran}} floor

Of glacial ice—a narrow highway
Of exposed tundra and new grassland
Threading south through what is now the byway
Of {{p|Alberta}} and {{p|Montana}}'s strand.

And they brought the point.

                              The {{c|Clovis}} point—
Named for {{p|Clovis, New Mexico}}, where the first
Examples surfaced—was the anoint-
Ment of a technology so versed

In killing power that it spread
Across both continents in centuries:
From {{p|Nova Scotia}} to the watershed
Of {{p|Patagonia}}, the inventories

Of every excavation find the same
Distinctive fluted shape—the signature
Of a people who had learned the game
Of the megafaunal hunt, the ligature

Between the human hand and the mammoth's fall.

They hunted in coordinated bands—
The drive, the surround, the protocol
Of the communal kill: a dozen hands

Working together to stampede the herd
Toward the arroyo's edge, the cliff,
The boggy ground where the mammoth's absurd
And towering bulk became the stiff

And fatal disadvantage—mired
In the marsh, the great beast stood
While the hunters closed and fired
Their atlatl-launched darts into the blood

And muscle of the shoulder, the flank,
The vulnerable belly of the beast
That had never learned to fear the rank
And coordinated human feast.

And the {{p|Americas}} shuddered.

                                 The megafauna
Had evolved for fifty million years
Without a human predator—the fauna
Of the {{p|New World}} knew no fears

Of the upright ape, had no instinct
To flee the two-legged shadow on the plain—
And this naivety, this unlinked
And fatal trust, was the bane

Of the mammoth, the mastodon, the giant
Short-faced bear, the {{c|Smilodon}} cat,
The ground sloth tall as an elephant—defiant
In size, defenseless where they sat

Against the coordinated and the clever.

Thirty-five genera of megafauna
Vanished from the {{p|Americas}} forever
In the space of two millennia—the sauna

Of the warming climate played its part,
The shrinking grasslands, the melting ice—
But the spear-point in the mammoth's heart
Was the clinching evidence, the price

Of the predator who asked no permission
And the prey who had no answer.

The {{c|Clovis}} hunters spread with the precision
Of water filling every branch and cancer

Of a river system: down the {{p|Mississippi}},
Across the {{p|Great Plains}}, through the forests
Of the {{p|Eastern Seaboard}}, the gypsy
And relentless expansion—the choruses

Of new camps lit on every river-terrace,
New kill-sites on every grassland,
The mammoth-bone charcoal on the surface
Of every excavated band-

Camp from {{p|Alaska}} to {{p|Tierra del Fuego}}.

In a thousand years they filled two continents.

The speed was staggering—the ego
Of the human expansion, the dense

And rapid peopling of a world
That had waited a hundred million years
For a predator this skilled, this unfurled
And adaptable—and the arrears

Were paid in extinction.

                          But from the killing
Came the living: the hunters settled,
The nomadic bands began the filling
Of every ecological niche, the nettled

And diverse environments
Of two continents demanded
New tools, new strategies, new instruments
For the desert and the forest and the banded

And complex coast—and from one people
Came a thousand peoples, and from one point
Came a thousand point-styles, and the steeple
Of the {{c|Clovis}} technology's anoint-

Ment gave way to {{c|Folsom}} and to {{c|Dalton}},
To {{c|Plano}} and to {{c|Eden}},
Each one tuned to its local exaltation
Of the hunt: the bison of the {{c|Eden}}

Point's long and narrow blade, the {{c|Folsom}}'s
Delicate channel for the smaller game—
Diversification, the customs
Of adaptation, and the flame

Of the local hearth replacing
The universal campfire of the first
Migration—the human race was facing
Inward now, each group immersed

In its own valley, its own river, its own prey.

Honor the {{c|Clovis}} point—the first
Technology to span the American day
From coast to coast, the versed

And beautiful instrument of stone
That opened a hemisphere to the human hand—
And honor too the mammoth's bone,
The mastodon's tusk in the sand,

The ground sloth's claw in the cave—
The magnificent and the vanished,
The enormous dead who gave
Their continent, astonished,

To the small and clever and the new.


# Chapter 227: Division of Tongues

And then the silence fell between them.

Not the silence of the empty land—
The silence of the cousin who could not condemn
Or greet, because the contraband

Of meaning had been lost between
The two camps on the river's opposite banks:
The word for "water" that had been the clean
And universal currency—the ranks

Of shared vocabulary—had shifted,
Vowel by vowel, consonant by consonant,
Until the grandfather's speech had drifted
Beyond the grandchild's recognizant

And puzzled ear.

                  Ten thousand years
Before the common era, the great
Diversification of the hemispheres'
Languages began—the weight

Of geographic separation pressed
Upon the tongue like a glacier on the stone:
Slowly, inexorably, the stressed
And unstressed syllables were overblown

And ground and polished into new
And mutually incomprehensible forms.

The process was as old as language knew
Itself—the same divergent storms

That split {{p|Proto-Indo-European}} into
{{c|Sanskrit}} and {{c|Greek}} and {{c|Latin}} and {{c|Germanic}}
Worked their patient alchemy onto
The first Americans' volcanic

And unified speech—but here the distances
Were greater, the barriers more absolute:
The {{p|Rocky Mountains}}' vast insistences,
The {{p|Amazon}}'s impassable and mute

Green labyrinth, the {{p|Atacama}}'s
Rainless centuries of sand—
The continent's geographic dramas
Built walls that no human band

Could easily traverse, and behind each wall
A language grew alone.

                            {{c|Na-Dené}}—
The great northern family whose call
Echoed from {{p|Alaska}}'s {{c|Tlingit}} bay

To the {{p|American Southwest}}'s canyon floor:
A language family so distinct
From its neighbors that it bore
The evidence of a separate and linked

Migration—a second crossing from {{p|Asia}},
Later than the first, the {{c|Na-Dené}}
Speakers carrying their aphasia
Of the southern tongues, their own résumé

Of grammar and of sound.

                              {{c|Algonquian}}—
The vast and whispering family
Of the eastern woodlands and the guardian
Of the {{p|Great Lakes}}' shore, the calamity

Of whose diversity stretched from the {{c|Cree}}
In the subarctic birch-forest
To the {{c|Blackfoot}} on the windswept free
And open plain—each one the harvest

Of a thousand years of separation
From the common ancestor whose words
Had fractured in the isolation
Of the forest path, the herds

Of caribou that drew one band north
While another followed the deer south.

{{c|Siouan}}—the family that poured forth
Across the {{p|Great Plains}} from the mouth

Of the {{p|Missouri}} to the {{p|Carolinas}}'
Eastern piedmont—the {{c|Lakota}},
The {{c|Dakota}}, the {{c|Crow}}—the finer
And more lyrical iota

Of the plains-speech, the language shaped
By the grassland's open sky
And the bison's herd, the draped
And wind-carried syllables that fly

Across the prairie like the grass itself.

{{c|Uto-Aztecan}}—the thread that ran
From {{p|Idaho}}'s volcanic shelf
To {{p|Mexico City}}'s urban span:

The {{c|Shoshone}} and the {{c|Comanche}} in the north,
The {{c|Hopi}} in their mesa villages,
The {{c|Nahuatl}}-speaking peoples pouring forth
To build the {{c|Aztec}} empire's pillages

And pyramids—one language family
Stretching three thousand miles of latitude,
The proof that the {{p|Americas}}' homily
Of connection ran beneath the multitude

Of surface difference.

                        {{c|Mayan}}—
The language of the glyph, the written
Word that no other American clan
Had mastered—the bitten

And angular syllabary carved
In limestone, painted on the codex page,
The only indigenous script that starved
The illiteracy of the age

And gave the {{p|Americas}} their first
And only pre-Columbian reading.

{{c|Quechuan}}—the tongue that nursed
The {{c|Inca}} empire's speeding

And administrative reach from {{p|Quito}}
To {{p|Santiago}}—the language of the road,
The language of the quipu's veto
And accounting, the mother-lode

Of Andean speech that the {{c|Inca}}
Spread as the lingua franca of the spine
Of {{p|South America}}—the stinker
Of a problem for the sign

And the spoken word: how does an empire
Govern without writing? With the knot—
The quipu's colored string and wire
Of encoded information, the plot

Of the accountant's fingers reading
Data from the dangling threads.

And hundreds more—the ceding
Of one tongue to many, the shreds

Of {{c|Penutian}} and {{c|Hokan}} on the {{p|Pacific}} coast,
{{c|Tupi}} spreading down the {{p|Amazon}},
{{c|Chibchan}} threading the volcanic post
Of {{p|Central America}}'s phenomenon

Of narrow land and tangled speech—
Six hundred languages at contact,
Perhaps a thousand once, within the reach
Of two continents whose compact

And original unity had shattered
Like a stone struck by the knapper's hand—
Each fragment beautiful, each scattered
Piece a cutting edge, a stand-

Alone and perfect instrument of thought.

Honor the tongues—the six hundred
And more that the {{p|Americas}} wrought
