As a hidden wisdom, a {{x|Gothic Kabbalah}}, a staff
Of the secrets of all the sciences, a cosmos in them:

The {{c|Adulruna}}, his own system, a cross of runes
Arranged as a ladder of the soul up to {{c|God}}, the key,
He believed, to the wisdom of the ancient {{p|North}}, the moons
And the planets and the {{c|Trinity}} in the futhark. He

Corresponded with the {{c|Rosicrucians}}, read the prophets,
Calculated the end of the world, and believed it near.
And he was a {{c|Gothicist}}: the {{c|Goths}} had come from {{p|Sweden}}, the profits
Of the old empire were the {{p|North}}'s, the first and clear

Rulers of {{p|Europe}} had been {{c|Swedes}}, and the {{x|Swedish}} tongue
Was the oldest of tongues, the first, or near enough.
This was the invented antiquity of a kingdom young
In power and hungry for a past. The stuff

Of the {{x|Thirty Years' War}} was fought by a king who believed it:
{{c|Gustavus Adolphus}} going south as the heir of the {{c|Goths}}.
His tutor had taught him. The kingdom received it
As a birthright. That is the invented tradition, the cloths

Of the spine of this book: a people reaching back
To make a past that would justify a present.
And here is the hardest thing on the {{x|Sixth Day of Awe}}: the track
Of the scholar and the inventor is one track. The pleasant

And the false grew from the same root as the true.
He drew the runestones exactly, and he dreamed them into a cosmology.
He recorded the family, and he gave it an ancestry it never knew.
And four hundred years later his kinswoman, in apology

And in love, is writing a scripture that does the same:
Reads the records exactly, and builds a past around the gaps,
And makes a family of all the world, and gives it a name.
Repent, then, the way he could not: say which is which. Perhaps

That is the whole lesson of the rune-keeper. Keep the stones.
Draw them exactly. Dream if you must. But mark the dream
As a dream, in the margin, so that the bones
Of the record stay the bones. He died in 1652. The stream

Of the runes he loved runs on: the revivals, the {{c|Ásatrú}},
The scholars of the futhark, the painted stones in the lawns
Of {{p|Uppland}} churches. The writer of this book reads them too.
She is his kin. She keeps his line. And the line, like the dawns

Of the {{p|North}} in summer, does not quite go dark. The rune-keeper
Kept the stones and the dream, and did not tell them apart.
His heir will. That is the vow: to be the keeper and the reaper
Of both, and to show the seam. Draw the stone. Know the heart.


# Chapter 269: The Sky Opens

In 1608 a spectacle-maker in {{p|Middelburg}}, in {{p|Zeeland}},
{{c|Hans Lipperhey}}, asked the {{c|States}} for a patent on a tube
With two lenses that made far things near. The steeple, and
The weathercock on it, across the town, came close. A cube

Of a toy, sold at fairs within the year. In {{p|Padua}}
A professor of mathematics heard the rumour in 1609,
{{c|Galileo Galilei}}, and without seeing one he knew what the parts would do,
And ground his own lenses, and made one, and made the line

Of sight stronger: three times, then eight, then twenty.
In August he climbed the bell tower of {{p|Saint Mark's}} in {{p|Venice}}
With the senators, old men panting up the stairs, and plenty
Of them saw ships two hours before the naked eye. The premise

Was war and trade, and they doubled his salary.
But that winter he turned it upward. Nobody had done that
In earnest. And the sky that had been a gallery
Of perfect lights, crystalline, unchanging, flat

Against the dark, opened. The {{c|Moon}} had mountains.
He saw their shadows lengthen at the edge of the light,
And measured them, and they were higher than the fountains
Of the {{p|Alps}}: a world, rough, like ours. The night

Of the seventh of January, 1610, he looked at {{c|Jupiter}}
And saw three little stars beside it in a line,
And the next night they had moved, and the night after, the cluster
Had changed again, and a fourth appeared, and the sign

Was clear: they were going around {{c|Jupiter}}. Moons.
Something in the sky that did not go around the {{p|Earth}}.
The {{c|Milky Way}} was not a mist: it was stars, in dunes
And drifts beyond counting, more than had ever had birth

In any catalogue. In March he printed it all in a little book,
*The {{x|Starry Messenger}}*, in {{p|Venice}}, and named the moons
For the {{c|Medici}}, and got a post in {{p|Florence}} for the look.
And later the phases of {{c|Venus}}, like the {{x|Moon}}'s, the tunes

Of a planet going round the {{x|Sun}}, as {{c|Copernicus}} had said.
And spots on the {{x|Sun}} itself: the perfect heaven had stains.
The sky was not another kind of stuff. It was made
Of world. The same world. Rock and fire and the rains

Of light. That is what the glass gave everyone who looked:
Not a new idea. A view. Anyone could climb a tower
And see it. The authority of the book was hooked
And pulled out of the sky. And that was the hour

The trouble came. In 1616 he was warned not to hold
That the {{p|Earth}} moves. In 1632 he wrote a dialogue
In which the defender of the old sky was a fool, and old,
And the {{c|Pope}} thought the fool was the {{c|Pope}}. The fog

Of the trial in 1633: an old man of sixty-nine
In the white shirt of a penitent, on his knees,
Abjuring, cursing and detesting the motion of the {{p|Earth}}, the line
Read out in {{x|Latin}}. The story says he rose, and the breeze

Of the last word was: *and yet it moves*. He did not say it,
Or not there. It was said for him, later, as the printers said
*Here I stand* for {{c|Luther}}. He was sent home to stay. Let it
Be told: under house arrest at {{p|Arcetri}}, blind, he fed

On the work, and wrote his greatest book, on motion,
Smuggled out to {{p|Leiden}} and printed by the {{c|Dutch}},
And died in 1642, the year, as if by a notion
Of the sky's own, that {{c|Newton}} was born. And as much

As this chapter is about a lens, it is about a sorry.
On the {{x|Seventh Day of Awe}}: in 1992, after a commission
Of thirteen years, a {{c|Pope}} stood up, and without hurry,
Said the {{x|Church}} had erred. Three hundred fifty-nine years. The admission

Came. Late, and it came. That is what repentance can look like
For an institution: slow, and true, and in public, and owned.
Look up tonight. The moons of {{c|Jupiter}} are there. The spike
Of a small telescope will show them. What was postponed

Is not undone. What was refused is not refused now.
Open the sky. Look. Let the evidence come in the window.
And when you are the one who was wrong, take the vow
He was never given: say so. Not in a whisper. Say it, and let it go.


# Chapter 270: The King of the Goths

The boy that {{c|Bureus}} taught came to the throne at sixteen, in 1611,
{{c|Gustav Adolf}}, grandson of {{c|Gustav Vasa}}, in a kingdom at war
On three sides, with {{p|Denmark}}, {{p|Russia}}, {{p|Poland}}, the heaven
Of the {{p|North}} a ring of enemies. And his tutor had taught him, before

Anything else, who he was: the heir of the {{c|Goths}}.
The kings of {{p|Sweden}} had long called themselves kings of the {{c|Swedes}},
The {{c|Goths}}, and the {{c|Wends}}. Now the title would wear clothes.
At the coronation festivities in 1617, to the needs

Of a court that wanted a past, the young king rode out
In the costume of {{c|Berik}}, the legendary first {{x|Gothic}} king,
Who, the old chronicles said, had sailed south from {{p|Sweden}}, about
The time of the {{c|Trojans}}, to found the {{x|Gothic}} nations. The ring

Of the tournament became a scripture of the state.
The {{c|Goths}} had sacked {{p|Rome}}. The {{c|Goths}} had ruled {{p|Spain}}.
The {{c|Goths}} were {{c|Swedes}}. So {{p|Sweden}}, small and poor and late,
Was the oldest and the greatest. The invented chain

Of ancestry, from {{c|Bureus}} and the old {{x|Swedish}} chroniclers,
Became the state myth: a {{c|Gothicism}} for an empire to come.
And it came. The king was a genius of war. The rumblers
Of his reforms: light cannon a few men could move, the drum

Of disciplined small brigades, musketeers firing by rank,
Cavalry that charged with the sword. And the conscription rolls,
Every parish in {{p|Sweden}} writing down its young men, the blank
Columns of the register filled with soldiers. The tolls

Of it on the villages: one man in ten taken, and most did not come home.
And the pride. In 1628 the great warship {{c|Vasa}},
Named for his grandfather's house, built higher than a dome,
Gilded, carved with lions and {{x|Roman}} emperors, to be the master

Of the {{p|Baltic}}, sixty-four guns on two decks, sailed out
Into {{p|Stockholm}}'s harbour on her maiden voyage before the crowd,
And a gust of wind heeled her over, and the water came in the gun-ports, and about
A mile from the quay she sank, with her flags flying. The proud

Ship was too tall for her keel. Hold that image on this day.
In 1630 he landed in {{p|Germany}}, in the middle of the war
Between the {{x|Catholic}} emperor and the {{x|Protestant}} princes, the way
Of the {{c|Lion of the North}}, they called him, the saviour, for

The {{x|Protestant}} cause, and paid by {{p|France}}, a {{x|Catholic}} crown,
For it suited {{p|Paris}} too. At {{p|Breitenfeld}}, in 1631,
He broke the emperor's army, and the cities opened, and the town
Of {{p|Munich}} paid him tribute. And the soldiers, under the sun

Of victory, did what armies do: they plundered,
And the peasants of {{p|Germany}} learned a new word,
The *{{x|Swedish}} drink*: filth poured down a man's throat. Hundred
After hundred villages burned by the {{x|Gothic}} heirs. The bird

Of the war had no side. And on the sixteenth of November, 1632,
At {{p|Lützen}}, in a fog like the fog at {{p|Sekigahara}},
The king, short-sighted, rode ahead of his men, and was shot through,
And fell from his horse, and was shot again, and the far

Cavalry did not find his body till the evening, stripped.
The {{c|Swedes}} won the battle. Their king was dead at thirty-seven.
{{p|Sweden}} became a great power for a century, gripped
By its {{x|Gothic}} dream: {{c|Rudbeck}} would prove it was {{c|Atlantis}}, the heaven

Of the ancients, the source of all wisdom. The myth grew wilder
As the empire grew. And in 1709 at {{p|Poltava}} it ended.
On the {{x|Eighth Day of Awe}}, look at the dream that made a builder
Build a ship too tall, and a nation pretend it had descended

From the conquerors of {{p|Rome}}. The farmers at {{p|Bure}} were real.
The {{c|Goths}} of the costume were not. And the conscript boys in the rolls
Were real, and died in {{p|Germany}}, for a king's ideal
Dressed in a legend. Repent of the legends that cost souls.

And keep the true things: the king was brave, and the cause
Of freedom of conscience in {{p|Germany}} was saved in part by his war.
The ship was raised in 1961 and stands in {{p|Stockholm}}, and the flaws
Are on display, for children, the tallest ship, and the shore

She never left. Go and see her. A nation keeps its wreck
On view, and teaches its children: this is what pride
Does to a keel. That is a better myth than {{c|Berik}}. The deck
Is the lesson. Stand on the quay. The water is on every side.


# Chapter 271: Two Fingers

{{p|Moscow}}, the town {{c|Yuri}} the {{c|Long-Armed}} founded on a hill above a river,
Was the head of an empire by 1600, and then it fell apart.
The old line of {{c|Rurik}} died out. The {{x|Time of Troubles}}: a fever
Of pretenders, famine, the {{c|Poles}} in the {{p|Kremlin}}, the heart

Of the country occupied. A butcher of {{p|Nizhny Novgorod}}, {{c|Kuzma Minin}},
And a prince, {{c|Dmitry Pozharsky}}, raised an army of the towns
And took {{p|Moscow}} back in 1612. And in 1613 an assembly of the land, in
The {{p|Kremlin}}, chose a boy of sixteen to wear the crown:

{{c|Michael Romanov}}, of a boyar family, whose great-aunt had been
{{c|Ivan the Terrible}}'s first and best-loved wife. A peasant, {{c|Ivan Susanin}},
It is told, led a {{x|Polish}} troop astray in the forest, unseen
Death in the snow, to save the boy. The {{c|Romanovs}} began

And ruled three hundred and four years. Hold the founding. Then the split.
In 1652 the {{c|Patriarch Nikon}}, a peasant's son of great will,
Set out to correct the {{x|Russian}} church: to make it fit
The {{x|Greek}}. The books had drifted, he said; the copyists' skill

Had failed; the {{c|Russians}} crossed themselves with two fingers,
And the {{c|Greeks}} with three; the {{c|Russians}} sang *{{x|Alleluia}}* twice, and the {{c|Greeks}}
Three times; the {{c|Russians}} walked the procession with the sun. The lingerers
In the old way must change. Three fingers. And the weeks

Became years of fury. The irony is this, on the {{x|Ninth Day of Awe}}:
The two-fingered sign was the older one. The {{c|Greeks}} had changed, not the {{c|Russians}}.
The {{x|Russian}} books kept a {{x|Byzantine}} use the {{c|Greeks}} forgot. The law
Of the reform called itself a return to the source. The discussions

Of the scholars would show it, centuries later: the "correction"
Was a modernization dressed as a restoration. Invented tradition
In reverse: the new disguised as the old, the defection
Disguised as fidelity. And the people who held the old position,

The {{c|Old Believers}}, would not cross themselves with three.
The council of 1666 cursed them. And the year itself, the number
Of the {{c|Beast}}, convinced them: the {{c|Antichrist}} had come, and the tree
Of the {{x|Church}} was cut. The archpriest {{c|Avvakum}}, from his slumber

In an earthen pit in the {{p|Arctic}}, wrote the first great book
In plain {{x|Russian}}, his own life, and was burned at the stake in 1682.
The {{c|Boyarina Morozova}}, a great lady, would not look
At the three-fingered cross; they starved her in a pit. And who

Can count the rest: whole villages, rather than submit,
Shut themselves in wooden churches and set them on fire,
Twenty thousand, perhaps more, over the years. The pit,
The fire, the fingers. For a gesture. Hold it, and the desire

To say they were fools. They were not fools. They knew
What a rite is: the body's memory of the holy.
To change the fingers was to say the fathers' prayer was untrue.
They would not betray their dead. And the state, slowly,

Hunted them to the edges of the empire, to the forests,
To {{p|Siberia}}, where some of them are still. In 1978
Geologists found a family, the {{c|Lykovs}}, whose fathers' choruses
Had fled in the 1930s into the taiga. The late

Twentieth century met them: they had never heard of the war.
They still crossed themselves with two fingers. Repent, on this day,
Of every reform that called the fathers wrong for
Being older than the reformers knew. And pray

As your fathers prayed, if you can, and change what must change,
And never burn anyone over the fingers of a hand.
The {{c|Old Believers}} are still in {{p|Russia}}, and in {{p|Alaska}}, and in the strange
Green valleys of {{p|Oregon}}. Two fingers raised. They stand.


# Chapter 272: The Sabbath of Sabbaths

It began with a window. On the twenty-third of May, 1618,
In the castle of {{p|Prague}}, {{x|Protestant}} lords of {{p|Bohemia}},
Furious that the {{x|Catholic}} king would take back what had been
Promised, their churches, their law, threw two of the king's men, the phobia

Of the moment made flesh, and their secretary, out of a high window.
They fell some twenty metres and lived. The {{c|Catholics}} said: angels caught them.
The {{c|Protestants}} said: they landed in a dung heap. The crescendo
Of thirty years began with a joke about how they fought them

Down. Then the war. At the {{p|White Mountain}} in 1620
The {{c|Bohemians}} were broken, and their leaders beheaded in the square.
Then {{p|Denmark}} came in, and was beaten. Then {{p|Sweden}}, and the plenty
Of {{c|Gustavus}}'s victories, and his death at {{p|Lützen}}, there

In the fog. Then {{p|France}}, {{x|Catholic}} {{p|France}}, against the {{x|Catholic}} emperor,
Because the war was no longer about {{c|God}}, if it had ever been.
It was about who would hold {{p|Europe}}. And the temper
Of the armies was the temper of hunger. Between

The battles, the armies lived on the land: they took
The grain, the cattle, the daughters, they burned what they could not take.
In May 1631 the city of {{p|Magdeburg}} was stormed, and the book
Of its dead was twenty thousand in a day; the wake

Of the fire left a few hundred houses standing. The verb
*To magdeburgize* entered the languages of {{p|Europe}}.
The great general {{c|Wallenstein}}, who had built an army no one could curb,
Was murdered by his own officers at {{p|Cheb}}, the scope

Of his ambition too large for the emperor to bear.
And the people of {{p|Germany}} died: of the sword, of plague, of famine,
Perhaps a fifth of them, perhaps a third, in some regions the share
Was half. Villages vanished from the map. The examen

Of the war's own chroniclers: wolves came back into the towns.
And then they talked. For five years, from 1643, in two cities,
{{p|Münster}} for the {{c|Catholics}}, {{p|Osnabrück}} for the {{c|Protestants}}, the crowns
And the princes and the free cities sent a hundred delegations; the pities

And the vanities: they argued for months over who would walk
Through a door first, who would sit at the head of a table.
And while they talked, the armies went on fighting. The talk
Went on. And at last, in October 1648, they were able

To sign. The {{c|Peace of Westphalia}}. Its terms were not beautiful.
Each prince would choose the faith of his own land, as before,
But now the {{c|Calvinists}} were counted too; and the dutiful
Minority, where it lived, could keep its worship, and more:

Could leave, with its goods, for a land of its own faith, and not be killed.
{{p|Switzerland}} was free. The {{p|Dutch}} were free, after eighty years.
And the idea grew from it, though the treaty never spelled
It out: that a state is sovereign within its borders, and the spheres

Of faith are not a reason for a war between them.
Not tolerance. Exhaustion. Not love. A truce
Between people who had learned that they could not condemn
Each other out of existence. That is the use

Of this day. The {{x|Lifeist}} {{c|Yom Kippur}} falls on a Saturday,
Always: the {{x|Sabbath of Sabbaths}}, the day of rest,
The day of atonement. And the old teaching says: the way
To atone with {{c|God}} for what you did to a person is not addressed

To {{c|God}}. You must go to the person. You must ask.
The day does not atone for that until you have. Hold it here.
{{p|Europe}} learned at {{p|Münster}} the slow, humbling task
Of sitting at one table with the enemy, year after year,

Arguing about the door, and signing anyway.
The bells rang in the cities when the news came. People wept.
Some had never known a year of peace. They had a day.
On the {{x|Sabbath of Sabbaths}}, rest. The promise kept

Is not that we love each other. It is that we stop.
That we lay down the sword and go home and plant the field
That the armies burned. Atone. Go to the one you wronged. Drop
The argument about the door. Sign. And let the land be healed.


# Chapter 273: The Closed Country and the Temple Book

The one who waited won the peace, and his grandson {{c|Iemitsu}} shut the door.
Between 1633 and 1639 the shogunate wrote the edicts:
No {{c|Japanese}} ship may sail abroad. No {{c|Japanese}}, on pain of death, may come ashore
From the outside world again. The {{c|Portuguese}}, with their padres and their contradicts,

Expelled, in 1639, their ships forbidden. When a {{c|Portuguese}} embassy
Came the next year from {{p|Macau}} to ask the trade back, sixty-one
Of them were beheaded, and a few sent home to tell it. The fantasy
Of the {{x|Christian}} century ended. What was left: the sun

Through four small windows. The {{c|Dutch}} on {{p|Dejima}}, a fan of land
In {{p|Nagasaki}}'s harbour, watched, and the {{c|Chinese}} merchants in their quarter;
{{p|Korea}} through the lords of {{p|Tsushima}}; the {{c|Ryūkyū}} kingdom's hand
Through {{p|Satsuma}}; the {{c|Ainu}} of the north through {{p|Matsumae}}. The water

Was a wall with four gates. Later they would call it {{c|sakoku}},
The locked country. It was not locked. It was watched.
And inside, the watching went into every house. The {{c|Taikō}}
Had measured the fields. Now the souls were notched

In a book. After the {{x|Christian}} rising at {{p|Shimabara}}, in 1637,
Which the next day of this book will tell, the shogunate decided
That every person in {{p|Japan}} must prove, each year, under heaven,
That they were not a {{x|Christian}}. And the proof was provided

By the temples. Every household was made the parishioner, the *danka*,
Of a {{x|Buddhist}} temple, and the temple certified each spring
That its families were {{x|Buddhist}}, and the village headman, the bookkeeper of the mura,
Wrote it in the *shūmon aratame chō*, the register of the inquiry: the thing

Every person in the land had to be written in. Name, age,
Household, relation to the head, the temple, the sect.
Births and deaths and marriages and servants hired, the page
Updated every year. By the 1670s the whole realm, correct

To the last fisher's child, was in the books. Some twenty-five million people.
And in {{p|Kyūshū}}, around {{p|Nagasaki}}, every {{x|New Year}}, the people
Were made to step on a bronze image of the crucified, the {{c|fumi-e}}, the simple
Test of the foot: tread on the {{c|Christ}}, or the steeple

Of the family's hidden faith falls on them all. They stepped.
Hold that. Mothers stepped on the {{c|Mother of God}} and went home and wept
And asked forgiveness in a hidden room. The register kept
Their names as {{c|Buddhists}}, and their secret kept

Itself. And the temples: they became the arm of the state,
Its clerks, its census-takers, its proof of loyalty.
They grew rich on the funerals every family had to celebrate
At its temple, by law. Buddhism in {{p|Japan}} became, in its royalty

And its poverty, the religion of the dead: the funeral faith,
The graves, the memorial tablets, the anniversaries. The cost
Came two hundred years later, when the new state, the wraith
Of the old resentment rising, smashed the temples, and the lost

Statues filled the rivers. That is another chapter, in {{c|Libra}}.
Here, on this day, see the book with both eyes.
It was a cage. It was a census of conscience, the fibre
Of a police state woven into every village. And it lies

On the historian's desk today as the greatest record of a people's lives
Ever kept in the old world: every family, every year, for two centuries.
The demographers read in it how long people lived, how wives
Married and left and returned, how many children, the plenties

And the famines, the age of mothers, the servants who came and went.
The names of millions of ordinary people who otherwise would have no name.
It was made to find the hidden. It found everyone. The intent
Was the cage. The gift is the record. They are the same.

That is the register's whole nature, and this book's too:
Every list that keeps a name can be used to hunt the named.
Keep the names. Keep the lists. And be one of the few
Who will not let the list become a cage. Be ashamed

For the foot on the image, and grateful for the page
That says a fisher's daughter lived, and married, and had two sons, and died,
In a village whose name you would never have known. The age
Of the locked country kept her. Read her. She is on our side.


# Chapter 274: Our Hearts Are the Same as Yours

On the peninsula of {{p|Shimabara}} and the islands of {{p|Amakusa}},
Across the bay from {{p|Nagasaki}}, the farmers had been {{x|Christian}}
For two generations, and their lords had been {{x|Christian}}, and the law
Had changed, and the lords had changed, and the new lord's mission

Was to squeeze. The {{c|Matsukura}} taxed the harvest past the bone,
In years of famine, and those who could not pay
Were wrapped in straw raincoats and set alight, it is said; the moan
Of the burning was called the dance of the straw coat. And one day

In December 1637 they rose. Peasants, fishermen,
Masterless samurai who had lost their lords, the poor,
And at their head a boy of sixteen, {{c|Amakusa Shirō}}, whom
They said could walk on the sea, and a dove had laid an egg, and more:

That a prophecy foretold a heavenly child would come
In the twenty-fifth year after the padres were driven away.
They marched under banners with the chalice and the {{x|Host}}, the drum
Of their war was a hymn, *{{x|Santiago}}*, and they swore that they would stay

Together. Thirty-seven thousand of them, men, women and children,
Took the ruined castle of {{p|Hara}} on its cliff above the sea,
And held it, all winter, against the armies of the shogun, the bewildering
Faith of the starving. A hundred and twenty thousand men, and the plea

Of the shogun's general to the {{c|Dutch}}: and the {{c|Dutch}} came,
The ship *{{x|De Ryp}}*, and fired its cannon into the castle walls
For two weeks, {{c|Protestants}} for the shogun against the papists, the same
Trade-loyalty that kept them on {{p|Dejima}}. The calls

Of the rebels shot back into the shogun's camp with arrows:
Are there no samurai in {{p|Japan}}, that you must ask foreigners for help?
The {{c|Dutch}} went home. In April 1638, in the burrows
Of the ruined castle, the defenders were eating seaweed, the kelp

Of the shore, and the shogun's men stormed it. Almost all were killed.
Thirty-seven thousand. {{c|Shirō}}'s head was set up at {{p|Nagasaki}} as a sign.
And the lord {{c|Matsukura}}, whose greed had begun it, was not stilled
By the victory: he was beheaded, the only daimyo of the line

Of the {{x|Edo}} peace to die like a common criminal. And then the silence.
The temple books. The image underfoot. The faith was dead,
They said. It was not dead. In the {{p|Gotō}} islands, in the hills, the violence
Of the search went on around it, and it went under, and was fed

From hand to hand, without a priest, without a church, for two hundred and fifty years.
In {{p|Sotome}}, in {{p|Ikitsuki}}, in {{p|Urakami}}, the villages kept
A baptizer, a calendar of feast days kept in secret, the fears
Of discovery in every prayer. The prayers themselves were kept

In a {{x|Latin}} and {{x|Portuguese}} no one understood any more,
Repeated, *orasho*, worn smooth like a stone in a stream.
They hid the {{c|Virgin}} in a white porcelain {{c|Kannon}}, the merciful one, the door
Of the {{x|Buddhist}} mercy opening on the {{c|Mother}}: {{c|Maria Kannon}}. The dream

Of the faith wore the robe of the other faith, and kept itself inside.
That is syncretism forced by fear, and it became their own.
They stepped on the image each {{x|New Year}}, and went home, and cried,
And said the contrition prayer, *konchirisan*, for the stone

Their foot had touched. And the centuries passed. And in 1865,
When the country had opened again to the foreigners, a {{x|French}} priest,
{{c|Bernard Petitjean}}, built a church at {{p|Ōura}} in {{p|Nagasaki}}, to keep alive
The faith of the foreigners. And on the seventeenth of March, the least

Expected thing: a group of women and men from {{p|Urakami}} came in,
And watched him at prayer, and one of them, a woman, came close,
{{c|Isabelina Yuri Sugimoto}}, and whispered: *Our hearts are the same as yours*.
And then: *Where is the image of {{c|Santa Maria}}?* And the rose

Of that moment: he showed them the statue, and they knelt.
Two hundred and fifty years. No priest. No book. They had kept it.
And the persecution came again, and they were exiled, and felt
The last cruelty of the old law, three thousand of them, and swept it

Away in 1873, when the ban came down at last.
Some went into the {{x|Catholic}} church. Some would not: they kept their own way,
The way of their grandparents, the hidden way, the past
They had carried, unchanged by the return. They are there today,

A few, on the islands. Their faith is their ancestors' faith,
And no priest from {{p|Rome}} could tell them it was wrong.
Here is the whole {{x|Gaiad}} in one village: the wraith
Of the faith that would not die, kept by the weak and the strong

Together, in the robe of another faith, under the eye
Of the register. Honor the boy on the wall of {{p|Hara}}. Honor
The woman at {{p|Ōura}}. Honor what is kept when the priests die, the keeper and the corner
Where it was kept. Where is the image of {{c|Santa Maria}}? Here. Our hearts are the same.


# Chapter 275: The Mandate Changes Hands

The {{c|Ming}} had held the {{x|Mandate of Heaven}} for two hundred and seventy-six years.
In the 1630s the sky turned against them: the long cold
Of the little ice age, the drought, the locusts, the tears
Of famine in the north, the silver from the {{p|Americas}}, gold

Of the world trade, drying up, so the peasants could not pay their tax.
The soldiers went unpaid. The eunuchs ruled the palace.
And out of the starving provinces, the axe
Of rebellion: {{c|Li Zicheng}}, a dismissed postal courier, the malice

Of the hungry behind him, took {{p|Xi'an}}, and named a dynasty, and marched east,
And in April 1644 his army came to the walls of {{p|Beijing}},
And the gates were opened from inside. The emperor, the last, the least
Fortunate of the line, {{c|Chongzhen}}, rang the bell to summon the ministers. The ring

Brought no one. He walked out of the palace with one eunuch
To the hill behind the {{p|Forbidden City}}, {{p|Jingshan}}, {{p|Coal Hill}},
And hanged himself from a tree. On his robe, the story says, he wrote: the fortune
Of the realm was lost by my ministers; let the rebels kill

Me, not my people. The tree they show today was planted later.
And at the {{p|Great Wall}}, at {{p|Shanhai Pass}}, where the wall comes down to the sea,
The general {{c|Wu Sangui}} held the gate against the {{c|Manchus}}, the greater
Danger, he had thought, until the capital fell, and he

Had to choose: the rebel who held {{p|Beijing}} and his family,
Or the enemy at the gate. The story says the rebel had taken his concubine,
{{c|Chen Yuanyuan}}, and that decided it. Love, or calculation, or the family
Of motives no one knows: he opened the pass. The line

Of the {{c|Manchu}} banners came through, and with {{c|Wu}}'s army broke the rebels,
And entered {{p|Beijing}} in June, and did not leave.
A boy of six, {{c|Shunzhi}}, was enthroned, his uncle {{c|Dorgon}} ruling. The levels
Of the {{x|Mandate}}: {{c|Heaven}} gives it, and {{c|Heaven}} takes it, and the reprieve

Is never long. The {{c|Manchus}} were few: perhaps one in a hundred
Of the people they now ruled. They ruled them by two things.
The first was the body. In 1645, the order: every {{c|Han}} man shall be sundered
From his hair: shave the forehead, braid the rest in a queue. The rings

Of the slogan: *keep your hair and lose your head, or keep your head
And lose your hair.* For a {{x|Confucian}}, the hair was the gift of the parents,
Not to be cut. Men chose death. At {{p|Yangzhou}}, the dead
Were counted for ten days after the city fell; the inherence

Of terror was the point. At {{p|Jiading}}, three massacres.
The braid, which the {{p|West}} would later think was simply {{c|Chinese}},
Was the mark of conquest, worn for two hundred and sixty years. The heirs
Of the {{c|Ming}} cut it off in 1911 as a declaration. Hold these:

Identity written on the body by the conqueror,
And worn until it felt like one's own. And the second thing:
The {{c|Manchus}} became more {{x|Confucian}} than the {{c|Ming}}. The honor
Of the classics, the examinations, the rites to {{c|Heaven}}, the king

Of the old cosmology: they kept it all, and patronized it,
And the great {{c|Kangxi}}, who ruled sixty-one years,
Compiled the dictionary, the encyclopedias, and was praised for it
By the very scholars whose grandfathers had died by the spears

Of his grandfather's men. That is how the {{x|Mandate}} is won:
By becoming the keeper of the thing you conquered.
And the {{c|Ming}} loyalists held out in the south, one by one
Falling, and one of them, {{c|Koxinga}}, a pirate's son, conjured

An army and a fleet, and in 1662 took {{p|Taiwan}} from the {{c|Dutch}},
The {{c|Company}}'s fort at {{p|Tainan}} surrendered after a siege of nine months:
The first time a {{c|Chinese}} army drove out a {{c|European}} power. Such
Things the ledger of {{p|Batavia}} did not foresee. The once-

Hunted loyalist became a god in {{p|Taiwan}}'s temples,
And a hero to the {{c|Qing}} who had hunted him, and to the {{c|Japanese}},
For his mother was {{c|Japanese}}, and to the {{c|Republic}}. The examples
Of the use of the dead multiply. Hold these

On this day: the {{x|Mandate}} passes; the conqueror becomes the keeper;
The body is made to carry the new order; the loyalist becomes a saint
Of all sides. And the peasant, the courier, the famine-sleeper
Who began it, died a year later in the hills of {{p|Hubei}}, no one sure how, without restraint

Of fame or a temple. The sky turned cold, and the grain failed,
And an empire fell. That is the oldest lesson in the book.
The {{x|Mandate}} is the harvest. When the harvest is assailed,
The {{x|Mandate}} goes. Feed the people. Then look

At the rites.


# Chapter 276: The Confluence of the Two Seas

{{c|Shah Jahan}}, the grandson of {{c|Akbar}}, built a tomb of white marble
At {{p|Agra}} for his wife {{c|Mumtaz Mahal}}, who died giving birth
To their fourteenth child. The {{c|Taj Mahal}}. And when he fell ill, the marvel
Of his empire, the richest on earth,

Went to war over him, in 1657, four sons against each other.
The eldest, {{c|Dara Shikoh}}, the father's favourite, the heir,
Was a scholar and a mystic, a {{c|Sufi}} of the {{c|Qadiri}} order, the brother
Who had sat with the {{x|Hindu}} sages and the {{x|Muslim}} saints, and in the air

Of their talk had found one truth. He wrote a book, *The Confluence
Of the Two Seas*, *{{x|Majma-ul-Bahrain}}*: that the {{c|Sufi}} way and the {{c|Vedanta}}
Were the same ocean, named twice; that the difference
Was only in words. And in 1657, with the pandits of {{p|Varanasi}}, the mantra

Of his life's work: he translated fifty {{c|Upanishads}} into {{x|Persian}},
And called them the hidden book the {{c|Quran}} itself had hinted at,
*{{x|The Greatest Secret}}*. That was {{c|Akbar}}'s {{x|House of Worship}}, the version
Of it in one man's heart. And his brother {{c|Aurangzeb}}, a different hat

Of the same house: austere, orthodox, a soldier, a scholar of the law,
Who prayed five times a day and knew the {{c|Quran}} by heart,
Beat {{c|Dara}} at {{p|Samugarh}} in 1658, and beat him again, and saw
Him handed over, betrayed by a host, and brought in chains, the part

Of the end: paraded through {{p|Delhi}} on a filthy elephant,
And tried by the clerics for apostasy, and his head cut off, in 1659.
The father, {{c|Shah Jahan}}, was shut in the fort at {{p|Agra}}, the remnant
Of his days spent looking across the river at the white line

Of the tomb he had built, for eight years, until he died.
And the son ruled for forty-nine years, as {{c|Alamgir}}, {{c|Seizer of the World}}.
Now hear it carefully. The historians divide.
Some say he was a bigot who undid what {{c|Akbar}} unfurled;

Some say he was a ruler of his time, who also granted land
To temples, and employed more {{x|Hindu}} nobles than his father did.
Both are true in part. Here is what is sure: by his command
The jizya, the tax on {{c|Hindus}}, came back in 1679; the lid

Came down on great temples, at {{p|Varanasi}}, at {{p|Mathura}}, and mosques
Rose on their ground; and the ninth guru of the {{c|Sikhs}}, {{c|Tegh Bahadur}},
Who had spoken for the {{c|Hindus}} of {{p|Kashmir}} against forced conversion, the tasks
Of conscience, was beheaded in {{p|Delhi}}, in 1675. The order

Of the {{c|Sikhs}} became an order of soldiers after that:
His son {{c|Gobind}} made the {{c|Khalsa}}. {{c|Nanak}}'s clearing of the ground
Had to grow a sword. And the emperor, in his hat
Of humility, sewed prayer caps and copied the {{c|Quran}} to be found

Paying for his own food, they say, and spent the last twenty-six years
Of his life in the {{p|Deccan}}, at war with the {{c|Marathas}} of {{c|Shivaji}},
Winning battles and losing the war, the empire at its greatest extent, and the tears
Of the treasury running dry. He died in 1707 at {{p|Ahmednagar}}, now {{p|Ahilyanagar}}, the free

Old man of eighty-eight, and asked to be buried in a plain grave,
Open to the sky, at {{p|Khuldabad}}, paid for with his caps. It is there.
And within fifty years the empire was a name. The save
Of the synthesis came from elsewhere. Hear where:

{{c|Dara}}'s {{x|Persian}} {{c|Upanishads}} were carried to {{p|France}}, and in 1801
A {{x|French}} scholar, {{c|Anquetil-Duperron}}, put them into {{x|Latin}}, and a young
{{x|German}} philosopher, {{c|Schopenhauer}}, read them, and wrote: it has been the consolation of my life, the sun
Of my death. And through him the {{c|Upanishads}} went into the tongue

Of {{p|Europe}}'s thinking. The brother who lost the war won the long game.
The confluence was closed in {{p|India}} and opened in {{p|Europe}}. The seas
Run where they will. Hold both brothers. The same
House, the same blood, the same faith, and the two keys:

The key that locks, the key that opens. The tomb by the river,
Built for love, watched by a prisoner. The plain grave on the hill.
The head of the mystic. The {{c|Upanishad}} in {{x|Latin}}. The giver
And the taker. The confluence is never closed. It is still

Running somewhere. Find it. Two seas, one water.
Sit with the sages. Do not cut off the head
Of the brother who found the same ocean in another's daughter
Faith. The two seas meet. Let them. Let the river be fed.


# Chapter 277: Take Nobody's Word for It

{{p|England}} had killed its king in 1649, and lived without one for eleven years,
And in 1660 called his son home, {{c|Charles}}, from exile, and the bells
Rang in {{p|London}}. And in the same year, the twenty-eighth of November, the peers
Of a different kingdom met: twelve men, after a lecture, the wells

Of their talk running over at {{p|Gresham College}}, where the young
Astronomer {{c|Christopher Wren}} had spoken. They had met before, for years,
In {{p|Oxford}} and {{p|London}}, through the wars, the invisible college, the tongue
Of experiment shared by men who had fought on both sides. The fears

Of the civil war were laid aside at the table of the air pump.
They agreed to meet each week, to do experiments, and to see them done.
The king gave them a charter in 1662: the {{c|Royal Society}}. The lump
Of the old learning, the authority of the ancients, the one

Who must be believed because he was {{c|Aristotle}}, they set aside
With a motto: *{{x|Nullius in verba}}*. Take nobody's word for it.
Not the king's, not the {{x|Church}}'s, not the philosopher's, not the pride
Of the learned. See it. Weigh it. Do it again. Commit

The result to the record, and let the others try.
That was the new rite: the public experiment, before witnesses,
Gentlemen who signed their names to what they saw. The why
Of the world would be settled by the eye, not the business

Of argument. {{c|Robert Boyle}} and his pump: a bird in a glass,
The air drawn out, and the bird dying, and the air let back in.
{{c|Robert Hooke}}, the {{x|Society}}'s curator of experiments, would pass
A flea under his microscope and draw it, the bristles, the skin

Of armour, enormous, in *{{x|Micrographia}}*, in 1665,
And look at a slice of cork and see little rooms, and call them *cells*.
The word is his. Every living thing is made of them. The hive
Of the body, the leaf, the whale, the child: cells.

And in the same year, {{c|Henry Oldenburg}}, the secretary, began
To print the letters that came in from every country: *{{x|Philosophical}}
{{x|Transactions}}*, the oldest scientific journal still in print. The plan
Was a register of discovery: who saw what, when. The radical

Idea that knowledge belongs to whoever saw it first and published it,
And that the date on the page decides the honour. The register again:
Not of souls, not of fields, but of facts, each one admitted
Only when another could repeat it. And then the men

Who were not gentlemen, and the women, who could not join.
When {{c|Margaret Cavendish}}, Duchess of {{p|Newcastle}}, a philosopher who wrote
Of atoms and of other worlds, asked to visit, in 1667, the coin
Of curiosity was paid for once: they let her come, and she took note

Of the experiments, and went home, and was mocked for it. She was the first
Woman at a meeting. The first woman elected a Fellow came in 1945.
Two hundred and eighty-five years. Hold it. The thirst
For evidence did not reach the evidence of who was alive

Around the table. And the {{x|Society}} ran out of money. In 1686 they printed
A *{{x|History of Fishes}}*, lavishly, and it did not sell.
So when {{c|Newton}}'s *{{x|Principia}}* came, in 1687, the book that minted
The laws of motion and of gravity, the {{x|Society}}, unable to tell

The printer yes, let {{c|Edmond Halley}} pay for it himself,
And paid {{c|Halley}} his salary, they say, in unsold copies of the fishes.
The greatest book of science came off the shelf
Because a young astronomer paid. The wishes

Of an institution are not the whole of its work.
{{c|Newton}} would be its president for twenty-four years, and a tyrant to his rivals.
Take nobody's word for it: not even his. The quirk
Of the motto is that it turns on its makers. The archivals

Of the {{x|Society}} keep the quarrels too: {{c|Hooke}} and {{c|Newton}}, the priority
Of the calculus, the committee {{c|Newton}} secretly wrote the report of himself.
Hold this, near the end of {{c|Virgo}}: the greatest authority
Of the modern age was founded on the refusal of authority. The shelf

Of scripture this book is making must keep the same rule.
Do not believe the {{x|Gaiad}} because it is scripture. Check it.
Repeat it. Where it dreams, it says so. Where it errs, the tool
Of correction is open to anyone. That is the oath. Respect it.


# Chapter 278: The Barrels Stayed Packed

In 1648 the {{c|Cossacks}} of {{c|Khmelnytsky}} rose in {{p|Ukraine}}
And killed the {{c|Jews}} of town after town, tens of thousands, the worst
Massacre the {{c|Jews}} of {{p|Europe}} had known in centuries. The stain
Spread through the communities like a fever. And then, as if the curse

Had to be answered by its opposite, the {{c|Kabbalists}} said the end was near.
In the teaching of {{c|Isaac Luria}}, the world was a broken vessel, its sparks
Scattered, and each good deed gathered one, and the year
Of the last gathering would bring the messiah. And the marks

Of the time were read as signs. In {{p|Smyrna}}, now {{p|İzmir}},
A young scholar, {{c|Sabbatai Zevi}}, born in 1626,
Of great charm and terrible moods, rose and fell, the sheer
Joy of illumination, then the dark, the swings

Of a mind that history would now call bipolar.
In his bright seasons he did forbidden things: spoke aloud
The {{x|Name of God}} that no one speaks, married a {{x|Torah}} scroll, the solar
Rites of a man who thought the law was over. The crowd

Of the rabbis expelled him. He wandered. And in 1665, in {{p|Gaza}},
A young prophet, {{c|Nathan}}, had a vision, and told him: you are the one.
And {{c|Sabbatai}} believed it, and the news ran out, a blaze, a
Rumour, a letter, a ship, from {{p|Gaza}} to {{p|Aleppo}}, the sun

Of it rising over {{p|Smyrna}} in December, where he took the synagogue,
And proclaimed himself, and gave his followers the kingdoms of the earth.
Then {{p|Amsterdam}}, {{p|Hamburg}}, {{p|Venice}}, {{p|Poland}}: the epilogue
Of exile seemed to be written. People sold their houses. The worth

Of everything was nothing beside the journey home.
In {{p|Hamburg}}, a woman named {{c|Glückel}} would remember, in her memoir,
How the people danced in the synagogue with the letters, and how, to roam
To the {{p|Holy Land}}, her father-in-law in {{p|Hameln}} packed his store

Of linen and dried food and peas and beans into barrels,
And kept them ready for the moment the messiah called.
1666. The year of the Beast for the {{c|Christians}}, the perils
And the hopes of all {{p|Europe}} pointing to it. And he was hauled

In chains, when he sailed to {{p|Istanbul}} to claim the sultan's crown,
And held in the fortress of {{p|Gallipoli}}, which his followers called
The {{x|Tower of Strength}}, and he held court there, and the town
Filled with pilgrims. And in September he was brought, enthralled

Or terrified, before the sultan's council at {{p|Edirne}},
And offered a choice: a miracle, or death, or {{x|Islam}}.
He took the turban. *{{c|Aziz Mehmed Efendi}}*. The journey
Was over. The messiah had converted. The calm

Of the morning after: shame, disbelief, the scattering.
Some said it was a mystery, a descent into the husks
To gather the last sparks. A few followed him into {{x|Islam}}, the battering
Of their faith turned inside out: the {{c|Dönme}} of {{p|Thessaloniki}}, the dusks

Of their secret rites kept for two hundred years. And most
Went home, and unpacked, and mourned. Except the barrels in {{p|Hameln}}:
{{c|Glückel}} says her father-in-law kept them packed, for the ghost
Of a hope, for three years, before he finally let them in

To the house again. He died in exile in 1676,
In {{p|Ulcinj}}, on the {{p|Adriatic}}, on {{c|Yom Kippur}}, they say.
Now, on {{c|Sukkot}}. The festival of booths: you leave the bricks
And live seven days in a hut of branches, open to the sky. The way

Of the holiday is joy, and it is commanded: *you shall rejoice*.
In a house you know is temporary. Under a roof
That lets in the stars and the rain. The choice
Of the sukkah is the choice to hope without proof

And not be destroyed when the proof does not come.
The barrels in {{p|Hameln}} were a sukkah. A hope, kept packed,
In a house where the stars came in. The sum
Of the story is not: the hope was a fool's. It is the fact

That a people who had just been massacred
Could still dance in the synagogue, and still pack the barrels, and still, when the hope
Turned to shame, unpack, and live, and wait. The word
Of the festival: rejoice in what does not last. The scope

Of the messiah was wrong. The joy was not wrong.
Sit in the hut tonight. It will not stand forever.
Sing anyway. The roof is thin. The night is long.
The barrels can be unpacked. The hope can be kept. Never

Confuse a man with the end of the world.
And never stop leaving the roof open to the stars.
Rejoice in the booth. The branches are curled
Over your head, and they let the light through the bars.


# Chapter 279: One Law for the Apple and the Moon

A child born early on {{x|Christmas Day}}, 1642, so small, his mother said,
He would have fit in a quart pot, at {{p|Woolsthorpe}} in {{p|Lincolnshire}},
The year {{c|Galileo}} died. His father was already dead.
His mother left him with his grandmother. The fire

Of that boyhood never cooled: he made lists of his sins, and one was
*Threatening my father and mother Smith to burn them and the house over them.*
He went to {{p|Cambridge}} as a servant-student. And then, because
Of the plague, in 1665 the university closed, and the stem

Of the modern world grew in an orchard at {{p|Woolsthorpe}}.
Twenty-three years old, alone, for eighteen months, he invented
The calculus, and split white light with a prism into the rainbow's gorge,
And wondered, watching an apple fall, the story is remembered

Or told by his own old age, whether the force that pulled it down
Reached up as far as the {{c|Moon}}, and held it in its orbit,
And weakened with the square of the distance. The crown
Of the idea he kept to himself for twenty years. The sorbet

Of fame did not interest him. Then, in 1684, {{c|Edmond Halley}}
Came to {{p|Cambridge}} and asked: if the force on the planets falls
With the square of the distance, what path do they follow? The rally
Of the answer: an ellipse. I have calculated it. The walls

Of his rooms were searched for the paper, and it was lost, and he promised
To do it again. Three years later the book came out:
*{{x|Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica}}*, the fifth of July, 1687, the honest
Size of it three books in {{x|Latin}}, paid for, as the last chapter told, without doubt,

By {{c|Halley}}. Three laws of motion. A body at rest stays at rest.
A force changes motion in proportion. Every action has its reaction.
And one law of gravity, the same for the apple and the planets, the test
Of the sky the same as the test of the orchard: one attraction

Between every two masses in the universe, falling with the square
Of their distance. The {{c|Moon}}'s orbit. The tides. The comets' return,
So that {{c|Halley}} could predict his comet would come back, and it did, there
In 1758, sixteen years after he had died. The burn

Of the old sky was over: the heavens were not made of a finer stuff.
They were made of world. The same law in the stars as in the hand.
That is the {{x|Gaiad}}'s first chapter, written in {{x|Latin}}. Enough
To know the universe is one: one law, one land.

And now the other {{c|Newton}}. The one who spent more years
On alchemy than on physics, hunting the philosopher's stone,
Writing a million words on the transmutation of metals, the tears
Of mercury and the green lion. The one who, alone,

Denied the {{x|Trinity}} in secret, and calculated from the {{c|Book of Daniel}}
That the world would not end before 2060. The one
Whose papers, sold in 1936, made {{c|Keynes}} write that he was not the first
Of the age of reason: he was the last of the magicians. The sun

Of the new science and the moon of the old wisdom in one man.
And here is the thing to keep, after {{c|Bureus}}: {{c|Newton}} knew which was which.
He published the laws, which anyone could check. The plan
Of the alchemy he kept in a box. He did not make the switch

Of dream into proof. The box was opened after he died,
And the world was surprised. That is the right shape. Dream, if you dream.
Keep it in the box, labelled. Publish what can be tried.
He wrote: *I frame no hypotheses*, about the cause, the seam

Of gravity he could not explain. He knew what he did not know.
And he was cruel: to {{c|Hooke}}, to {{c|Leibniz}}, and, as {{x|Master of the Mint}},
To the counterfeiters he hunted himself, and sent to the gallows. So
Hold the whole man. Not a saint. A mind, and a temper, and a stint

Of loneliness that lasted his whole life. He wrote, of himself, near the end,
That he had been like a boy on the shore, playing with a smoother pebble,
A prettier shell, while the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered. Attend
To that: the greatest mind of the age, and the ocean, and the treble

Of the waves on a beach. He died in 1727 and lies in {{p|Westminster}}.
*Nature and Nature's laws lay hid in night;
God said, Let {{c|Newton}} be! and all was light.* The poet's tinder.
Better the shell on the shore. Better the boy. Better the ocean, and the sight

Of the apple falling, and the {{c|Moon}} held, by one thing.
The universe is one law. And the ocean is still there.
Pick up a shell. Check it. Keep your dreams in a box, labelled. And sing
For the orchard where the plague sent a boy, and he looked up, and saw it there.


# Chapter 280: One and Nothing

{{c|Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz}}, born in {{p|Leipzig}} in 1646, the son
Of a professor of ethics who died when the boy was six,
Taught himself {{x|Latin}} from the books of his father's library, and won
A doctorate in law at twenty, and then refused the fixed

Life of a professor, and became a courtier, a diplomat, a librarian,
A historian of the house of {{p|Brunswick}}, a writer of letters, fifteen
Thousand of them, to everyone in {{p|Europe}} and beyond, the clarion
Of a mind that wanted to join every mind it had seen.

He found the calculus at the same time as {{c|Newton}}, alone,
And wrote it in the signs we still use: the long S of the integral,
The *d* of the differential. And the quarrel over whose it was, the bone
Of the {{c|Royal Society}}'s committee, as the earlier chapter told, the minimal

Justice of it came late. But this chapter is about two numbers.
In 1679 he wrote out a way of counting with only one and zero:
One, ten, eleven, a hundred. Two digits for all the numbers. The slumbers
Of the idea lasted twenty years. He saw in it, as a hero

Of the old theology might: the world made from God and nothing.
One is God. Zero is the void. And from the two, all things.
*{{x|Omnibus ex nihilo ducendis sufficit unum}}*: the clothing
Of the motto on a medal he designed: to draw all things from nothing, the wings

Of one suffice. And he built a machine that could multiply,
A stepped drum of brass, and showed it to the {{c|Royal Society}} in 1673.
And he dreamed of more: a universal language, a *characteristic*, a way to try
Every argument by calculation, so that two philosophers, the sea

Of their quarrel too deep for words, would sit down with pens
And say to each other: *calculemus*. Let us calculate.
The dream of a machine that reasons. The lens
Of the next three hundred years is in that word. The weight

Of everything that {{c|Ophiuchus}} will tell is in it. Hold it.
And he loved {{p|China}}. He read everything the {{c|Jesuits}} wrote,
And published their letters, *{{x|News from China}}*, in 1697, and told it
To {{p|Europe}}: their ethics are better than ours; we should note

That we need {{x|Chinese}} missionaries to teach us natural theology,
As much as they need ours to teach revealed religion.
He defended {{c|Ricci}}'s way, the rites for the ancestors, the apology
Of the accommodation, against {{p|Rome}}. And then, the vision:

In 1701 a {{c|Jesuit}} in {{p|Beijing}}, {{c|Joachim Bouvet}}, who had read
His binary, sent him a diagram of the sixty-four hexagrams
Of the {{c|I Ching}}, the *{{x|Book of Changes}}*, in the order {{c|Shao Yong}} had spread,
And {{c|Leibniz}} looked at the broken and unbroken lines, the grams

Of yin and yang, and saw: zero and one. The hexagrams in that order
Counted from nothing to sixty-three in binary. The oldest book
Of {{p|China}}, ascribed to {{c|Fuxi}}, the sage of the beginning, a border
Crossed four thousand years before, he believed, by the same look

At the world as his own. He was wrong about the history.
The order was a {{x|Song}} scholar's, not the ancient sage's. But the mystery
Was real: two minds, a world apart, building the same ladder of change. The registry
Of that meeting is a letter. And in 1703 he published his binary, the history

Of it ending with the hexagrams. Within two hundred and fifty years,
Every machine that thinks would think in one and zero.
The register of every soul, the census, the ledgers, the tears
Of the {{x|Company}}, the temple book: all of it, in the next era,

Would be written in his two digits. That is the bridge.
{{c|Virgo}} ends here: the early modern world, its saints and its massacres,
Its registers and its telescopes, its kings on the ridge
Of invented pasts. And it ends with a man who joined the actors

Of {{p|East}} and {{p|West}} in two numbers, and dreamed of reasoning by machine.
He died in 1716 in {{p|Hanover}}, out of favour, his king gone to {{p|London}},
And only his secretary followed the coffin. The lean
Grave of the man who joined the world. And {{c|Voltaire}} would make fun

Of his *best of all possible worlds*. Let him. The one and the nothing
Are in every phone. Every message to the ones you love goes in them.
Tomorrow begins {{c|Libra}}: the {{x|Rites}}, the reckoning, the clothing
Of the {{x|Enlightenment}}. From one and nothing, the world. Hold the hem.

---

# Libra (11宮) - Days 281-308


# Chapter 281: The Harvest at the Ancestors' Hall

In autumn in {{p|China}}, when the grain was in, the family
Went to the ancestors' hall, and set the first of the harvest
Before the tablets of the dead: the rice, the millet, the homily
Of the incense, the bowing, the names read out. The darkest

Winter would come; first, the thanks. This is the day of the harvest.
Hold that table in your eye, because {{p|Rome}} would forbid it.
{{c|Ricci}} had made his wager: these were civil rites, the starkest
Honouring of the parents, not worship. A {{x|Christian}} could do it.

His order, the {{c|Jesuits}}, kept the wager for a hundred years.
Other orders came to {{p|China}}, the {{c|Dominicans}}, the {{c|Franciscans}},
Who worked in the villages, not the court, and saw, among the peasants' tears
And offerings, food set out for the dead to eat, the stances

Of prayer to spirits, and said: this is idolatry. And they said:
The words {{c|Ricci}} used for God, *{{x|Tian}}*, {{x|Heaven}}, and *{{x|Shangdi}}*,
The {{x|Lord on High}}, are pagan words. The quarrel spread
To {{p|Rome}}, to the universities of {{p|Paris}}, where the clergy

Argued for decades about a country none of them had seen.
The {{c|Jesuits}} asked the emperor himself. And in 1700 the great {{c|Kangxi}},
Who had made the {{c|Jesuits}} his astronomers, signed a statement, clean
And clear: the rites to {{c|Confucius}} are to honour a teacher; the ancestry

{{x|Rites}} are to show love and remember; *{{x|Tian}}* means the {{x|Lord of Heaven}}.
Nothing in them is a prayer for blessing from the dead.
The emperor of {{p|China}} had settled it. And {{p|Rome}}, the leaven
Of whose authority could not be shared, said: it is not his to settle. Instead,

In 1704, {{c|Clement XI}} decreed: no *{{x|Tian}}*, no *{{x|Shangdi}}*, only *{{x|Tianzhu}}*,
{{x|Lord of Heaven}}, {{c|Ricci}}'s coinage; no tablets saying *seat of the soul*;
No {{x|Christian}} to take part in the rites of {{c|Confucius}}, nor do
The seasonal offerings at the ancestors' hall. The whole

Of the accommodation, refused. A legate, {{c|Tournon}}, carried it to {{p|Beijing}},
And the emperor received him, and heard what he had come to say,
And questioned the bishop who had begun it, {{c|Maigrot}}, who could not read a single thing
Of the characters, and was furious that such a man should judge the classics. The way

It ended: the legate expelled to {{p|Macau}}, where the {{x|Portuguese}},
Jealous of their own rights, held him, and he died in 1710.
{{p|Rome}} confirmed the ban in 1715. And the emperor, with ease
And contempt, wrote on the papal decree with his red brush: *the men

Of the {{p|West}} are small; they do not understand the great principles of {{p|China}}.
From now on they need not preach here, to avoid trouble.*
In 1724 his son banned {{x|Christianity}}. The fine
Work of a century fell like a house to rubble.

And in 1742 {{c|Benedict XIV}} closed it for good: every missionary
To {{p|China}} had to swear an oath against the rites. For two hundred years
A {{x|Chinese}} {{x|Christian}} could not bring the harvest to his fathers. The adversary
Was not the emperor. It was a refusal to see. The tears

Of the converts who had to choose: their God, or their dead.
Hold that, on {{x|Harvest Day}}. And then hold this: in 1939,
In {{c|Pius XII}}'s first year, {{p|Rome}} reversed itself. The rites, it said,
Are civil. A {{x|Christian}} may bow. The tablets may be in line

With the faith. One hundred and ninety-seven years, from the final no
To yes. The wager {{c|Ricci}} made was right. The emperor was right.
The thanks at the harvest to those who came before, the bow
To the tablet with the grandmother's name, was love. The light

Of this day in the {{c|Gaian}} calendar falls on many harvests:
The first fruits of the {{p|Americas}}, given thanks by its first peoples;
The rice of {{p|Japan}}; the turkey of {{p|Canada}}; and the ancestral hall, where the fastest
And the slowest of the family come home. The steeples

And the shrines and the ancestors' halls: the harvest belongs to all of them.
Give thanks for the food. Give thanks to the hands that grew it.
Give thanks to the ones who came before, and set the bowl at the hem
Of their memory. No one has the right to forbid it. Do it.


# Chapter 282: The Names of Everything

In {{p|Småland}}, in {{p|Sweden}}, a country pastor's son was born in 1707,
At {{p|Råshult}}, in the parsonage among the birches.
His father, {{c|Nils}}, the son of a farmer named {{c|Ingemar}}, had been given, as was common,
No surname: *{{c|Nils Ingemarsson}}*. When he went to university, the churches

And the learned wanted a {{x|Latin}} name. So he made one up,
From a great linden tree, a *lind*, that grew on the family's farm:
*{{c|Linnaeus}}*. Hold that, in a book of genealogy: the cup
Of a name was filled by a tree. The family line, the charm

Of the patronymic, {{c|Ingemar}}'s son, {{c|Nils}}'s son, gave way
To a name you choose. And the son, {{c|Carl}}, would spend his life
Giving names to every living thing. His father had a garden; the way
The boy learned the flowers was by asking, and the strife

Of forgetting them made his father say: I will not tell you again.
He did not forget again. He went to {{p|Uppsala}}, poor,
With shoes he mended with birch bark, and walked, in 1732, the plain
Of {{p|Lapland}}, two thousand kilometres, and wore

The costume of the {{c|Sámi}} afterward for his portrait, the drum
And the reindeer boots, and learned from them, and wrote it down.
In 1735, in {{p|Leiden}}, in the {{p|Netherlands}}, the sum
Of his system came out: *{{x|Systema Naturae}}*, a crown

Of eleven large pages: all of nature, the three kingdoms,
Animal, plant and stone, in classes, orders, genera, kinds.
And the plants sorted by their sex: the stamens and the pistils, the stem's
Husbands and wives, how many of each in the flower. The minds

Of the pious were shocked. A professor called it *loathsome harlotry*.
{{c|Linnaeus}} named an ugly weed after him. And in 1753
He gave every plant two names, a genus and a species, a clarity
That made botany possible: *{{x|Bellis perennis}}*, the daisy. The key

Of the binomial still opens the whole living world. And in 1758,
The tenth edition, he did the boldest thing. He put us in.
*{{x|Homo sapiens}}*: wise man, among the primates, beside the great
Apes, in the same order as the monkeys. The sin

Of it, to the theologians: man among the beasts.
He wrote to a friend: tell me one difference between man and ape
That follows the rules of natural history. I know of none. The feasts
Of human pride had their first plain mirror. And then the shape

Of the harm. In the same pages he divided *{{x|Homo sapiens}}*
Into four varieties by continent, *americanus*, *europaeus*, *asiaticus*, *afer*,
And gave each a temperament, and ranked them, the {{x|European}} in the sense
Of governed by laws, the {{x|African}} by caprice: the seed of a horror

That would grow for two hundred years. The register of life
Had a racist line in it, written by the hand that put us among the apes.
Hold both. He sent his students out across the world, the strife
And the joy of it: seventeen apostles, he called them, to the capes

And jungles and the ice, to collect, and a third of them died on the road.
He was ennobled in 1761: *{{c|Carl von Linné}}*.
He said of himself, *God created, {{c|Linnaeus}} ordered*. The load
Of the boast was heavy and half true. He died in 1778, the day

Coming when they laid him in the cathedral of {{p|Uppsala}}.
This is a book that begins with the birth of the universe and of life,
And comes down through the fish and the reptiles and the patterns
Of the mammals to us. It owes him its names. The knife

Of his system cut the living world into a register,
And the register is a gift: to know the names of the beings we share the earth with
Is the first respect. A {{x|Lifeist}} calls each one by its name, a barrister
Of the living, an advocate. Learn the names. The pith

Of reverence is attention. And cross out the line he got wrong:
There are no ranked varieties of us. The register of humankind is one.
*{{x|Homo sapiens}}*. One species. One family. One song.
The linden tree in {{p|Småland}} is gone. The name it gave is in the sun.


# Chapter 283: No Place Empty

After the messiah who took the turban, the {{c|Jews}} of {{p|Poland}} and {{p|Ukraine}}
Were ashamed, and poor, and the learned were proud of their learning,
And the poor who could not read the {{x|Talmud}} stood outside the plain
Of the scholars' world, and prayed the words without discerning

What they meant, and were told they were nothing. And in {{p|Podolia}},
Among the villages of the borderland, around 1700,
A boy was born, an orphan, {{c|Israel}}, son of {{c|Eliezer}}, who would be holier
Than the scholars and never write a book. They sent

Him as a helper to the teacher, to walk the little children
To the schoolroom in the morning, and he walked them singing,
And taught them to sing the prayers. He was a watchman, a clay-digger in
The {{p|Carpathian}} hills, a hidden man, and the bringing

Of his secret out came late, when he was thirty-six, the story says.
He was a *baal shem*, a master of the Name: a healer, a writer of amulets,
And they called him the {{c|Baal Shem Tov}}, the {{c|Master of the Good Name}}, the praise
Of the villages. He settled at {{p|Medzhybizh}}, around 1740. The lets

And hindrances of the old way he did not abolish. He kept the law.
But he taught a different heart in it. God is everywhere:
*There is no place empty of Him.* In the field, the straw,
The tavern, the stranger, the evil thought, the prayer.

Every spark of the broken vessels the {{c|Kabbalists}} had mourned
Was here, in the ordinary, waiting to be lifted with joy.
Not with fasting. With joy. The sad are far from God; the scorned
And the simple are near. And the story they tell of the boy:

On {{c|Yom Kippur}}, a shepherd boy who could not read the prayers
Stood in the synagogue all day, and his heart was full, and he had a whistle,
A shepherd's pipe, and at the end of the day, in the airs
Of the closing prayer, he could not hold it, and blew it, a thistle

Of a sound in the solemn room, and the men were furious.
And the {{c|Baal Shem Tov}} said: the gates of heaven were shut,
And all our prayers could not open them, and that boy's pipe, the curious
Note of a heart with no words, broke them open. The rut

Of learning was not the road. The heart was the road.
He wrote nothing. His students wrote him down: the great {{c|Maggid}}
Of {{p|Mezhyrichi}}, and the others, and the stories, the load
Of the tales passed on by the poor, the parables, the rigid

Made soft. And the movement spread like water through the villages:
{{c|Hasidism}}, the way of the pious, dancing in the prayer house,
Following a holy man, a *rebbe*, a righteous one, whose courtyard and its images
Of feasting and song drew the poor in. And the {{c|Vilna Gaon}}, who would house

No compromise, the greatest scholar of the age in {{p|Vilnius}},
Excommunicated them in 1772: these are dancers, not scholars, a sect.
The quarrel lasted a generation, and then, like the illness
Of every quarrel, cooled, and both sides were what kept

The {{c|Jews}} of the East {{x|Jewish}} when the modern world came for them.
And here is the thing for this book. The rebbes' courts became dynasties.
The holiness passed from father to son, and son-in-law, the hem
Of the rebbe's coat held by his heirs: genealogies

Of the holy, kept as carefully as any king's.
His own great-grandson, {{c|Nachman of Breslov}}, would teach
That the whole world is a narrow bridge, and the main thing
Is not to be afraid at all. And the grave and its reach

At {{p|Uman}} draws tens of thousands every new year still.
Hold the two: the teaching that holiness is in everyone, everywhere,
And the dynasties that made it run in families. The will
Of the movement was for the simple; the courts grew rich. The prayer

Of the shepherd's pipe is the part to keep. And this, which the {{x|Gaiad}} shares
With the {{c|Master of the Good Name}}: there is no place empty.
The divine, or the sacred, or the life, is in all of it: the stairs,
The straw, the stranger, the smallest thing. The plenty

Is everywhere. Lift it with joy. Do not be sad; the sad
Are far from the sacred. Sing on the way to school.
And if you have no words, blow the whistle. What you had
Was enough. It always was. The heart is the rule.


# Chapter 284: The Pact at Diriyah

In {{p|Najd}}, the high desert at the heart of {{p|Arabia}}, a long way
From {{p|Istanbul}} and from {{p|Cairo}}, in the oasis towns of palm and mud brick,
Where the people visited the tombs of holy men, and hung rags on trees to pray,
And asked the saints to carry their prayers, a scholar, quick

And severe, {{c|Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab}}, born in 1703,
Came home from his studies in {{p|Medina}} and {{p|Basra}} and preached:
This is not {{x|Islam}}. God is one. No saint, no tree,
No tomb, no prophet even, may be asked to intercede. He reached

Back past a thousand years of what the {{c|Muslims}} had done,
The {{c|Sufi}} orders, the shrines, the feasts of the saints, the schools
Of law and their commentaries, to the {{c|Quran}} and the sayings, the one
Pure beginning, as he read it. His book was *{{x|The Oneness of God}}*. The rules

Were simple and absolute. And he acted. At {{p|Al-Uyaynah}},
With the town's emir, he cut down a sacred tree, and pulled down the tomb
Of {{c|Zayd ibn al-Khattab}}, a companion of the {{c|Prophet}}, the venerated
Dome over his grave, and had a woman stoned. The room

Of the town grew afraid, and the emir's own overlord made him send the preacher away.
He went to {{p|Diriyah}}, a small town on a dry riverbed,
And there, in 1744, he met its emir, {{c|Muhammad ibn Saud}}, and the day
Of their meeting made a pact that still holds: the preacher said,

You give me your sword and protection; I give you the faith, and the right
To rule in its name. The emir agreed. The {{c|Saud}} would hold the land;
The family of the sheikh, the {{c|Al ash-Sheikh}}, would hold the light
Of the religion. Two dynasties, in one hand,

Married to each other, generation after generation, to this day.
Hold that, in a book of genealogy: a faith and a state
As two family trees, bound by a promise in a mud-brick town. The way
Of the alliance was conquest. Their followers called themselves, as they relate,

*{{c|Al-Muwahhidun}}*, the people of God's oneness. The word *{{x|Wahhabi}}*
Was what their enemies called them, and it stuck. They took {{p|Najd}},
And then, in 1802, they rode north to {{p|Karbala}} in {{p|Iraq}}, the shrine-crowned
And holy city of the {{c|Shia}}, where {{c|Husayn}}, the {{c|Prophet}}'s grandson, had died

And is buried, and they killed thousands in its streets, and stripped the shrine.
In 1803 and 1805 they took {{p|Mecca}} and {{p|Medina}}, and pulled down
The domes over the graves of the {{c|Prophet}}'s family, the line
Of the saints, at the {{p|Baqi}} cemetery, and the pilgrims of every town

Who would not pray their way were turned back. The {{c|Ottomans}} sent {{c|Muhammad Ali}}'s
{{x|Egyptian}} army, and it took seven years, and in 1818 {{p|Diriyah}} was razed,
And the emir {{c|Abdullah}} was taken to {{p|Istanbul}} and beheaded. The steel
Of the empire had won. The idea had not. It was praised

And kept in the desert, and came back. In 1902 a young {{c|Ibn Saud}}
Retook {{p|Riyadh}}, and by 1932 the kingdom was named for his family.
In 1925 the domes at {{p|Baqi}} were pulled down again. And the flood
Of oil, found in 1938, would carry the preaching, quietly and loudly,

To mosques and schools across the world. Now hold this carefully, because it is the spine
Of this book: the movement said it was a return to the pure beginning.
But what it built had never existed: a state church in a desert, a line
Of two families, a faith stripped of the saints that the beginning

Had grown in a thousand places, the {{c|Sufi}} lodges, the shared shrines
Where {{c|Muslims}} and {{c|Christians}} and {{c|Jews}} had sometimes prayed side by side.
A purification is always a new thing wearing the old lines.
The {{c|Old Believers}}' persecutors said they were restoring the pure rite. The pride

Of every reformer is to be the first faithful one since the founder.
And what is cut away is the life that grew in between:
The grandmother at the saint's tomb with her rag on the tree, the wonder
Of the feast day, the shrine where two faiths met. The green

Of the oasis was not a corruption. It was the faith alive.
This book does not condemn the many {{c|Muslims}} who keep this way with sincerity.
It names the pattern: the return that is an invention, the drive
To purity that splits. Hold the tree that was cut down. Its charity

Was shade. Somebody prayed under it. Remember them.
God is one, the preacher said, and he was right. The oneness
Is wide enough for the rag on the tree, and the saint's dome, and the hem
Of the grandmother's prayer. The sacred has room. Make room. That is the oneness.


# Chapter 285: The Assessor of the Board of Mines

His father was {{c|Jesper Swedberg}}, a bishop of {{p|Skara}}, a man who said
He had seen angels and talked with them. In 1719 the family
Was ennobled, and the name was changed, as {{x|Swedish}} nobles' names were made,
To {{c|Swedenborg}}. Another name made new, as the linden named the family

Of {{c|Linnaeus}}. The son, {{c|Emanuel}}, born in {{p|Stockholm}} in 1688,
Was the most practical of men. For thirty years he sat as an assessor
On the {{c|Board of Mines}}, inspecting copper and iron, the weight
Of ore and the safety of shafts, a dutiful professor

Of the kingdom's wealth. And a scientist of everything:
He designed a flying machine in 1714, on paper, with a fixed wing;
He studied the brain and guessed that its outer layer, the ring
Of the cortex, held the mind, and that each part of it did a separate thing,

A century before the anatomists proved it; he wrote of the planets
Forming from a cloud around the sun. He learned {{x|Hebrew}}. He was famous.
And at fifty-five, in 1743, the dreams came. The granite
Of the assessor cracked. He kept a journal of them, the infamous

And tender night journal of a man undone: temptations, terrors,
{{c|Christ}} appearing. And in April 1745, in a {{p|London}} inn,
After dinner, he said, a man appeared in the corner, and the errors
Of the meal were the first thing: *do not eat so much*. And then, within

The same night, the Lord appeared to him, he wrote, and gave him
A task: to explain the inner meaning of the {{x|Scriptures}} to the world.
He gave up science. He gave up everything but that. The whim
Of a madman, his enemies said. He was calm. He unfurled

Thirty years of books, in {{x|Latin}}, published anonymously in {{p|London}}:
*{{x|Heavenly Secrets}}*, eight volumes on {{c|Genesis}} and {{c|Exodus}}; *{{x|Heaven and Hell}}*.
He said he walked in the spiritual world daily, the way one
Walks down a street, and talked with the dead, and could tell

What they said: that heaven is not a reward but a state of love,
That the angels were once human, that married love goes on,
That every natural thing corresponds to a spiritual one: the dove,
The light, the water, the tree. That the {{x|Last Judgment}} had come and gone,

In the spiritual world, in 1757, and no one on earth had noticed.
And the evidence: in July 1759, at a dinner in {{p|Gothenburg}},
Four hundred kilometres from {{p|Stockholm}}, he turned pale and, it is noticed,
Went out and came back: a great fire has broken out in {{p|Stockholm}}. The church

Of the guests listened while he reported it, hour by hour,
And at eight o'clock he said: thank God, it has stopped, three doors
From my house. Two days later the courier came, and it was so. The power
Of that story reached {{c|Kant}} in {{p|Königsberg}}, who looked into it, wrote scores

Of pages on it, *{{x|Dreams of a Spirit-Seer}}*, and mocked it, and could not let it go.
Hold the man whole, as this book has held {{c|Bureus}} and {{c|Newton}}.
A mind of the mines and the brain and the cloud of the sun, and the glow
Of visions; and unlike {{c|Newton}}, he did not keep the box shut: the button

Of the seer and the scientist was the same button, and he pressed it,
And said: I have seen. Believe me or not. He did not ask
For a church. He died in {{p|London}} in 1772, and he had guessed it:
When {{c|John Wesley}} wrote to say he wished to meet him, the task

Was answered: I shall die on the twenty-ninth of March. He did.
His readers made the church after him, the {{c|New Church}}, in 1787.
And it went where the {{c|Swede}} had never gone. The seed of it hid
In a strange pocket in {{p|America}}: a man named {{c|John Chapman}}, a heaven

Of a different kind in his head, barefoot, walked the frontier
For forty years with a sack of apple seeds and {{c|Swedenborg}}'s pages,
Planting orchards ahead of the settlers, and tearing out the sheer
Leaves of the books to leave with the families, like wages

Of the spirit. {{c|Johnny Appleseed}}. A visionary's church became
An orchard across {{p|Ohio}} and {{p|Indiana}}. The poets read him: {{c|Blake}},
{{c|Emerson}}, {{c|Balzac}}; and {{c|Helen Keller}}, who could not see or hear, whose flame
Was lit by his heaven of correspondences. Make

Of him what you will. The {{x|Gaiad}} says: here is a man who was sure
He saw the other world, and the other world in him planted trees.
Every natural thing corresponds to something. The tree, the water, the pure
Light. Plant the tree. Leave the page. Walk barefoot on your knees

If you must, in a strange country, with a sack of seeds. The harvest
Is for people you will never meet. His bones are in {{p|Uppsala}} now, brought home,
In the cathedral, near {{c|Linnaeus}}'s. The farthest
Visions and the nearest names lie under one dome.


# Chapter 286: All Knowledge in One Structure

It began as a translation job. A {{p|Paris}} publisher, {{c|Le Breton}},
Wanted to put an {{x|English}} reference book, {{c|Chambers}}'s *{{x|Cyclopaedia}}*, into {{x|French}},
And hired a poor writer, the son of a cutler from {{p|Langres}}, {{c|Denis Diderot}}, a sort of wanton
Philosopher, and a mathematician, {{c|d'Alembert}}, to edit it. The wrench

Of the job in their hands: they would not translate it. They would make
A new thing: a dictionary of everything, *raisonné*, reasoned,
The sciences, the arts, the crafts, all of human knowledge, for the sake
Of changing, {{c|Diderot}} wrote, the common way of thinking. Seasoned

By prison already (he had spent three months in the fortress of {{p|Vincennes}}
For a letter on the blind that doubted God), {{c|Diderot}} knew the risk.
The first volume came out in 1751. And the chart at the front, the means
Of its order, was a tree: the tree of human knowledge, the brisk

Branches drawn from {{c|Francis Bacon}}: Memory, which grows history;
Reason, which grows philosophy; Imagination, which grows the arts.
And where was God? Theology was a twig on the branch of Reason. The mystery
Of faith was filed under the human mind. The parts

Of the world, and the parts of heaven, in one human scheme.
That was the scandal before a word was read. And the words:
Seventy-two thousand articles, over twenty years, a team
Of a hundred and fifty writers: {{c|Voltaire}}, {{c|Rousseau}} on music, the herds

Of the lesser and the forgotten, and one man, the Chevalier {{c|de Jaucourt}},
Who wrote seventeen thousand of the articles himself, for no pay,
Hiring secretaries with his own money. Hold his name. The sure
Labour of the unglamorous. And the subversion: in the way

Of a dictionary, a dull article on cannibals would say, at the end,
*See: {{x|Eucharist}}*. The cross-references were the weapon.
And the plates: eleven volumes of engravings, the most beautiful the century would send
Into the world, not of kings, but of workshops: how to step in

To the forge, the loom, the printing press, the mine, the stocking frame,
The glassworks, the pin factory, every tool drawn, every motion.
The knowledge of the hands was set beside the knowledge of the name,
And given the same dignity. That was the deepest devotion

Of the book: the artisan was a philosopher of his craft.
Of course they banned it. The king's council in 1752. In 1759
The privilege revoked, the {{c|Pope}} condemning it, the draft
Of the remaining volumes illegal. And the line

Of the story turns on two men. The head of the censorship himself,
{{c|Malesherbes}}, who believed in it, warned {{c|Diderot}} of the raid,
And hid the manuscripts in his own house, on his own shelf,
