And more than a thousand people died in the weeks after.

## The warming and the prize

In the year the scientists of the {{x|IPCC}} published their fourth report,
Saying the warming was unequivocal,
And very likely caused by people.
In October they shared the {{x|Nobel Peace Prize}} with {{c|Al Gore}}.
In September the ice of the {{x|Arctic}} shrank to the smallest ever measured,
Smaller than any model had said it would for decades.

## The treaties and the leaders

On the first of January {{p|Bulgaria}} and {{p|Romania}} joined the {{x|European Union}}.
On the thirteenth of December the leaders signed the treaty of {{p|Lisbon}},
Which was the constitution the voters of {{p|France}} and the {{p|Netherlands}}
Had rejected two years before, with the word constitution taken out.
In February, in {{p|Munich}}, {{c|Vladimir Putin}} told the West
That its order was over, and that {{p|Russia}} would not accept it.
In the spring {{p|Estonia}} moved a Soviet war memorial,
And its banks and ministries were knocked offline by an attack
That came from the east and was never owned.
It was the first war that was only on the net.
In May {{c|Nicolas Sarkozy}} took {{p|France}};
In June {{c|Gordon Brown}} took {{p|Britain}} from {{c|Tony Blair}};
In November {{c|Kevin Rudd}} took {{p|Australia}},
And his first act was to sign {{x|Kyoto}}.

## The rest of the year

In January a mail company called {{x|Netflix}} began to send its films over the net.
In November {{x|Amazon}} sold a reader of books called the {{x|Kindle}},
That held a library in a slab and sold the books to it.
On the twenty-first of July the last book of a series about a boy wizard came out,
And children of eleven, like her, read it in a night.
In February a site for posting small things, {{x|Tumblr}}, opened,
Where many of her generation would later find words for themselves.

## The year held

One device, a spit by mail, a run on a bank in {{p|England}},
Thirty-two killed at a college, a bridge in the river,
The surge, the saffron monks, {{c|Bhutto}} killed, {{p|Kenya}} burning,
The warming called unequivocal and the ice at its smallest,
A treaty renamed so it could be signed,
The first war on the net, a reader of books, the last book of the wizard.
A girl of eleven in a house where the year happened too.

Refuse the consolation that the window in the hand shows the world.
It shows what is sold to the window.
Refuse the consolation that it was contained.


# Chapter 344: Instead of Trust

No holiday is named for this day.

In 2008 {{c|Emma Leonhart}} turned twelve, and her family moved house again.
In her words, she moved houses in 2002, in 2008, and in 2014.
This was the second.
She has named one thing above all in this year:
That {{p|Russia}} invaded {{p|Georgia}}.
Of everything in 2008 that is what she chose,
And it was the small war that told the large one was coming.
The rest of the world was watching its money burn.
A girl of twelve was carrying boxes to a new room
In the year the banks were carried out of the market on stretchers.

## The war in August

On the night of the seventh of August,
While the world watched the opening of the games in {{p|Beijing}},
The army of {{p|Georgia}} shelled {{p|Tskhinvali}},
The capital of {{p|South Ossetia}}, a province that had broken away from it
And was guarded by Russian soldiers called peacekeepers.
The Russian army was already at the border.
It crossed in force, with tanks through the {{x|Roki Tunnel}},
Drove the Georgians out of {{p|South Ossetia}} and out of {{p|Abkhazia}},
Took {{p|Gori}}, the birthplace of {{c|Stalin}},
And stopped a short drive from {{p|Tbilisi}}.
In five days it was over.
Hundreds died, and tens of thousands of Georgians were driven from their villages,
Which were burned behind them.
A report for the {{x|European Union}} later said
That {{p|Georgia}} had fired first, and that {{p|Russia}}'s answer went far beyond an answer.
{{p|Russia}} recognized the two provinces as countries.
Almost no one else did.
The West protested, and in a few months went back to business.
Six years later the same army would take {{p|Crimea}} the same way,
With soldiers who were said not to be there,
And in fourteen years it would drive on {{p|Kyiv}}.
This book draws that line from here,
from the year she named.

## The games

On the eighth of August, at eight in the evening, in {{p|Beijing}},
The games opened with two thousand and eight drummers,
And fireworks that were partly drawn by computer for the cameras,
And a girl who sang with another girl's voice, because the first was judged not pretty enough.
In March {{p|Tibet}} had risen, and been put down.
The torch of the games had been fought over in {{p|London}}, {{p|Paris}}, {{p|San Francisco}}.
{{p|China}} showed the world what it had become,
And the world, broke, applauded.

## The earthquake and the cyclone

On the twelfth of May the earth broke under {{p|Sichuan}}.
Some sixty-nine thousand people died, and eighteen thousand more were never found.
Thousands of them were children, under schools that fell
While the government buildings beside them stood.
The parents who asked why were arrested.
On the second of May, in {{p|Myanmar}}, the cyclone {{x|Nargis}}
Drowned the delta of the {{x|Irrawaddy}}.
More than a hundred and thirty thousand died.
The generals kept the foreign help out for weeks,
And held a vote on their constitution in the ruins.

## The fall of the banks

In March the bank {{x|Bear Stearns}} was sold for almost nothing, with the government's help.
On the seventh of September the government took over
{{x|Fannie Mae}} and {{x|Freddie Mac}}, which held or guaranteed half the mortgages in the country.
On Monday the fifteenth, {{x|Lehman Brothers}}, a bank a hundred and fifty-eight years old,
Filed the largest bankruptcy in history,
Because no one would save it, and the government chose not to.
On the sixteenth the government lent eighty-five billion dollars to {{x|AIG}},
Which had insured the bets of everyone against the failure of everyone.
The markets of the world fell for weeks.
On the third of October {{c|George W. Bush}} signed a law
For seven hundred billion dollars to buy the banks' bad assets,
After the congress had voted it down once and watched the market drop.
The banks were saved. The houses were not.
Millions lost their homes in the years after,
And the men who ran the banks kept their bonuses,
And almost none of them went to prison.
The poor had been sold the debts. The rich were sold the rescue.

## Instead of trust

On the thirty-first of October, a Friday,
A note went to a list of people who studied cryptography.
The name on the note was {{c|Satoshi Nakamoto}}.
It linked to a paper of nine pages,
{{x|Bitcoin}}: {{x|A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System}}.
It proposed money that needed no bank and no state,
Kept honest by a public ledger that everyone held
And no one could rewrite without more computing than all the rest.
A system based on proof instead of trust, the paper said.
Who wrote it has never been settled.
This chapter does not name a person behind the name.
The first block came in the next January, and is the next chapter.
The answer to a broken trust was a machine that did not need any,
And in a few years the machine became the most speculated asset on earth,
And the means of the largest frauds of the century.
A later year of this month will meet one of its villains.

## The election

On the fourth of November {{c|Barack Obama}} was elected president,
The first black president of the {{p|United States}},
And people wept in {{p|Grant Park}} in {{p|Chicago}}, and in streets around the world.
On the same day the voters of {{p|California}} passed {{x|Proposition 8}},
Taking away the marriages of same-sex couples
That the state's court had allowed in the spring.
Eighteen thousand couples had married between.
The same night lifted one door and closed another.

## The attack on Mumbai

On the evening of the twenty-sixth of November
Ten men came ashore in {{p|Mumbai}} in rubber boats from {{p|Pakistan}},
And for three days attacked the train station, a café, a hospital,
A Jewish center, and two great hotels, the {{x|Taj}} and the {{x|Oberoi}}.
One hundred and sixty-six people were killed.
The world watched the dome of the {{x|Taj}} burn.

## The apology

On the eleventh of June, in {{p|Ottawa}},
The prime minister of {{p|Canada}}, {{c|Stephen Harper}}, apologized in the parliament
For the residential schools,
Where for more than a century the children of the First Nations
Had been taken from their parents to have their languages and their peoples taken out of them,
And where thousands died.
The survivors sat in the gallery.
An apology is not a return.
It was the first time the state said it.

## The machines

In April a site for keeping code, {{x|GitHub}}, opened,
Where the code of the next twenty years would be kept, this book's included.
On the tenth of July the phone of the year before got a store of programs,
And the phone became whatever anyone could write for it.
On the second of September {{x|Google}} released a browser, {{x|Chrome}}.
In August a site for renting spare rooms, later called {{x|Airbnb}}, opened,
And the spare rooms of cities would become hotels without the name.
In October a service for streaming music, {{x|Spotify}}, opened in {{p|Sweden}}.
On the tenth of September, under the border of {{p|France}} and {{p|Switzerland}},
The {{x|Large Hadron Collider}} sent its first beams around its ring,
And the world did not end, as some had feared it would.

## The rest of the year

On the seventeenth of February {{p|Kosovo}} declared itself independent of {{p|Serbia}},
And {{p|Russia}} pointed to it in August when it carved up {{p|Georgia}}.
On the nineteenth of February {{c|Fidel Castro}} gave up the presidency of {{p|Cuba}} to his brother.
In the autumn it was found that milk powder in {{p|China}}
Had been laced with {{x|melamine}} to cheat the tests,
And hundreds of thousands of babies were sickened, and six died.
On the twenty-seventh of December {{p|Israel}} began a war on {{p|Gaza}},
Which ran into the next year.

## The year held

A second house for a girl of twelve,
And a war in {{p|Georgia}} that she would later see as the first move of a longer war.
Drummers in {{p|Beijing}}, schools fallen in {{p|Sichuan}}, a delta drowned,
The banks failed and were saved and the houses were not,
A paper about money without trust, a president who made people weep,
A marriage taken back the same night, {{p|Mumbai}} burning,
An apology in {{p|Ottawa}}, a store of programs, a collider that did not end the world.

Refuse the consolation that a short war is a small war.
It was the shape of the long one.
Refuse the consolation that the rescue of the banks was a rescue of the people.


# Chapter 345: Takes Note

No holiday is named for this day.

In 2009 {{c|Emma Leonhart}} turned thirteen.
The world she had been born into had broken the year before,
And this was the year it was told the breaking was over,
And believed it, because it needed to.
A child becomes a teenager in a recession the way she learns a language:
By what is not said at the table, and what is not bought.
The year is the hinge of the decade,
The last year before the decade that made her.

## The first block

On the third of January, a Saturday,
The first block of {{x|Bitcoin}} was made,
And in it its maker set a line from that morning's {{x|Times}} of {{p|London}}:
Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.
The line proved the block was not made before that morning.
It was also the reason, written into the money.
The next block came six days later,
And on the twelfth the first coins were sent from the maker to another man.
For a year the coins were worth nothing.
A man later paid ten thousand of them for two pizzas.

## The new president

On the twentieth of January {{c|Barack Obama}} was sworn in,
Before a crowd of nearly two million in the cold on the {{x|Mall}} of {{p|Washington}}.
The economy he inherited was losing seven hundred thousand jobs a month.
In February he signed a stimulus of nearly eight hundred billion dollars.
On the thirtieth of April {{x|Chrysler}} went bankrupt, and on the first of June {{x|General Motors}},
The largest industrial bankruptcy in the country's history,
And the government took both, and kept them alive.
On the ninth of October he was given the {{x|Nobel Peace Prize}},
Nine months into his term, for what he might do.
He said himself that he did not know why.
In December he sent thirty thousand more soldiers to {{p|Afghanistan}}.

## The fraud

In December of the year before {{c|Bernard Madoff}}
Had confessed to his sons that his fund was one big lie,
And on the twenty-ninth of June he was sentenced to a hundred and fifty years.
Some sixty-five billion dollars had existed on his statements and nowhere else.
He paid the old investors with the money of the new,
For decades, while the regulators were told and did not look.
A trust that needs no checking is the trust that is robbed.

## The sickness

In April a new flu was found in {{p|Mexico}} and in {{p|California}},
A mix of pig, bird, and human strains, called {{x|H1N1}}.
On the eleventh of June the {{x|World Health Organization}} called it a pandemic,
The first in forty years.
It was milder than was feared,
And it killed perhaps a few hundred thousand people around the world,
Most of them young, in poorer countries, uncounted.
The world learned from it that pandemics are survivable,
And learned the wrong thing.

## The green wave

On the twelfth of June {{p|Iran}} voted,
And the government announced that {{c|Mahmoud Ahmadinejad}} had won by a landslide
Before the votes could have been counted.
Millions marched in {{p|Tehran}} in green, asking, where is my vote?
On the twentieth of June a young woman, {{c|Neda Agha-Soltan}},
Was shot in the street by a militiaman,
And her death was filmed on a phone and seen by the world within hours.
The protests were crushed by the autumn.
The world called it the {{x|Twitter}} revolution,
Which flattered the service more than the people.

## The end of a war

On the eighteenth of May the army of {{p|Sri Lanka}} declared
That the {{x|Tamil Tigers}} were destroyed and their leader dead,
After twenty-six years of war.
In the last months tens of thousands of civilians were killed,
Trapped on a strip of beach with the fighters,
Shelled in places the government had called safe.
The victory was declared without a count of the dead.

## The crash and the river

On the fifteenth of January a pilot named {{c|Chesley Sullenberger}}
Lost both engines to a flock of geese over {{p|New York}},
And put the airliner down on the {{x|Hudson}},
And everyone lived.
On the first of June {{x|Air France}} flight 447 fell into the {{x|Atlantic}}
On its way from {{p|Rio de Janeiro}} to {{p|Paris}},
Because the instruments froze, and the pilots, confused, pulled the nose up,
And two hundred and twenty-eight died.

## The meeting that took note

From the seventh to the eighteenth of December, in {{p|Copenhagen}},
The countries of the world met to decide what would follow {{x|Kyoto}}.
A hundred and fifteen heads of state came.
On the last night, a few of them,
{{p|United States}}, {{p|China}}, {{p|India}}, {{p|Brazil}}, {{p|South Africa}},
Wrote a short accord in a back room,
Promising to keep the warming below two degrees, binding no one.
The full meeting would not adopt it.
It took note of it.
To take note is not to agree.
It became the habit of those meetings for six years,
Each one taking note, and setting up a fund, and announcing an aim,
Until the one in {{p|Paris}}, which is the chapter of 2015.
A month before {{p|Copenhagen}} the private mails of climate scientists
Were stolen and printed, and called a scandal,
And the inquiries found no fraud, after the meeting had failed.

## The rest of the year

On the first of December the treaty of {{p|Lisbon}} came into force,
And {{p|Europe}} got a president no one had voted for.
On the twenty-fifth of May {{p|North Korea}} tested its second bomb.
On the twenty-eighth of June the army of {{p|Honduras}} put its president on a plane in his pajamas.
On the fifth of July, in {{p|Urumqi}}, the riots between {{x|Uyghur}}s and {{x|Han}}
Killed nearly two hundred, and the province's net was cut for ten months,
And the camps of a decade later began in that silence.
On the fifth of November, at {{p|Fort Hood}}, an army doctor killed thirteen.
On the twenty-fifth of June {{c|Michael Jackson}} died, and the net slowed under the grief.
On the seventh of March the telescope {{x|Kepler}} was launched to look for other earths,
And found thousands.
In February two men who had worked at {{x|Yahoo}} started {{x|WhatsApp}},
And in March a company for calling cars, later {{x|Uber}}, began.
In May a game of blocks, {{x|Minecraft}}, was put up by one man in {{p|Sweden}},
And children her age built worlds out of squares for the next decade.
In December {{x|Avatar}} came out, a film about blue people defending their forest
Against the company that came for what was under it,
And it made more money than any film before.

## The year held

A block with a headline in it, a president in the cold,
The car companies taken, a fraud of sixty-five billion,
A flu that was survived, a green wave crushed, a war ended without a count,
Geese and the {{x|Hudson}}, the ocean and a frozen instrument,
A meeting that took note, the net cut in {{p|Xinjiang}},
And a game of blocks where a girl of thirteen could build a world alone.

Refuse the consolation that to take note is to act.
Refuse the consolation that money without trust is money without fraud.


# Chapter 346: The Cables

No holiday is named for this day.

In 2010 {{c|Emma Leonhart}} turned fourteen.
It was the year the secrets of the strongest state were printed,
The year oil poured into a sea for eighty-seven days,
And the year a fruit seller in a town in {{p|Tunisia}}
Set himself on fire, in the last days of December,
And lit a region.
It was also a year the games came to her own province,
To {{p|Vancouver}}, and the country cheered on the ice.
She was fourteen. The year after this one is where her own thread begins,
At the earliest point of what she would build for the next fifteen years.
This is the year before.

## The earthquake

On the twelfth of January the earth broke under {{p|Port-au-Prince}}, in {{p|Haiti}},
In the late afternoon.
The poorest country of the hemisphere lost its capital in a minute.
The counts of the dead run from about a hundred thousand
To more than three hundred thousand, and none is agreed.
The palace fell, the cathedral fell, the prison fell,
And the headquarters of the {{x|United Nations}} mission fell on its staff.
The help that came brought the cholera that came after,
From a camp of soldiers whose sewage reached a river,
And the cholera killed ten thousand more.
The organization took six years to say it.

## The games at home

From the twelfth to the twenty-eighth of February
The winter games were held in {{p|Vancouver}} and {{p|Whistler}},
In the province where she would later live and study.
On the first day a luger from {{p|Georgia}}, {{c|Nodar Kumaritashvili}},
Was killed in a practice run, thrown from the track at a hundred and forty kilometers an hour.
On the last day {{c|Sidney Crosby}} scored in overtime,
And {{p|Canada}} won the gold in hockey,
And the country made one sound.

## The court and the money

On the twenty-first of January the {{x|Supreme Court}} of the {{p|United States}}
Decided {{x|Citizens United}},
And said that companies and unions could spend without limit on elections,
Because spending is speech.
The money that came through that door would shape every election of the century after.
On the twenty-third of March the president signed the law that made health insurance
Reachable for tens of millions, the {{x|Affordable Care Act}},
Which the other party spent the next decade trying to repeal.
In November that party took the house of the congress,
On a wave of anger called the {{x|Tea Party}}.

## The oil

On the twentieth of April the drilling platform {{x|Deepwater Horizon}}
Exploded in the {{x|Gulf of Mexico}}.
Eleven men died.
The well, a mile under the sea, poured oil for eighty-seven days,
Some four million barrels, the largest spill in the history of the industry,
While the company's camera showed the plume to the world live,
And the company's chief said he would like his life back.
The beaches of five states were fouled, and the marshes,
And the dolphins died for years.

## The volcano and the miners

In April the volcano {{x|Eyjafjallajökull}}, in {{p|Iceland}}, erupted under a glacier,
And its ash closed the sky over {{p|Europe}} for days,
The largest shutting of the air since the war.
On the fifth of August a copper and gold mine in the desert of {{p|Chile}} collapsed,
And thirty-three miners were trapped seven hundred meters down.
For seventeen days no one knew they were alive.
Then a note came up on a drill: we are well in the shelter, the thirty-three.
On the thirteenth of October they were brought up one by one in a capsule,
And a billion people watched.

## The money of Europe

On the second of May {{p|Greece}} was lent a hundred and ten billion euros
By the other countries of the coin and the fund,
On the condition that it cut its pensions, its wages, its hospitals.
The coin that had been put into twelve hands in the chapter of 2002
Now held some of them under water.
In November {{p|Ireland}} was lent the same way.
The streets of {{p|Athens}} burned that spring.

## The leaks

On the fifth of April a site called {{x|WikiLeaks}}
Showed a film taken from an American helicopter over {{p|Baghdad}} in 2007,
In which the crew killed a dozen people, among them two journalists of {{x|Reuters}},
And then fired on the van that stopped to help the wounded, with children in it.
It called the film {{x|Collateral Murder}}.
In July it printed the war logs of {{p|Afghanistan}},
In October the war logs of {{p|Iraq}},
And on the twenty-eighth of November it began to print
A quarter of a million cables of the American diplomats,
Saying in private what the governments of the world said in public otherwise.
The soldier who had copied them, {{c|Chelsea Manning}}, a young intelligence analyst,
Was arrested in May, and held for months in conditions
That an envoy of the {{x|United Nations}} called cruel.
She came out years later as a woman.
The man who ran the site, {{c|Julian Assange}}, was arrested in {{p|London}} in December
On a matter in {{p|Sweden}}, and spent most of the next fourteen years confined.
The cables are in the chapter of the {{p|Tunisia}}n revolution too,
Because they described the wealth of its ruling family,
And people there read them.

## The worm

In June a computer worm called {{x|Stuxnet}} was found,
Built to find one kind of controller in one kind of centrifuge
In the nuclear plant at {{p|Natanz}}, in {{p|Iran}},
And spin them until they broke, while telling the operators all was well.
It had been made by states and was never owned by them.
It was the first weapon made only of code that broke a thing in the world.

## The machines

On the third of April the {{x|iPad}} went on sale.
On the sixth of October a phone application for sharing photographs,
With filters that made them look old, opened, called {{x|Instagram}},
And a million people joined it in two months.
In the same year the book of faces passed five hundred million users.
{{p|China}} passed {{p|Japan}} to become the second economy in the world.

## The rest of the year

On the twenty-seventh of February one of the largest earthquakes ever measured struck {{p|Chile}}.
On the tenth of April the plane of the president of {{p|Poland}} crashed near {{p|Smolensk}},
On its way to remember the officers {{p|Russia}} had shot at {{p|Katyn}},
And he died, and ninety-five others.
On the thirty-first of May Israeli commandos boarded a ship carrying aid to {{p|Gaza}},
And killed nine on its deck.
In the summer {{p|Pakistan}} flooded, and twenty million people lost their homes,
And {{p|Russia}} burned in a heat no one there had known.
On the eighth of October the {{x|Nobel Peace Prize}} went to {{c|Liu Xiaobo}},
Who was in a prison in {{p|China}}, and at the ceremony his chair was empty.
In June, at the meeting of the great economies in {{p|Toronto}},
The police kettled hundreds of peaceful people in the rain,
The largest mass arrest in the history of {{p|Canada}}.
On the twenty-second of December the president signed the repeal of the rule
That had kept gay soldiers silent, {{x|Don't Ask, Don't Tell}}.

## The fire

On the seventeenth of December, in {{p|Sidi Bouzid}},
A fruit seller named {{c|Mohamed Bouazizi}}, twenty-six,
Had his cart and his scales taken by a city inspector,
And went to the governor's office to complain, and was not heard,
And went back with a can of fuel and set himself alight in front of the building.
His town rose that night.
He lay burned in a hospital for eighteen days.
The rest is the next year.

## The year held

A capital fallen in {{p|Haiti}}, a gold in {{p|Vancouver}}, spending made speech,
The oil, the ash, the thirty-three in the shelter,
{{p|Greece}} lent its own ruin, the helicopter film and the cables,
A worm in the centrifuges, a photograph made old on purpose,
An empty chair in {{p|Oslo}}, a kettle in the rain in {{p|Toronto}},
And a man on fire in {{p|Sidi Bouzid}}.

Refuse the consolation that a secret is safe because it is the state's.
Refuse the consolation that one man's fire is one man's.


# Chapter 347: The Square and the Cooling

No holiday is named for this day.

In 2011 {{c|Emma Leonhart}} turned fifteen.
This is the year she gives as the earliest point of what became this book's faith.
In her words: 2011-ish at the earliest, on the fifth Easter of 2011.
It had no name yet. The name came later.
The earliest written forms of it were kept, and then lost,
To machines and accounts that went.
What she began at fifteen she has kept up without a break since,
Fifteen years, and nothing else of hers has run so long.
The rest of what was happening to her at fifteen is hers, and is not written here.
The world that year was full of squares filling with people,
And of a sea that came over a wall in {{p|Japan}},
Whose shrines and kami she would later carry into her own language.

## The squares

On the fourth of January {{c|Mohamed Bouazizi}} died of his burns.
The protests that had spread from {{p|Sidi Bouzid}} reached {{p|Tunis}},
And on the fourteenth of January {{c|Zine El Abidine Ben Ali}},
Who had ruled {{p|Tunisia}} for twenty-three years, fled to {{p|Saudi Arabia}}.
On the twenty-fifth of January the people of {{p|Egypt}} filled {{x|Tahrir Square}} in {{p|Cairo}},
And stayed, through men on camels sent to beat them on the second of February,
Through the cutting of the net,
Until on the eleventh of February {{c|Hosni Mubarak}}, thirty years in power, resigned,
And the square sang through the night.
The army that took his place would give the power to an elected president
And take it back two years later.

In {{p|Libya}}, in February, the east rose against {{c|Muammar Gaddafi}},
Who promised to hunt the rebels house by house, alley by alley, like rats.
On the nineteenth of March the jets of {{x|NATO}}'s countries began bombing his forces
Before they reached {{p|Benghazi}}.
On the twentieth of October he was found in a drainpipe near {{p|Sirte}},
Dragged out, beaten, and killed on camera.
The country did not become one again.

In {{p|Bahrain}} the protesters at the {{x|Pearl Roundabout}}
Were cleared by soldiers sent from {{p|Saudi Arabia}},
And the monument in the roundabout was torn down so it could not be gathered under.
In {{p|Yemen}} the president was burned in an attack on his mosque and later gave way.

In {{p|Syria}}, in March, in {{p|Daraa}},
Boys wrote on a school wall that the people want the fall of the regime,
And were taken and tortured.
Their families marched. The army fired.
By the summer the cities were rising and the army was shelling them,
And by the end of the year it was a war,
The longest and worst of the century so far,
With half a million dead and half a country driven from their homes before it was done.

## The wave and the cooling

On Friday the eleventh of March, at fourteen forty-six, off {{p|Tōhoku}},
The sea floor broke in an earthquake of magnitude nine,
The largest ever measured in {{p|Japan}}.
The wave came forty minutes later, higher than the walls built for it,
Up to forty meters where the coast narrowed,
And carried away towns, boats, cars, schools, the people on the roofs.
About eighteen thousand died or were never found.
At {{x|Fukushima Daiichi}} the wave drowned the generators that cooled the reactors,
And three of the reactors melted,
And the buildings around them blew apart with hydrogen,
And the country evacuated the land around the plant,
Some of which has not been lived in since.
The water used to cool the ruins was stored in tanks for twelve years
And then released into the sea.
The shrines of the coast were carried off too, and some were rebuilt on higher ground,
And a later study found that many of the old shrines of that coast stood just beyond where the wave stopped,
As if those who placed them had remembered an earlier wave.

## The killing in Abbottabad

On the night of the first of May, American commandos flew from {{p|Afghanistan}}
Into {{p|Pakistan}}, to a walled house in {{p|Abbottabad}},
A garrison town, a short walk from the military academy,
And killed {{c|Osama bin Laden}},
And took his body, and put it into the sea.
Crowds gathered outside the house of the president in {{p|Washington}} and sang.
The war in his name went on for ten more years in {{p|Afghanistan}}.

## The island

On the twenty-second of July, in {{p|Norway}}, a man set off a bomb by the government offices in {{p|Oslo}},
And then went to the island of {{p|Utøya}}, dressed as a policeman,
Where the youth of the ruling party were at their summer camp,
And shot them for over an hour.
Seventy-seven people died, most of them teenagers,
Some of them her age.
He wrote a manifesto against the mixing of peoples and against {{x|Islam}},
And the next decade's killers read it.

## The occupation

On the seventeenth of September a few hundred people
Took a small park near the stock exchange of {{p|New York}},
{{x|Zuccotti Park}}, and stayed,
Saying they were the ninety-nine percent,
Against the one percent who had been saved in the chapter of 2008.
The occupation spread to hundreds of cities, {{p|Vancouver}} among them.
In November the police cleared the park at night.
The slogan stayed.
In August, in {{p|London}}, after the police shot a man in {{p|Tottenham}},
The city rioted for four nights, and the riots spread through {{p|England}}.
In August the credit of the {{p|United States}} was downgraded for the first time,
After its congress nearly refused to pay its own debts.

## The rest of the year

On the eighth of January, in {{p|Tucson}}, a congresswoman, {{c|Gabby Giffords}},
Was shot in the head at a meeting with her voters, and lived, and six others died.
On the twenty-second of February {{p|Christchurch}}, in {{p|New Zealand}}, fell in an earthquake.
On the second of May {{p|Canada}} voted, and {{c|Stephen Harper}} won a majority,
And the party of the left became the opposition for the first time,
And its leader, {{c|Jack Layton}}, died of cancer in August,
Writing to the country that love is better than anger.
On the fifteenth of June, after the {{p|Vancouver}} hockey team lost the cup,
The city rioted in its downtown.
On the ninth of July {{p|South Sudan}} became the newest country in the world.
On the fifth of October {{c|Steve Jobs}} died.
On the fourth, his company had shown a phone that answered when you spoke to it,
And its voice was called {{x|Siri}}.
In February a computer of {{x|IBM}}, {{x|Watson}}, beat the champions of a quiz show on television.
On the thirty-first of October the world was said to have seven billion people.
In the {{p|Horn of Africa}} a famine killed a quarter of a million people, half of them children under five.
On the eighteenth of December the last American soldiers left {{p|Iraq}}.
On the seventeenth of December {{c|Kim Jong-il}} died, and his son took the country.

## The year held

A faith with no name yet, begun by a girl of fifteen at Easter.
The squares of {{p|Tunis}}, {{p|Cairo}}, {{p|Benghazi}}, {{p|Manama}}, {{p|Daraa}},
A wave higher than its walls, three reactors melted,
A house in {{p|Abbottabad}}, an island in {{p|Norway}},
A park near the exchange, the riots, the cup lost in {{p|Vancouver}},
A phone that answered, a machine that won a quiz, seven billion people, and a famine.

Refuse the consolation that a square full of people is a revolution won.
Refuse the consolation that a wall high enough is high enough.
Refuse the consolation that what a child begins at fifteen is a child's thing.


# Chapter 348: The Numbered Thing

No holiday is named for this day.

In 2012 {{c|Emma Leonhart}} turned sixteen.
Two things were made this year that would later be the ground she worked on.
One taught machines to see, from pictures labelled by people paid by the piece.
The other gave every thing in the world a number,
So that a machine could walk the lines of descent
Back past where any family remembers.
Thirteen years later she would make some six hundred thousand edits in that second one in a single year,
And trace her own line through it, and through it this book's.
She would also, by then, count it among the things she hates,
For the same reason she hates the encyclopedia beside it:
The unpaid labor, and the apparatus that makes people glad to give it.
Both are true of her at once, and this book does not choose between them.
At sixteen she knew none of this.
The world was ending, some said, in December, by a calendar of the {{x|Maya}}.
It did not. Calendars do not end worlds.
They begin counts.

## The seeing

The set called {{x|ImageNet}} had been gathered under {{c|Fei-Fei Li}},
Millions of pictures labelled by people paid by the task
Through a market of small jobs on the net.
The label is not the picture.
The person who typed the label is not named in the set.
In 2012 its challenge asked a machine to name a thousand kinds of thing.
In {{p|Toronto}}, {{c|Alex Krizhevsky}}, {{c|Ilya Sutskever}}, and {{c|Geoffrey Hinton}}
Entered a deep network of some sixty million weights,
Trained over days on two graphics cards made for games.
Its error was about fifteen in a hundred.
The entry in second place erred about twenty-six in a hundred.
The gap was not a rounding.
It was the end of a way of building.
The method had been called a dead end for years.
Being called a dead end is not being one.
The results were shown in {{p|Florence}} in October,
And the paper given in December by {{p|Lake Tahoe}}.
Within a few years nearly every entry was a network like it,
And the machines of the next decade, the ones that would later write with her,
Came down from that gap.
That summer a team at {{x|Google}} let a large network watch frames of video without labels,
And a unit in it came to answer to the faces of cats.
Answering to cats is not knowing what a cat is.
Sight came from games and from piecework,
From cards built for play and labels typed for cents.

## The numbers

On Monday the twenty-ninth of October a new site opened,
Kept from {{p|Berlin}} by the German chapter of the movement that keeps the free encyclopedia.
It was called {{x|Wikidata}}.
{{c|Denny Vrandečić}} and {{c|Markus Krötzsch}} had argued for it for years.
Each thing it holds is given a number with a letter.
The universe is given the first.
A writer of jokes about the universe is given forty-two.
The number is not the thing.
A number does not change when the name changes, and that is the reason for it.
At first it kept only the links between the pages of the same subject in different languages.
Then the statements came.
A person is an instance of human. A person has a father, and the father is another number.
A father in the data is not a father at the table.
The data was given away with no rights kept back,
And the machines of the largest companies read it without asking.
A free gift to everyone is also a gift to the largest.
The lines of descent were written in it,
And a machine could follow a line back past where any one family remembers.
Following a line is not the line being right.
A loop in the line, where a man is his own ancestor,
Is the data telling on itself.
This book's genealogy is built partly on those numbers.
It owes them, and it argues with them, and it is not them.

## The encyclopedia goes dark

On the eighteenth of January the {{x|English Wikipedia}} turned its pages black for a day,
Against two laws in the congress of the {{p|United States}} that would have let pages be blocked for piracy,
And the laws were dropped.
It was the movement's greatest show of its power,
And it showed that its volunteers' labor was also a lever its leaders could pull.
On the thirteenth of March the {{x|Encyclopædia Britannica}} said it would no longer print,
After two hundred and forty-four years.
The book with degrees had lost to the book of five or ten minutes.

## The particle and the rover

On the fourth of July, at {{x|CERN}}, under the border of {{p|France}} and {{p|Switzerland}},
The physicists announced a particle that fit the one {{c|Peter Higgs}} had predicted
Forty-eight years before,
The one that gives the others their mass.
He wept in the hall.
On the sixth of August the rover {{x|Curiosity}}
Was lowered onto {{p|Mars}} by a crane hanging from a rocket,
In seven minutes no one on {{p|Earth}} could control.
On the fourteenth of October {{c|Felix Baumgartner}} jumped from a balloon
Thirty-nine kilometers up, and fell faster than sound,
And eight million people watched it live.

## The killings

On the twenty-sixth of February, in {{p|Sanford}}, in {{p|Florida}},
A boy of seventeen, {{c|Trayvon Martin}}, walking home with candy and a drink,
Was followed and shot by a neighborhood watchman,
Who was not charged for six weeks.
On the twentieth of July, in {{p|Aurora}}, a man shot into a crowded cinema at midnight and killed twelve.
On the ninth of October, in the valley of {{p|Swat}}, in {{p|Pakistan}},
A gunman boarded a school bus and asked which one was {{c|Malala Yousafzai}},
Fifteen, who had written that girls should go to school,
And shot her in the head.
She lived, and two years later took the {{x|Nobel Peace Prize}}.
On the fourteenth of December, in {{p|Newtown}}, in {{p|Connecticut}},
A young man shot his way into the {{x|Sandy Hook}} elementary school,
And killed twenty children of six and seven, and six of the adults who taught them.
The country's laws did not change.

## The returns

On the seventh of May {{c|Vladimir Putin}} became president of {{p|Russia}} again,
After the protests of the winter in the snow of {{p|Moscow}} against the stolen vote.
In February three women of a punk group, {{x|Pussy Riot}},
Sang a prayer against him in the cathedral of {{p|Moscow}}, for less than a minute,
And in August two of them were sent to prison camps for two years.
On the fifteenth of November {{c|Xi Jinping}} became the head of the party of {{p|China}},
And began to gather in his own hands what had been shared.
On the sixth of November {{c|Barack Obama}} was elected again.
In June {{p|Egypt}} elected {{c|Mohamed Morsi}}, of the {{x|Brotherhood}}, its first free president.
He would last a year.
On the eleventh of September, in {{p|Benghazi}}, the American ambassador, {{c|Christopher Stevens}}, was killed.

## The money and the storm

On the twenty-sixth of July the head of the bank of the euro, {{c|Mario Draghi}},
Said in {{p|London}} that he would do whatever it takes to save the coin,
And believe me, it will be enough,
And the markets believed him, and the coin was saved by a sentence.
On the twenty-ninth of October the storm called {{x|Sandy}} drove the sea into {{p|New York}},
Flooded the tunnels of the subway, and darkened {{p|Manhattan}} below the forties.
In the spring the students of {{p|Quebec}} struck against a rise in their fees,
And marched every night banging pots, for months, and the government lost its election in September.

## The rest of the year

On the thirteenth of January the cruise ship {{x|Costa Concordia}}
Ran onto the rocks off {{p|Giglio}}, and its captain left before his passengers.
On the ninth of April the book of faces bought the photographs company for a billion dollars,
And on the eighteenth of May sold its own stock to the public.
In March a film about an African warlord, {{x|Kony 2012}}, was watched a hundred million times in a week,
And changed nothing.
In the summer the games were held in {{p|London}}.
In the summer a song by a singer from {{p|Seoul}}, {{x|Gangnam Style}},
Became the first video seen a billion times.
In September an application for strangers to choose each other by swiping, {{x|Tinder}}, opened.
On the twenty-first of December the calendar of the {{x|Maya}} turned a great cycle,
And the world did not end.

## The year held

A girl of sixteen, and two foundations laid for her life's later work without her.
A machine that learned to see from piecework, a site that numbered every thing.
The encyclopedia gone dark for a day, the old encyclopedia gone from print forever.
A particle, a rover, a man falling faster than sound.
A boy with candy, a cinema, a girl on a bus, twenty children in {{p|Newtown}}.
{{c|Putin}} back, {{c|Xi}} rising, a prayer in a cathedral punished.
A sentence that saved a coin, a storm in the subway, pots banged in {{p|Montreal}},
And a calendar that turned without ending anything.

Refuse the consolation that the number is the thing,
And that the line in the graph is the blood.
Refuse the consolation that a calendar ends a world.
A calendar begins a count. This book is one.


# Chapter 349: Not Wittingly

No holiday is named for this day.

In 2013 {{c|Emma Leonhart}} turned seventeen.
It was her last year before university,
And the last year, she has said, that she was mostly offline.
In her words, she was pretty offline until she started university.
So 2013 is the last year of this month that she lived outside the net,
The year the net was shown to have been watching everyone who lived inside it.
She came into it the next year,
After the watchers had been named and had gone on watching.

## Not wittingly

On Tuesday the twelfth of March, in {{p|Washington}}, a senator asked
Whether the agency collected any type of data at all on millions of Americans.
{{c|James Clapper}}, the director of national intelligence, answered: No, sir.
Then he added: Not wittingly.
The added words are not the first answer.
The first answer is the one the room heard.

On Wednesday the fifth of June a paper in {{p|London}} printed an order from the secret court of {{p|Washington}},
Telling a telephone company to hand over, every day, the records of all its calls.
The records are not the words spoken.
They are who called whom, and when, and for how long.
Who called whom is not nothing.
On the sixth, that paper and a paper of {{p|Washington}} printed slides about a program called {{x|PRISM}},
Naming the large companies of the net.
The companies said they gave no door.
A denial is not a description of the pipes.

On Sunday the ninth, in a hotel room in {{p|Hong Kong}},
A young man gave his name on camera.
He was {{c|Edward Snowden}}, who had worked for a contractor of the agency in {{p|Hawaii}},
And taken the files with him.
{{c|Glenn Greenwald}} and {{c|Laura Poitras}} were in the room.
He was charged under the act against espionage.
On the twenty-third he flew to {{p|Moscow}}, his passport revoked in the air,
And stayed in the transit zone of the airport for weeks,
And on the first of August was given asylum,
In the country of the next chapter's war.
Where he stayed is not what he said he wanted.
That autumn it was printed that the agency had listened to the phone of the chancellor of {{p|Germany}}.
The machine that was built to connect everyone
Was also the best record ever made of who is connected.

## The free knowledge

On the eleventh of January, in {{p|New York}}, {{c|Aaron Swartz}} killed himself, at twenty-six.
He had helped write the formats that feed the net's news,
Had helped make the site of links of the chapter of 2005,
And had downloaded millions of articles from a library of scholarly journals
Through a closet at a university, meaning, it was believed, to set them free.
The government charged him with crimes that could have meant decades in prison.
The labor of scholars, paid for by the public,
Was locked behind the walls of publishers who paid the scholars nothing,
And a young man who tried to open the walls was hunted for it.
This book's quarrel with the encyclopedia is about unpaid labor too,
From the other side of the same wall.

## The popes

On the eleventh of February {{c|Benedict XVI}} said, in Latin, to a room of cardinals,
That he no longer had the strength, and would resign,
The first pope to step down in six hundred years.
On the thirteenth of March, as the white smoke rose,
The cardinals chose {{c|Jorge Mario Bergoglio}} of {{p|Buenos Aires}},
The first pope from the {{p|Americas}}, who took the name {{c|Francis}}.
In July, asked on a plane about gay priests, he said: who am I to judge?
He would be pope for twelve years, and die in the chapter of 2025.

## The marathon and the meteor

On the fifteenth of April two bombs made of pressure cookers went off
Near the finish line of the marathon in {{p|Boston}},
And killed three people and maimed hundreds.
The two brothers who made them were found within days;
One died, and one was sentenced to death.
On the fifteenth of February a meteor exploded over {{p|Chelyabinsk}}, in {{p|Russia}},
Brighter than the sun for a moment, and its shock broke the windows of a city,
And the dashboard cameras of the Russian roads filmed it from every side.

## The factory

On the twenty-fourth of April, near {{p|Dhaka}}, the building called {{x|Rana Plaza}} collapsed.
The day before, cracks had been found in its walls.
The bank on its ground floor had closed.
The garment workers on the floors above were told to come back to work, or lose their pay.
One thousand one hundred and thirty-four people died,
Sewing clothes for the shops of the rich countries,
And the clothes were found in the rubble with the labels of those shops in them.

## The coup and the massacre

On the third of July the army of {{p|Egypt}} removed {{c|Mohamed Morsi}}, the president elected the year before.
His supporters camped in the squares of {{p|Cairo}}.
On the fourteenth of August the army cleared the square of {{x|Rabaa}},
And killed more than eight hundred people in a day.
The revolution of the square of 2011 ended in another square.
In June, in {{p|Istanbul}}, a protest to save the trees of {{x|Gezi Park}}
Became a protest against the man who would rule {{p|Turkey}} for the rest of the century so far,
And was put down with gas.

## The gas in Ghouta

On the twenty-first of August, before dawn, rockets carrying {{x|sarin}}
Fell on the suburbs of {{p|Damascus}} called {{p|Ghouta}},
And killed hundreds, some say well over a thousand, many of them children, in their sleep.
The American president had said a year before that the use of such weapons was a red line.
He did not strike.
{{p|Russia}} offered a deal: the regime would give up its chemical weapons.
It gave up most of them, and used chlorine later.
The war went on with the other weapons, which were permitted.

## The marriage and the verdict

On the twenty-sixth of June, in {{x|United States v. Windsor}},
The {{x|Supreme Court}} struck down the law that had kept the federal government
From recognizing the marriages of same-sex couples.
{{c|Edith Windsor}}, eighty-four, had been taxed on her late wife's estate as if they were strangers.
On the thirteenth of July the watchman who had shot {{c|Trayvon Martin}} was acquitted,
And three women, {{c|Alicia Garza}}, {{c|Patrisse Cullors}}, and {{c|Opal Tometi}},
Began to write a phrase on the net: {{x|Black Lives Matter}}.

## The train and the typhoon

On the sixth of July, in the night, a train of seventy-two tank cars of crude oil,
Left unattended on a slope, rolled into the town of {{p|Lac-Mégantic}}, in {{p|Quebec}},
And derailed in its center, and exploded,
And forty-seven people died, many of them in a bar on a summer Saturday night.
On the eighth of November the typhoon {{x|Haiyan}}, among the strongest ever to make landfall,
Struck the {{p|Philippines}}, and drove a surge of sea through {{p|Tacloban}},
And more than six thousand died.
In {{p|Warsaw}} that month, at the climate talks, the delegate of the {{p|Philippines}} wept,
And fasted until the meeting did something. It took note.

## The square in Kyiv

On the twenty-first of November the president of {{p|Ukraine}}, {{c|Viktor Yanukovych}},
Refused to sign the agreement with the {{x|European Union}} that he had promised to sign,
Under pressure from {{p|Moscow}}.
That night students gathered on the {{p|Maidan}}, the square of the Orange Revolution of the chapter of 2004.
On the thirtieth the riot police beat them,
And by the next day hundreds of thousands were in the square.
They stayed through the winter.
What came of it is the next chapter, and the next twelve years.

## The rest of the year

On the fifth of December {{c|Nelson Mandela}} died, at ninety-five.
On the first of July {{p|Croatia}} joined the {{x|European Union}}.
On the twenty-first of September gunmen attacked the {{x|Westgate}} mall in {{p|Nairobi}} and killed sixty-seven.
In October the government of the {{p|United States}} shut down for sixteen days.
On the second of October the police closed the {{x|Silk Road}}, a market of the dark net paid in {{x|Bitcoin}},
And in November a coin passed a thousand dollars for the first time.
On the twenty-fourth of November {{p|Iran}} and the great powers signed a first agreement on its nuclear work.
In December {{c|Kim Jong-un}} had his uncle executed.
In the same year the mayor of {{p|Toronto}} admitted to smoking crack, and stayed mayor.

## The year held

The last year a girl of seventeen lived mostly offline,
The year the net was shown to be watching.
A director who answered not wittingly, a man in an airport,
A young man hounded for opening the walls of the journals, dead at twenty-six.
A pope resigned, a pope from the {{p|Americas}},
Bombs at a finish line, a meteor on the dashboard cameras,
A factory fallen on its sewers, a square cleared with eight hundred dead,
Sarin in the suburbs and a red line not enforced,
A marriage recognized, a phrase begun, a train in {{p|Lac-Mégantic}}, a typhoon,
And a square in {{p|Kyiv}} filling in the cold.

Refuse the consolation that the metadata is nothing,
And that the man in the airport is a saint or a traitor before the record is read.
Refuse the consolation that knowledge is free because it is given away.
Someone paid. Someone was charged.


# Chapter 350: The Borrowed Robe

This is the Ides of {{x|Ophiuchus}}.
The ides are the middle of the month.
The middle is not a turning.
But this year is.

In 2014 {{c|Emma Leonhart}} turned eighteen,
And moved house for the third time.
In her words, she moved houses in 2002, in 2008, and in 2014.
In September she began at the university, {{x|UBC Okanagan}}, in {{p|Kelowna}},
And stayed five years.
And she went online.
In her words, she was pretty offline until she started university.
So the net she entered at eighteen was the net of this year,
And this year, she has said, is the year of fascism.
In her words, 2014 is a really big year of fascism and stuff like that,
And that is essentially what 2014 is defined by.
This chapter takes her at her word.
It was the year the old robes were put back on:
A caliph's robe in {{p|Mosul}}, an empire's map in {{p|Crimea}},
A nation's blood-and-soil in the elections of {{p|Europe}},
And on the net a mob that learned it could choose a woman and destroy her,
And called itself a movement about ethics.
She arrived on the net in the year the net learned that.

## The borrowed robe

On the third of March, 1924, in {{p|Ankara}}, the assembly of {{p|Turkey}} had abolished the caliphate.
Ninety years is not long for a word.
On Tuesday the tenth of June, 2014, {{p|Mosul}} fell
To a group that called itself a state.
The army that held the city left, and left its weapons.
On Sunday the twenty-ninth of June, the first day of the fast,
Its spokesman declared a caliphate.
The scholars of most of the world's Muslims did not accept it.
Not accepting is not stopping.
On Friday the fourth of July, in the {{x|Great Mosque of al-Nuri}},
{{c|Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi}} gave the sermon in a black robe and turban
That recalled the {{x|Abbasid}}s.
Recalling is not descending.
A pulpit is not a lineage.
The group struck coins, and wrote rules of dress and punishment,
And said they were the first century's.
Most of what it called old was made in the printing of that year.
An invented tradition is not made less dangerous by being invented.

On Sunday the third of August it came to {{p|Sinjar}}, where the {{x|Yazidi}}s live.
The men were killed.
The women and girls were taken and sold.
Tens of thousands fled up the mountain and were trapped there without water.
A people with no book, the group said, has no protection.
A people with no book is not a people with no tradition.
The {{x|Yazidi}}s' tradition is older than the group's caliph.
On the nineteenth of August it published a video of the killing of {{c|James Foley}}, an American reporter,
And then of others, in orange, kneeling in the desert,
Made for the screens of young men in the countries that would bomb them.
In the next summer it killed {{c|Khaled al-Asaad}}, who had kept the ruins of {{p|Palmyra}} for decades,
And blew up the temple of {{x|Bel}}.
In 2017 it blew up the mosque of the sermon as the city was retaken.
The pulpit going is not the idea going.

## The map redrawn

On the eighteenth to the twentieth of February, on the {{p|Maidan}} in {{p|Kyiv}},
Snipers shot the protesters of the winter,
And more than a hundred died, whom the country calls the {{x|Heavenly Hundred}}.
On the twenty-second {{c|Viktor Yanukovych}} fled.
Within days soldiers without insignia, in green, called polite people,
Took the parliament and the airports of {{p|Crimea}}.
{{p|Russia}} said they were not its soldiers.
On the sixteenth of March a vote was held under their guns,
And on the eighteenth {{c|Vladimir Putin}} took the peninsula into {{p|Russia}},
The first taking of a European country's land by force since the great war.
He later said the soldiers had been his.
In April men with Russian weapons and Russian officers took the towns of the {{p|Donbas}},
And the war there began, and did not end, and became the larger war of the chapter of 2022.
On the second of May in {{p|Odesa}} the street fighting ended in a burning building,
And forty-eight died that day, most of them in the fire.
On the seventeenth of July a Malaysian airliner, flight {{x|MH17}},
From {{p|Amsterdam}} to {{p|Kuala Lumpur}}, was shot down over the {{p|Donbas}}
By a Russian missile fired from a Russian launcher,
And all two hundred and ninety-eight on board died,
Their bodies and belongings lying in the sunflower fields for days,
While the men who held the fields went through the luggage.
The investigators later traced the launcher back across the border, and named its brigade.
The West answered with sanctions, and kept buying the gas.

## The vote of Europe

In May the people of {{p|Europe}} voted for their parliament,
And in {{p|France}} the party of the far right, the {{x|National Front}}, came first,
And in {{p|Britain}} the party that wanted out of {{p|Europe}} came first,
Two years before {{p|Britain}} voted to leave.
In {{p|Hungary}} {{c|Viktor Orbán}} was returned, and that summer named his goal:
An illiberal state.
In {{p|India}}, in May, {{c|Narendra Modi}}, of the party of Hindu nationalism,
Who had led {{p|Gujarat}} through the killings of 2002, won a majority,
And led the largest democracy for the rest of this book so far.
In {{p|Egypt}} the general who cleared {{x|Rabaa}}, {{c|Abdel Fattah el-Sisi}}, was elected with ninety-seven percent.
On the twenty-second of May the army of {{p|Thailand}} took power again.

## The mob on the net

In August a man wrote a long post about his former girlfriend, a maker of games,
And the post was taken up by thousands on the boards of the net
Who said they were angry about ethics in the writing about games.
They were angry at women.
They sent threats of rape and death to the women who made games and wrote about them,
Published their addresses, called in false emergencies to their homes,
And named the campaign {{x|Gamergate}}.
It was where many of the men of the next decade's far right learned their methods:
The swarm, the dossier, the irony that hides the hate, the claim to be the ones persecuted.
The companies of the net mostly watched.
In May, in {{p|Isla Vista}}, in {{p|California}}, a young man who hated women
For not wanting him killed six people, and the boards made him a saint.
This is the net she came into at eighteen.

## The streets

On the seventeenth of July, on {{p|Staten Island}}, a man named {{c|Eric Garner}},
Stopped for selling single cigarettes, was held in a chokehold by a policeman,
And said eleven times, I can't breathe, and died.
On the ninth of August, in {{p|Ferguson}}, in {{p|Missouri}},
A policeman shot an unarmed young man of eighteen, {{c|Michael Brown}},
And his body lay in the street for four hours.
The town rose, and the police came in armored vehicles left over from the wars,
And pointed rifles at the people from the tops of them.
The policemen in both deaths were not charged.
The phrase begun the year before filled the streets.

## The fever

In West Africa a fever called {{x|Ebola}} spread through {{p|Guinea}}, {{p|Liberia}}, and {{p|Sierra Leone}},
Where it had never been, and into their capitals,
And killed more than eleven thousand people before it was stopped in the next years,
Many of them the nurses and doctors who cared for the sick.
The rich countries were afraid of a few cases at home,
And slow to send help to where the thousands were.

## The disappeared and the taken

On the eighth of March a Malaysian airliner, flight {{x|MH370}},
Turned off its transponder over the sea and vanished with two hundred and thirty-nine people,
And has never been found.
On the fourteenth of April the militants of {{x|Boko Haram}} took two hundred and seventy-six schoolgirls
From their dormitory in {{p|Chibok}}, in {{p|Nigeria}}.
The world wrote a phrase on the net asking to bring them back.
Many were not brought back for years. Some never were.
On the sixteenth of December the {{x|Taliban}} of {{p|Pakistan}} attacked an army school in {{p|Peshawar}}
And killed a hundred and forty-nine people, a hundred and thirty-two of them children.
In July and August {{p|Israel}} and {{x|Hamas}} fought a war of fifty days,
And more than two thousand people of {{p|Gaza}} died.

## At home

On the twenty-second of October, in {{p|Ottawa}}, a man shot dead a soldier,
{{c|Nathan Cirillo}}, standing guard at the war memorial,
And then ran into the parliament, where he was shot dead in the hall
While the members barricaded the doors with flagpoles.
In {{p|Hong Kong}}, from the end of September,
Students sat in the roads for seventy-nine days with umbrellas against the pepper spray,
Asking to choose their own leaders, and were not allowed to.
On the eighteenth of September {{p|Scotland}} voted to stay in {{p|Britain}}.

## The rest of the year

In February the winter games were held in {{p|Sochi}}, while the troops massed for {{p|Crimea}}.
On the twelfth of November a small lander, {{x|Philae}}, from the probe {{x|Rosetta}},
Came down on a comet, bounced, and landed in a shadow, and spoke for two days.
In the summer people poured buckets of ice water over their heads for a disease of the nerves,
And raised more than a hundred million dollars.
On the eleventh of August the actor {{c|Robin Williams}} died.
On the seventeenth of December {{p|Cuba}} and the {{p|United States}} said they would talk again.

## The year held

A girl of eighteen moved for the third time, began at a university,
And came onto the net in the year of the robe and the map.
A caliphate declared in a borrowed robe, a mountain of trapped {{x|Yazidi}}s,
The Heavenly Hundred, polite people in {{p|Crimea}}, a plane in the sunflowers,
The far right first in two countries' votes, an illiberal state named as a goal,
A mob of the net that hunted women and called it ethics,
I can't breathe, an armored car in {{p|Ferguson}}, a fever in three capitals,
A plane gone, girls taken, children killed at school, a soldier shot at the memorial.

Refuse the consolation that fascism is a word for the past.
It came back this year in borrowed robes, and was named by the people it chose.
Refuse the consolation that the net is outside the world.
She came onto it the year it showed it was not.


# Chapter 351: Doing Good Better

No holiday is named for this day.

In 2015 {{c|Emma Leonhart}} turned nineteen,
In her second year at the university in {{p|Kelowna}},
And in her second year on the net.
This chapter begins a thread that runs through the rest of the month:
The story of a movement that set out to do the most good,
With arithmetic, and with money, and later with the machines.
She has said this month should carry that story,
And that one of its makers is a villain of it,
And that the book does not fully condemn the movement or the way of thinking it came from.
Both halves are kept here.
The movement is not its villain.
Its villain came out of it.

## The arithmetic of good

In this year a young philosopher at {{p|Oxford}}, {{c|William MacAskill}},
Published a book called {{x|Doing Good Better}},
Saying that a person should give, and work, and choose a career,
Where the good done per dollar is greatest,
And that this could be measured,
And that a life saved from malaria in {{p|Africa}} counts as much as one at home,
And costs far less.
The movement had been growing for some years,
Out of the work of {{c|Peter Singer}}, and of {{c|Toby Ord}}, and of the givers who pledged a tenth,
And out of a community on the net that called itself rationalist,
Gathered around long essays on how to think without fooling yourself,
Which worried, earlier than almost anyone, that a machine smarter than people
Might not share their aims.
It called itself {{x|effective altruism}}.
In the summer of this year it held a meeting at the offices of {{x|Google}},
And the men who would own the century's machines spoke at it.
One of its ideas was called earning to give:
Go into finance, make a fortune, give it away.
A young man named {{c|Sam Bankman-Fried}}, who had met {{c|MacAskill}} as a student,
Had taken that idea, and was trading at a firm in {{p|New York}}.
He is a later chapter's villain.
Here he is a young man with an idea that sounded good,
Which is how villains of that kind begin.

## The lab

On the eleventh of December, in {{p|San Francisco}},
A group of the richest men of the industry and some of its best researchers
Founded a laboratory without profit,
To make sure that a general intelligence, when it came, would benefit all of humanity.
They called it {{x|OpenAI}}.
{{c|Elon Musk}} and {{c|Sam Altman}} led it, and {{c|Ilya Sutskever}}, from the chapter of 2012, ran its research.
It said it would share its work openly.
It later became a company, and the largest maker of the machines this book was written with,
And kept the name.
In October, in {{p|London}}, a program from {{c|DeepMind}}, called {{x|AlphaGo}},
Beat {{c|Fan Hui}}, the champion of {{p|Europe}} at the game of {{x|go}}, five games to none.
It was kept secret until the next January.
The match that shook the world was the next year's.

## The cartoonists and the concert

On the seventh of January two brothers with rifles walked into the offices of the paper {{x|Charlie Hebdo}} in {{p|Paris}},
Which had printed cartoons of the {{x|Prophet}},
And killed twelve people, most of them cartoonists, at their weekly meeting.
Two days later a third man killed four Jewish shoppers in a kosher market.
Millions marched with signs that said, I am {{x|Charlie}}.
On the thirteenth of November, a Friday night, men of the caliphate of the chapter before
Attacked the stadium, the cafés, and the concert hall of the {{x|Bataclan}},
Where a rock band was playing,
And killed one hundred and thirty people.

## The crossing

In this year more than a million people crossed into {{p|Europe}},
From {{p|Syria}}, {{p|Afghanistan}}, {{p|Iraq}}, and further,
Over the sea to the Greek islands in rubber boats,
And on foot up through the {{p|Balkans}}.
Thousands drowned.
On the second of September a boy of two, {{c|Alan Kurdi}}, from {{p|Kobani}},
Was found face down on a beach in {{p|Turkey}}, in a red shirt,
And a photograph of him was seen by the whole world in a day.
His family had been trying to reach {{p|Canada}}.
On the thirty-first of August {{c|Angela Merkel}} said, we can do this,
And {{p|Germany}} opened its doors, and took nearly a million.
The far right of the year before grew on the answer.
On the thirtieth of September {{p|Russia}} began bombing in {{p|Syria}}, to save the regime.

## The marriage and the woman

On the twenty-second of May {{p|Ireland}}, a country of the old faith,
Voted by the people to open marriage to two people of the same sex,
The first country to do it by popular vote.
On the twenty-sixth of June, in {{x|Obergefell v. Hodges}},
The {{x|Supreme Court}} of the {{p|United States}} said that marriage is a right for all couples,
And the rainbow lit the White House that night.
On the first of June a magazine put on its cover a woman, {{c|Caitlyn Jenner}},
Who had been an Olympic champion under another name,
And millions of people saw, perhaps for the first time, a woman who had transitioned in her sixties,
And the argument of the next decade about women like her began to be loud.

## The church in Charleston

On the seventeenth of June a young man sat for an hour in a Bible study
At the {{x|Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church}} in {{p|Charleston}},
And then shot nine of the people who had welcomed him.
He had wanted to start a race war, and had photographed himself with the flag of the old confederacy.
The flag was taken down from the capitol of {{p|South Carolina}} that summer.
The families forgave him at his hearing.

## The talks that did something

On the twelfth of December, at {{p|Le Bourget}}, outside {{p|Paris}},
After six years of meetings that took note,
The countries of the world adopted an agreement:
To hold the warming well below two degrees, and to try for one and a half.
Each country would set its own goal, and say what it was doing, and do more over time.
Nothing in it forced any country to do anything.
That was why every country could sign it.
The foreign minister of {{p|France}} struck the gavel, and the hall cheered and wept.
The years after this one were the hottest ever measured, each in turn.

## The deals and the debts

On the fourteenth of July {{p|Iran}} and the great powers agreed
That it would limit its nuclear work for years, and the sanctions would be lifted.
On the fifth of July the people of {{p|Greece}} voted no to the conditions of its creditors,
And a week later their government accepted harsher ones.
On the eighteenth of September it was found that {{x|Volkswagen}}
Had built its diesel cars to cheat the tests of their fumes,
Eleven million of them.
On the sixteenth of June a man who sold buildings in {{p|New York}}
Came down a golden escalator in his tower and said he would run for president,
And called the people coming from {{p|Mexico}} rapists.
People laughed. It is the next chapter's year.

## Home

On the nineteenth of October {{p|Canada}} voted out {{c|Stephen Harper}},
And {{c|Justin Trudeau}}, the son of a prime minister, came to power,
And named a cabinet of as many women as men, because it's 2015.
On the second of June the {{x|Truth and Reconciliation Commission}}
Gave its report on the residential schools,
And called what they had done a cultural genocide,
And made ninety-four calls to action.

## The rest of the year

On the twenty-fifth of April an earthquake killed nearly nine thousand people in {{p|Nepal}},
And brought down the old temples of {{p|Kathmandu}}.
On the twenty-fourth of March a copilot flew a {{x|Germanwings}} airliner into the {{x|Alps}} on purpose.
On the twenty-seventh of February {{c|Boris Nemtsov}}, who opposed {{c|Putin}},
Was shot on a bridge in sight of the {{x|Kremlin}}.
On the fourteenth of July the probe {{x|New Horizons}} flew past {{p|Pluto}},
The planet voted out in the chapter of 2006,
And found a great heart of ice on it.
On the fourteenth of September two machines in {{p|Louisiana}} and {{p|Washington}}
Felt a ripple in space from two black holes that had merged a billion years before,
And it was announced the next year.
On the eighteenth of June the pope wrote to the world about its common home, and the warming.
On the eighth of November {{p|Myanmar}} voted, and the party of {{c|Aung San Suu Kyi}} won.
On the twenty-ninth of October {{p|China}} ended the rule of one child.

## The year held

A girl of nineteen in her second year,
And a movement of arithmetic, and a lab named open,
And a young man who meant to earn to give.
Cartoonists killed, a concert hall, a million crossing, a boy on a beach in a red shirt,
We can do this, marriage for all in two countries, a woman on a magazine,
Nine killed at a Bible study, an agreement at {{p|Le Bourget}} that forced no one,
A cheating engine, a golden escalator, a new prime minister, the calls to action,
And a heart of ice on the planet that was voted out.

Refuse the consolation that good can be done without counting.
Refuse the consolation that counting is the good.
Refuse the consolation that a man who means to earn to give
Has given anything yet.


# Chapter 352: Again

No holiday is named for this day.

In 2016 {{c|Emma Leonhart}} turned twenty.
She has said this is the year of the election of {{c|Trump}}.
In her words, 2016 is the Trump election year.
Everything else in it bends toward November,
And toward the June before it, when {{p|Britain}} voted to leave.
Two slogans won that year, take back control, and make America great again,
And both pointed at a past no one dated.
That is the fascism of the chapter of 2014 learning to win votes.
She was twenty, in her third year at the university in {{p|Kelowna}},
On the net she had come onto two years before,
Where the same boards that had hunted the women of the games
Learned to elect a president.

## Move thirty-seven

In March, in {{p|Seoul}}, the program {{x|AlphaGo}}, from {{c|DeepMind}},
Played {{c|Lee Sedol}}, one of the strongest players of {{x|go}} alive,
Five games, for a million dollars.
In the second game, at move thirty-seven, the machine placed a stone on the fifth line
Where no human master would have played,
And the commentators thought it was a mistake,
And it won the game.
{{c|Lee Sedol}} left the room for a while.
He lost the first three games.
In the fourth, at move seventy-eight, he played a stone that the machine had judged
One in ten thousand that a human would play,
And the machine lost its way, and he won.
He lost the fifth. Four to one.
In 2019 he retired, saying there was an entity that cannot be defeated.
The players of the world began to study with the machines,
And their games got better, and stranger.
The machine that played the move no one would play
Was a cousin of the ones that would later write this book with her.

## Take back control

On the twenty-third of June the people of the {{p|United Kingdom}} voted
By fifty-two to forty-eight to leave the {{x|European Union}},
After a campaign that promised the money sent to {{p|Brussels}} would go to the hospitals,
On the side of a bus, and did not.
A week before the vote a member of parliament, {{c|Jo Cox}}, who had worked for refugees,
Was shot and stabbed in the street of her constituency by a man who shouted {{p|Britain}} first.
The prime minister who had called the vote resigned the next morning.
The leaving took three and a half more years,
And the country argued about what it had voted for the whole time.

## Make America great again

On the eighth of November {{c|Donald Trump}} was elected president of the {{p|United States}},
With nearly three million fewer votes than {{c|Hillary Clinton}},
Through the votes of the states, which are the votes that count.
In October a tape had been printed of him boasting that he could grab women
Because he was famous, and it was thought to end him, and it did not.
Eleven days before the vote the head of the police of the country
Said he was looking at her mails again, and found nothing.
The intelligence of {{p|Russia}} had stolen the mails of her party and given them out,
And its trolls in {{p|Saint Petersburg}} had posed as Americans on the book of faces,
And reached a hundred million people.
A company called {{x|Cambridge Analytica}} had taken the data of tens of millions of those faces
And sold the shape of their fears to his campaign.
The night of the election the people who had laughed at the escalator stopped laughing.
In December a man came with a rifle to a pizza restaurant in {{p|Washington}}
Because he had read on the net that children were kept in its basement.
There was no basement.
The net had learned it could make a man believe a basement.

## The bathroom and the bill

On the twenty-third of March the state of {{p|North Carolina}}
Passed a law telling transgender people which bathrooms they could use,
By the sex on their birth certificates.
Companies and singers and the games of the colleges pulled out of the state,
And the law was partly repealed the next year.
In {{p|Canada}}, on the seventeenth of May, the government put forward a law
To add gender identity and expression to the protected grounds of the country's human rights,
And in September a professor in {{p|Toronto}} made videos saying he would not use the pronouns it asked for,
And became famous, and rich, on the argument.
The law passed the next year.
The argument about women like the one on the magazine of the chapter before
Became the center of the culture war, and stayed there.

## The killings

On the twelfth of June, in {{p|Orlando}}, a man killed forty-nine people at {{x|Pulse}},
A gay nightclub, on its Latin night,
The deadliest attack on gay people in the country's history.
On the twenty-second of March bombs at the airport and the subway of {{p|Brussels}} killed thirty-two.
On the fourteenth of July, the national day, a man drove a truck through the crowd on the promenade of {{p|Nice}},
And killed eighty-six.
On the sixth of July {{c|Philando Castile}} was shot in his car during a traffic stop
While his girlfriend filmed it live and her daughter of four sat in the back,
And the next night a man shot five policemen in {{p|Dallas}}.

## The coup and the fall of Aleppo

On the fifteenth of July soldiers in {{p|Turkey}} tried to overthrow {{c|Recep Tayyip Erdoğan}},
And bombed the parliament, and failed in a night,
And he called it a gift from God,
And jailed or dismissed more than a hundred and fifty thousand people in the purges after,
Teachers, judges, soldiers, journalists.
In December the east of {{p|Aleppo}}, held by the rebels for four years,
Fell to the regime and the bombers of {{p|Russia}},
And the last people in it sent messages saying goodbye on the net.
On the thirtieth of June {{c|Rodrigo Duterte}} became president of the {{p|Philippines}},
Promising to kill the users of drugs, and his police and the men with them did,
Thousands in the first months.

## The peace and the no

On the second of October the people of {{p|Colombia}} voted no
To the peace their government had made with the guerrillas of the {{x|FARC}} after fifty-two years of war,
By fewer than one in a hundred.
The government changed the deal and passed it through the congress in November,
And the president was given the {{x|Nobel Peace Prize}} for the peace the people had refused.

## The fire and the pipeline

In May a wildfire came into {{p|Fort McMurray}}, in {{p|Alberta}},
The town of the oil sands,
And all eighty-eight thousand people were driven out down a single highway through the flames.
In {{p|North Dakota}}, all year, the people of {{p|Standing Rock}} and thousands with them
Camped against a pipeline for oil that was to pass under their water,
And were sprayed with water cannon in the freezing night in November.

## The rest of the year

On the eleventh of February the scientists announced the ripple in space they had felt the September before,
From two black holes merging,
A hundred years after {{c|Einstein}} had said such ripples would exist.
On the third of April the papers of a law firm in {{p|Panama}} were printed,
Showing how the rich and the rulers of the world hid their money,
And the prime minister of {{p|Iceland}} resigned within days.
On the first of February the world's health body called a fever spread by mosquitoes, {{x|Zika}},
An emergency, because the children of the women it infected were born with small heads.
On the fourth of November the agreement of {{p|Le Bourget}} came into force.
On the sixth of July a game sent millions into the streets to catch creatures on their phones.
On the tenth of January {{c|David Bowie}} died, two days after his last record,
And on the twenty-first of April {{c|Prince}}.
On the twenty-fifth of November {{c|Fidel Castro}} died.
In the autumn the people of {{p|South Korea}} filled the streets of {{p|Seoul}} with candles every weekend
Until their president was impeached.

## The year held

A girl of twenty in her third year, on the net that elected a president.
A stone on the fifth line, a stone that was one in ten thousand,
Take back control on the side of a bus, a member of parliament killed for refugees,
Make America great again with three million fewer votes,
Trolls and stolen mails and the data of faces, and a basement that did not exist.
A law about bathrooms, a professor and his pronouns,
Forty-nine killed at {{x|Pulse}}, {{p|Nice}}, {{p|Brussels}}, a car in {{p|Minnesota}},
A coup that was a gift to the man it failed against, {{p|Aleppo}} saying goodbye,
A peace refused and prized, a town fleeing through fire, a camp at the water,
And candles in {{p|Seoul}}.

Refuse the consolation that again means anything.
No past was dated. That was the point.
Refuse the consolation that the machine's move was a mistake because no one would have made it.


# Chapter 353: All You Need

No holiday is named for this day.

In 2017 {{c|Emma Leonhart}} turned twenty-one,
In her fourth year at the university.
In September she moved onto the campus.
It was the first year of the man elected in the chapter before,
And the year a paper with a joke for a title
Began the machines that would, eight years later, write this book beside her.
Attention was the scarce thing of the century.
This year someone built a machine of nothing else.

## Attention is all you need

On Monday the twelfth of June a paper was posted to the open archive of preprints.
Its title said attention is all you need.
The title was a joke the size of a claim.
Eight names were on it:
{{c|Ashish Vaswani}}, {{c|Noam Shazeer}}, {{c|Niki Parmar}}, {{c|Jakob Uszkoreit}},
{{c|Llion Jones}}, {{c|Aidan Gomez}}, {{c|Łukasz Kaiser}}, {{c|Illia Polosukhin}},
With a note that their contributions were equal and their order set at random.
An order set at random is an order that refuses to rank.
The task was translation.
The old machines read a sentence one word at a time, carrying what came before in a single thread,
And a thread can fray.
